Possible spoilers if you haven't read the book or seen the movie, in which case you should do so right now. This will undoubtedly end up as a comparison between the two--me being the Kubrick fan-boy that I am-so having experienced both versions would probably help understand what I'm talking about. 
 The Shining is probably my favorite horror movie of all time. It takes a medium based on cheap pop-out scares and uses the horror in a way that gives legitimate depth to the characters. To me, it's a prime example of how horror ought to be done. It's not a perfect movie. The characters aren't entirely believable and don't always act, um, like normal people (this seems to be a trend in Kubrick movies, though I don't love them any less for it). If I had to praise the book for any one thing, it would be how well developed the characters were in comparison to the movie. There was a lot of depth to the characters as well as--surprisingly--all of the symbolism and motifs being thrown around throughout the book. The book was also very unnerving in parts and almost certain scarier than the movie (not to brag or anything, but I'm not one to find horror movies scary). Books and written word in general leave far more up to the imagination, and I find horror is far more effective when it's psychological. The unknown is usually scarier than anything you can see and that where this book gets most of it's horror from. 
 So, you say, with all this praise surely I must think the book is better than the movie, right? 
 WRONG!!!!! 
 For all the awesome storytelling and its near-brilliance, The Shining horribly fails in one regard. Stephen King is a horrible writer. Perhaps I should rephrase that. Stephen King is a horrible editor. The page count of The Shining could have been cut in half without losing any important information. He fills these pages with useless explanation and almost redundant character development. I didn't know it was possible to spend too much time developing character but King did it. In the movie Jack's alcoholism is only briefly mentioned during the opening scenes, but King decides to spend 500 chapters describing how each member of the family and his career have all been affected by Jack's addiction. I suppose this is asking a lot considering King is a mainstream pop-lit author, but some subtlety would be nice. I think Hemingway's iceberg theory could have been applied here with extraordinary results. Kubrick's version was far more subtle than this, and a lot more interesting because of it (what's this, you say, a subtle horror movie!?). Everything was just executed better. Plus Jack Nicholson is absolutely amazing at portraying insanity. 
 Another thing, the novel starts getting downright absurd around the climax. The overall scariness of the novel took a nosedive right when the "scary" stuff started happening. For some reason the anticipation of what was going to happen was more frightening than it actually happening. Oh well. 
 Inexplicably King didn't like Kubrick's adaptation of the novel, but I won't judge him too harshly. It is his story after all. Kubrick made it his own, and I'd probably be pretty ticked if someone did that with my work. Just don't expect me to watch King's TV mini-series adaptation.
Very solid, original story about a boy whose real-world illness transports him to a world beyond touched by his own imagination.
Stephanie didn't really like uncle Fred, but misplacing an uncle is careless and she does like a good mystery. She meets up with Randy Briggs and starts her freelance job with RangeMan.

So I... really liked this one? I know, I'm surprised too... I found the protagonist weirdly relatable (not going to delve into details about that though) and the whole plot was kind of cute. So, yeah, I'm satisfied. A nice, fluffy contemporary YA romance - that's what this book is.

Contemporary romance / new adult 
 Sequel to Thoughtless and NOT a standalone book. The third and final book is scheduled to be released in early Spring 2013. 
 This author once again had me laughing, screaming, crying, frustrated beyond belief, you name it, I undoubtedly felt it. Whereas Thoughtless focused on two people coming together in what I feel are not the best circumstances - seriously - this story follows Kiera and Kellan through that first official year-plus of their relationship. 
 It's a relationship filled with many complexities and rough patches due to the weak foundation the relationship was built on. As I was reading, I also kept wondering if they could in fact make it in the long run due to the serious trust issues they both have for very real and justified reasons, without forgetting the nasty fights these two have once they've both reached their limits. Having said that, even with their bucket loads of issues, you can't help but cheer for the couple and really really hope they overcome all the obstacles in their way. 
 What I love about Stephen's writing is the fact that she never shies away from outlining every detail and emotion when it comes to Kiera and Kellan's relationship. And I mean at 400+ pages, you get everything! But that's what makes this so great. There's a realism to it that is quite frankly, at times, frightening. I really hope the final book has an HEA because these two have caused, done, been through A LOT, and I would be upset if at the end of it, they didn't work out. I've become attached, so I NEED them to be okay forever!!!!! 
 I also loved the side characters and storylines in this one. There's a particular side story I definitely want to know and read more about (Anna and Griffin), and of course I love reading that all the other resident couples in the series are continuing to flourish too. I really can't wait to read more, and I am so happy to have found this author and series. 
 Give this series a try by reading Thoughtless first. And although Kiera can be annoying at times, it's worth it long run with the obvious internal growth I witnessed by her by the end of Effortless (god I hope it continues into book 3).

I read this book in a few hours. To be honest, while I was reading it I thought it was a great book though there were things that confused me. When I got to then end and was sitting considering what had happened in the book though, that's when I started to realize just how much of the I hadn't actually understood. 
 I didn't not understand the book because I wasn't reading carefully, trust me, I rarely misunderstand things in books. I didn't understand why people were acting the way they were. Why was Kate seemingly so oblivious to Henry's affections when the stories about past events clearly show that she knew he loved her and she knew that she loved him? Why would she have asked him to propose to her three times if she knew he had once loved her (and, as any girl who kept noticing a guy watching them would know) still cared deeply for her? 
 Why did there have to be questionable scenes throne in? Like the scene at night by the sea and the scene from her past where Henry claims she loves him. What's up with her mother? What's up with his mother? If Kate's family was really full of flirts and scandalous people, why wouldn't she have just run away with her aunt? Obviously her mother and sisters weren't acting in a way they should and Kate shouldn't have been listen to them...which brings me to the premise of the whole plot. Why would you make a deal with your mother, who flirts with men as a living it seems, to get three proposals? Just the fact that Kate didn't want to marry because of what she had seen from her mother and sisters is enough for me to think the very idea of that proposal would have been revolting to her. If I was her, I would have refused immediately...and most likely run away...as I said before. 
 As to Henry's mother...if she didn't like Kate's mother so much (for very valid reasons...that family is really messed up) why in the world would she let her children play with Kate all the years of their lives? She was just asking for trouble... 
 And this is why I can't find a reason to give the book a good rating. I liked the plot, the idea, but a book should make you ask many questions throughout that are answered at the end, that's what a great book does. It leaves you with an amazed, happy feeling. This book just left me wondering and wondering.

This is my first time reading a middle grade book, and I did enjoy it, just not as much as I wanted to. I randomly saw this book available to rent at the library and I had no idea what it was about (I actually just saw the gorgeous cover and decided to download it and go into it completely blind.) I didn't even know it was a middle grade book until I started listening to the audiobook. 
 This book follows two twelves year old kids: Cedar Lee, a young girl who's Dad and brother recently just died, and Leo Bishop, a local kid who she meets that introduces her to the towns "Summerlost" festival. They both have jobs at this festival and they make a tour to show the locals around, and they are both obsessed with this old movie actress. There's also a kind of random side story line happening with this mysterious shit happening to Cedar Lee's bedroom at night. 
 I thought this book was okay. It was written really beautiful and I think the story is interesting, but it didn't interest me personally very much. I wasn't drawn into the characters and the story in the way I wanted to be, but I think this is still a decent middle grade book. But unfortunately this story is something I won't remember for very long, it's pretty forgettable.

 I read this book about a month ago now. I was jonsing for a good YA spy book and in the span of five days I read four different spy books. Sad to say out of the four, Two Lies and a Spy was the only one that left me feeling like I had to have the second book RIGHT NOW! 
 I mean OMG what a fab book. There was everything you could want: fast paced plot, edge of the seat griping action, more that enough mystery and plot twists I wouldn't have expected. PLUS two very hot guys. One that Kari had been crushing on for ages, Luke, and another foreign boy, Evan, that drives her mad and is always turning up at the most inopportune times and when he's not really wanted, for Kari at least. 
 Kari is the main hero who is well developed and is a character that I related too almost instantly! (All the characters were actually really well developed, even the annoying characters. Kari is the daughter of two spies working for the CIA. She is at her high school when things go bad and she gets a distress text from her parents. Cleverly she plans to ditch but ends up having to escape the school through the window of the girls bathroom because said foreign hottie, Evan, was hovering like a creeper stalker. Once free she immediately flees to get her younger, genius brother Charlie, so they can flee with their parents. And that's where things go really bad!
OH. MY. GOD. I cannot wait that long till next year I wanna read it now no I need to read it now.

I couldn't put this one down. Wavy would be three years younger than me, so I really got the time this was set in. I loved Wavy and Kellen -- all of the characters were interesting, and if it wasn't all completely realistic, well, it was still a heart wrenching and thought provoking story.

First let me start by saying that this book is not the best on the series. It takes a while to get into it and there is a lot of world building but it is worth it. This is my all time favorite YA book series. This book is about a 15/16 year-old girl named Clary who finds out she is a Shadowhunter (an ancient race pf demon hunters). The world that Cassandra Clare has built is magical and wonderful while still incorporating aspects from our world that make the book all the more enjoyable. I highly recommend this book and all other books by Cassandra Clare.

I was a little disappointed in this book, actually. Though I guess that happens a lot when a book gets such great reviews. My main problems with the book were the slow start and errors I kept finding in my print. When I finally got into the book, I enjoyed the story and wanted to find out what was going to happen. I'll definitely read the next one as well. But I was never blown away by the writing or the story. It's a fast read with a couple of interesting characters, but nothing that made me fall in love with it. Just as a warning, it does deal with depression and has some scenes with cutting.

The first time I read this book was 7 years ago - I was 13 years old. With Shadowhunters having just started and Lady Midnight coming out in a month or so, I want to reread this series. 
 I had forgotten how much I loved it and I am so happy I waited a while to do it. That might sound weird, but to me it felt like I was reading it for the first time all over again. I obviously knew the plot and certain aspects. But the details! I had forgotten a lot of the little details of the story, and the sarcastic dialogue. 
 I never really cared that much for Alec as a character when I was younger (i know, blasphemy) - but I think I understand him more now and will grow to love him as a reread the series. AND JACE!! He is still, to this day, one of my favorite characters of all time. AND POOR BB SIMON! I feel for him, I really do. 
 I think I put this series into a category in my mind where all I loved was Clary and Jace. The Clace scenes were what I lived for. And though I still absolutely adore seeing their relationship progress (and then digress for a little bit... haha), I think this time around I really enjoyed other aspects of the novel, too. The themes of love and family and betrayal, etc. I enjoyed the world building and history of the shadow world. I enjoyed the father-daughter relationship between Clary and Luke. 
 I can't wait to reread this whole series, and read Cassandra's next series for the first time.

I have been wanting to read this book FOREVER! And I'm so glad that I finally did. I loved Dexter the tv show first so it was really great to finally be able to read what started it all. I actually have a really high appreciation for both the book and the tv show. I can see why certain liberties were made with the tv show and how it really worked with the overall feel of the story! 
 Dexter is a serial killer that happens to work for a police department as a blood splatter analyst, he also happens to kill other serial killers that slip through the fingers of the police department in order to appease his "dark passenger". He was so well written as a flawed vigilante doing justice while still breaking the law. The personalities were well described in the book and the scenarios were vividly brought to life! I LOVED this. I can't wait to read more of the series!

First of all, this cover.. Wow.. I love it! It is super cool!! I am a person who judges books by their covers and this one was very pleasing to the eyes. 
 Secondly, this story isn't what I was expecting but I enjoyed it. I was confused a lot of the time but the ending definitely answered a lot of questions that I had while reading this book. 3 stars...3 very GENEROUS stars. Review to come.

I went back and forth a little about this book. 
 On the one hand, I thought the concept was very creative and I really enjoyed that we got to hear so many different characters' perspectives. On the other, I did see a lot of similarities to other YA dystopian books. I eventually came to the conclusion that this was inevitable -- as a genre, there are a lot of repeated ideas and themes, but it's the execution that matters. 
 I found the execution of this book to be very good. I liked the world that was created -- it had a solid reason for existing and for the population limits in place. As mentioned above, I also liked hearing from multiple characters. I got a better sense for things this way and it helped drive me forward in the story. I also really liked the ads/articles/etc. at the end of each chapter. They helped to create an immersive experience in the world, which is often difficult. 
 I definitely appreciated that we did find out how and why the head of Pop Con had an unauthorized child. I had wondered about that through most of the book and found the answer to be a satisfying one. 
 I'm interested to see how the family dynamics play out and how the characters learn to exist together. I'm not sure how I feel about the Lifers -- turning Benson into a symbol reminds me too much of The Hunger Games, so I hope it doesn't play out in too similar a manner. I also wasn't a huge fan of the early interactions between Benson and Luce, but as we got further, it wasn't horrible. The romance element in the book seems unnecessary to me, but I get that it's almost always part of books in the genre. 
 For a long time, I had essentially stopped reading YA dystopian novels because they all started to sound the same to me. I appreciated the differences I saw here, while remembering why I stopped reading them in the first place. I did enjoy this book, and I will probably continue to read the rest of the books in the trilogy.

I love that Maas has the ability to surprise me. There are quite a few major twists that I did not see coming in this book. Once again, I love that Celaena is strong, intelligent, powerful, and yet not infallible. She lets her emotions control her at times, she can be too trusting, and she can be naive when she thinks she has control over the situation. The friendship with Nehemia was a highlight of this book and I adore the love shared between them (even as they each kept secrets from each other). Chaol remains a character I find fascinating and love reading his perspective. But I truly loved the brief chapter where we saw the world from the King's eyes. The ending left me wanting so much more--thank goodness I already have Heir of Fire on hand!

This was pretty good. The middle dragged a bit for me, but the beginning and the end were quick reads. It's definitely from the school of Harry Potter, that Greek gods series, etc. However, this one is a stand-alone (I think....there was room for more at the end, but I don't think there will be). So, you can just read it and be done. Worth it as an easy read. 
 I'm not sure who this book is really intended for, though. It's definitely not for adults, but not really for young people, either, given that it uses the word "blow" (as in blow job), and some other adult themes. Unless the term blow job is now used and/or accepted for children? Oh god, having kids is scary...

Much like another book I read recently (The Third Gate by Lincoln Child) Alpha reads like the middle book in a series, but in fact is the first book (although the subtitle of 'A Jad Bell Novel' indicates that there will be more books to come). You figure out along the way that Jad Bell is a special forces type operative, and he is divorced with a deaf teenaged daughter. He has a team, that you don't really get to know well, although one of them at least is 'Uncle' to the daughter. 
 The book starts out with a prologue of a mission gone bad. After that, you meet Jad, who comes across as depressed. Then he is contacted about going to work at WilsonVille, a park to rival Disney (with a little history of the fictional Wilson company), as second in command of security. 
 We also meed Mattias, a young drug runner who was sent to the US as a sleeper agent. And his boss has plans for WilsonVille. 
 At this point, anyone could see what was coming. A terrorist attack on the park, with hostages that innevitably include Bell's ex-wife and daughter. There may or may not be a dirty bomb in the park as well. 
 I've read and enjoyed books in Greg Rucka's other series (Queen and Country, and Atticus Kodiak) as well as his comic book work, but I did find this one... well, serviceable to damn him with faint praise. It wasn't *bad*, but compared to some of his other books this one was a bit paint-by-numbers. There were a few twists here and there, but it doesn't get much beyond average. 
 Still, when Greg Rucka is being just okay, he's still better than a lot of other thriller writers, and I will be checking out the next book when it comes around.

This is definitely a dark taboo book. And although I loved the subject matter, I felt the execution of the story was choppy. This isn't to say there weren't parts that I didn't enjoy, because I did enjoy it but it was an okay read, not a read one. 
 I'll talk about the things I loved about this story because I dive into the things did not work for me. 
 When Luciano showed his fierce love and protection for Belen, I loved him. He was a great source of strength to her when she needed him the most, at the end. I also liked how unafraid Belen was to always profess her love for Luciano. She knew at a very young age that she loved him and she never deviated from that. She was initially the first one to make a physical move to progress their relationship, which is VERY hard for a girl to do some times (not to mention to it was her cousin). She was always able to do something with her actions or words that was demonstrating her undying love for him. Also, other relationships in the story were cool to read about, like when Belen and Luc's mother would hang out or when the kids where with friends. I thought it was interesting and different to read about the infusion of the Hispanic daily lifestyle of people from DR & PR. And lastly but not the least of my favorite things, the epilogue! What and ending. Loved it. It could not and should not have ended in another way. BIG props to the author for taking that big risk. 
 On to things that didn't work for me in the story, <>, Luciano'a manwhore!! It is very seldom when I read a story where the MAN (our hero) can keep it in his pants. How is this attractive?! Half the time i'm worried my Heroine will get an STI. I guess I'm in the minority because authors keep on writing about this. But I think what bothers me the MOST is that all the while our Hero is out having fun, our heroine is left mopping for me. Why isn't it possible too for the girl to have a guy friend with benefits or another way of reliving her stress?! I have seen VERY FEW author do this, (Presently Perfect by Alison Bailey) but when they did, I loved it! I mean its only fair right?! I did not like Luciano felt whoring was his way of "protecting" Belen from him. LOL REALLY?! Come on. Come on. If anything this behavior of his kept her prison in her need for him. He never, until the end really acknowledged her feelings towards him. When he did I think she was already so messed up by him. 
 Luciano even admits it here; "I know. That's partly my fault. I think she needed the reassurance that she wasn't crazy, that she wasn't alone in it [love]. I never gave that to her. I fucked up, big time..." 
 I just felt this realization came to late for me in the story. Also, the time line in the story was not always clear. The plot was so detailed at the beginning of the story, yet towards the end it was breezing by years. Time, LOTS OF IT, would pass without much explanation or detail. 
 But all was forgiven because of that ending. One of my top favorite EPILOGUES in a loooooong while. The author finally gave our heroine what she had been holding hostage from us ALL through out the story!! I think that ending was even sweeter because Belen gave it to herself. She made the choice (well from what she what to chose from). She chose to be happy, and by her accounts, truly happy. 
 This book had a PERFECT ending. I REALLY, REALLY hope that author DOES NOT write a sequel. It would completely ruin the story. This was my first book from Mara White and she intrigued me. I will definitely be reading more from her.

I know that the author is very well versed in the Young Adult Lit circles and has published incredible works. This is my first book by her. She is an excellent writer and definitely speaks to her audience. She wrote an amazing character by introducing us to Doug. I didn't like anybody else in the book. 
 Truth be known, I think I would probably rename this book, "How to Lose Your Virginity at 17." Zoey seemed intent on doing exactly that. The secondary theme of Zoey trying to control her surroundings due to her lack of life control was excellent. I really wish there was more on this compulsion. 
 I know I am part of the "parent crowd" but as a high school counselor, I pride myself on knowing a little more about the teenage culture. There were parts of the story where Zoey seems to jump from thought to conclusion without letting me into the process. I really didn't understand how Brandon continued to be her "boyfriend" when he didn't show up. I thought Zoey was really rather stupid. 
 I didn't love the book and I wouldn't recommend it to any teenagers I know. On the other hand, I thought the writing style was strong and I would probably read another title by the author before deciding whether or not I like her books. This one just didn't draw me in.

This was adorable, if nothing else. Sadly, I didn't like it as much as Danika did but I'm still glad I read it, nonetheless. 
 I'll have a full review up shortly!

Some day I might actually be able to write a review of this. But I'll have to re-read it first. For now, though: holy shit. I did not know what I was getting into at all with this one. And it's not an easy one, but so so so worthy it. Wow. The structure is what I am most marvelling at, but the layers of stories and connections and just wow. Brilliant.

Wow! This was so absolutely terrible! Why do you always polarise me Gaiman? Sometimes I love what you do and at other times I absolutely hate it. I just have no middle ground with you. 
 Gaiman subverted the standard fairy-tale so much that his ending, one that was clearly meant to be surprising, was so blatantly obvious to the point of actually being mundane. I called this one from the get go. Certainly, some of the changes he makes are, indeed, praiseworthy. We have a gallant hero, one ready to wake the sleeping beauty. So to spice things up a bit Gaiman makes the hero a woman. This was a good move, but nothing overly remarkable. It's been done before, and will be done again. By reversing such things, the story that followed was easy to predict; it was just the opposite of what you'd normally expect to see. I yawned through the entire thing. 
 Now the artwork was undeniably wonderful, but this story doesn't deserve it. . The plot is simple at best, and the final ending just doesn't deliver what it needed to. It relies on its reversal so much. It was disappointing as a story, and not worthy of being in an edition like this by itself. It was weak, so weak. There's no time for anything to develop, and the eventual villain that revealed itself was practically an overdone caricature. There's so little to this. I actually have nothing else to say because there is not much else here to criticise. It's like the bear bones of a story. Gaiman can do so much better than this.

 After the ghastly events at the end of Prince of Fools, Jalan and Snorri are locked in the northern town of Trond by the icy grip of the Norse winter. As spring rolls around, Snorri, equipped with Loki's key, is hell-bent on finding the door to hell itself, regardless of what lies between him and it or or beyond, to try and wrest his wife and children from death's cold embrace. Throughout their journey, however, the pawns of the Dead King, a pawn himself, will be relentlessly hounding the duo, and it remains unclear whether their darkspawn and lightspawn guardians are even guardians at all. 
 Back when I began King of Thorns in mid-2013, I actually ended up shelving the book because it wasn't one that fit my mood at the time. It took me about 10 months to pick it back up again and finish it. Looking back and having finished all of Lawrence's books to date, I cannot even fathom doing that again. The man takes something for every reader, be it prose, worldbuilding, plot, characterization, or whatever else tickles your fancy, and tackle it with an incredibly deft hand. His prose is second to none in the genre (yes, right next to Guy Gavriel Kay), and his ability to write beautifully without being wordy is mind-boggling. It's this exact balance that he utilizes in his worldbuilding as well, where you know just enough about the Builders and the apocalypse that annihilated our civilization that you're content, but he drip-feeds more and more details that leave you subconsciously craving more. 
 When you open a Lawrence book, you know you're in for a ride, as the way he plots never leaves you feeling underwhelmed. There are plenty of times in books I've enjoyed that I find myself thinking that a particular passage is slow or some sort of lull. With The Broken Empire and The Red Queen's War, you're never below a 5 or a 6, and often you're closer to a 10. That's not something many authors can accomplish, and it leaves his books at the sweet spot for length: 350-600 pages. 
 Because I'm apparently incapable of doing anything other than praise his work, let's talk about Lawrence's characters. By the end of Emperor of Thorns, many readers empathized with Jorg in some way (insofar as one can empathize with a cold-blooded killer), and in Prince of Fools and now The Liar's Key, Jalan and Snorri have an especially complex relationship that is ever-evolving. Jalan begins the tale a selfish, womanizing coward, and in this middle novel, he's still a selfish, womanizing coward, but he clearly grows as the tale moves along. Picture this: Snorri's pinned to the ground by some Red Vikings and about to be axed. Will Jalan run? The old one almost certainly would have, but would the new one? The one who's traveled for months alongside Snorri while the Silent Sister's bond grows weaker in contrast to their bond of friendship? The way it's written, you're left with a feeling of doubt that keeps you reading and reading despite what you think you know, wondering if people really can change. 
 Lawrence continues with the compelling...well, everything, and injects the humor we saw in Prince of Fools at the most perfect times. The same themes resonate with yet greater impact: love and loss, courage and friendship, and Lawrence continues to improve, even when it seems like he has nothing to improve upon.
Shirley Jackson has been on my list to read for what seems like a very long time. I'll have to read some more now. Quite a few really great snippets of oddness.

 This book is the friends-to-lovers trope brought to life. 
 Macallan and Levi meet in seventh grade and are with each other trough awkward firsts, fights, and developing feelings, and we follow them trough it all. The story is cute, well-structured and humorous. The intro/outro to each chapter really gives insight to Macallan and Levi's personalities and relationship dynamics. 
 This book is such a cute, harmless read and you can't help but root for Macallan and Levi and cheer when they get together. Recommoend for fans of fluffy contemporary and best-friends-to-lovers stories.

It's pretty decent, with good characters and setting, but the heroine is WAY too stupid to live. It's not just her making bad decisions, it's her literally not figuring things that are in front of her face (I knew who the villain was the exact moment (view spoiler)[one of the characters assured Owl, on his honour, that the other person who she thought was the villain "had no intention of using the magical bomb she was supposed to acquire" HINT. HIIIINT. HIIIIIINT (hide spoiler)] 
 After that, I lost all respect for Owl, and I wanted to see more adventures that didn't involve her.

 Except.

I had been really looking forward to this as I loved Dylan, what can I say I love them big and brooding, but this left me feeling disappointed and it's not because Heidi isn't the girl in this story. I was one of the few who didn't want this to be about Heidi. I felt that we had already had the story of high school love and beyond with Cam and Lucy and honestly, it could never be as good as that. I liked that Dylan and Heidi were left unresolved because sometimes thats how it happens in life, you grow apart and never really get closure. All that being said I didn't care for the girl in the beginning. She's such a mess that's it's hard to feel sorry for her and I didn't completely connect with her in the beginning. I do think this is on purpose as she's drowning in grief and alcohol that even she doesn't know what's going on in her head. As she pulled herself together I really liked her and I did connect with her. 
 The first two thirds of this was a 5* read for me, it was the last third probably 2*. Dylan messed up so much and so big that I felt that he never really redeemed himself. Even at the end I wasn't sold on him. My other big problem was the epilouge, I've read all 5 books and I wanted some sort of goodbye to these characters and that epilouge just plain sucked.

Loved how the narrator describes the detail as if writing from a distance but the very things described have depth, power and emotion and the reader is quickly drawn in and taken along for a ride in this horrifiically, beautiful,honest and powerful encounter of the Vel' d'Hiv'. Contrasted by the personal account of a journalist discovering the events of the summer of 1942 and just how closely her life is intwined with the horrors of Vel' d'Hiv'. 
 Retelling a portion of WWII history I previously had no knowledge of. Not a fun book to read, but important.

I recently finished editing the Bulgarian translation. In all honesty, this isn't a 2 star book. I was harsh when I rated it, but that's got more to do with the genre it's required to fit in than with the quality of the writing. I'm not sure I'd recommend it to anyone over 15, or to any 15 year olds of my acquaintance, for that matter - I'm BEYOND tired of dystopias, vampires (of the modern and supposedly improved variety, anyway), and vampire involving love stories, so recommending a 3 in 1 to anybody... unlikely, I'm afraid. 
 NEVERTHELESS, the book is quite all right for what it is. Which is yet another post viral outbreak dystopia. This one features zombie-like villains, ruthless vampires that have enslaved humankind, and a doomed love story between one of the two nice vampires in the land (a 17 year old Japanese American girl wielding a katana) and a noble, selfless, fearless, perfectly-self-sacrificing-and-all-loving-leader (who's also really cute) human boy, henceforth referred to as PYF (Perfect Young Fella). 
 (Could anyone please direct me to a YA novel where the male love interest is neither an abusive / womanizing / borderline sociopathic weasel who's just DIFFERENT with our girl, nor too good to be true? I will admit that to me, the latter cliche (featured here) seems less damaging as far as bringing up girls is concerned - at least they aren't being brainwashed into thinking love can change an asshole - but I'm tired of having to settle for the least of however many evils.) 
 The plot is engaging, if rushed in places. Dialog flows well, and the concept of loyalty in the face of betrayal, plus the protagonist's struggle to remain human while having to feed on other humans, are handled nicely. 
 Excepting the "they'll kiss, no, they won't kiss; oh, oh, they're kissi... no, they didn't kiss" couple and the hardass, seemingly steel hearted priest who turns out to also be a scientist (and thinks a line such as "So you don't believe in god? Well, he has LEFT us so it really doesn't matter if you do" would leave a non-believer totally awestruck), character development is non-existent. Which is understandable. What isn't is that the one other major female character in the book exists for the sole purpose of hating the heroine while being in love with PYF, then dying. She's shrill and possessive, and totally uncool because she's sorta girly. (The horror.) Annoyingly, 60% of the other women also crush on PYF, including one in what sounded like her 70s. 
 Nevertheless, the writing is tight and polished, the ambiance is there, and the characters that are meant to be memorable would be, to less experienced readers. Who are, after all, the intended audience. I'd say this is a solid 3.

I was unfortunately not surprised by much of anything.

Elegy was quite the conclusion to the Watersong series. When I look back at Wake, the story has just come so far in terms of character development and plot. What was once a very predictable story with decent characters has turned into something unexpected with characters I've come to love. Hocking continues with her unique spin on Greek mythology to create something really special in Elegy. 
 There is so much tension in Elegy. We have couples who don't know if they'll ever make it through their siren adventure alive, family in danger of losing loved ones, a centuries old mystery to solve, and a long-lost goddess to track down. Whew! Sounds like a lot for one book, doesn't it? Even though there was so much going on though, the plot was perfectly balanced between mystery and adventure and the heart-felt moments where the characters just try to enjoy each other in the face of so much uncertainty. 
 I was truly taken aback by how much I loved Harper, Gemma, Alex, and Daniel by the end of the story--especially Gemma. At the beginning of the series, Gemma was unbelievably reckless--to the point of being stupid. I was so frustrated with her choices that it put a damper on the book for me, but she did a lot of growing up as the series continued and by the end of Elegy she is a very strong main character with a sense of responsibility. Alex ended up being great too, which was nice since I wasn't very connected to him in the beginning. Harper and Daniel I have actually always liked, although I am thrilled that Harper finally took a chill pill and let loose. 
 Elegy was a great conclusion to a wonderful mythology series. Hocking's take on the way myths are told and events unfolded was truly original, and she breathed new life into the stories I have loved so much for so long. While I am sad to see this one come to an end, I am looking forward to whatever Hocking has in store for us next.

I just wanted to squash him under my thumb! Ughhhh. But yes, he does play an important role not only in the story itself, but also, it seems, in the previous book and most likely a little in the final book. Then we meet fire, a half-human, half-monster. I felt like "monster" was such a vague term, or maybe not the right term to describe what Fire herself is.

I will admit that I did not expect too much from SHATTER ME. The plot seemed quite interesting, but most plots do and after the wave of dystopian YA books lately, I figured this story would be a nice read, but nothing special. I have to give it four stars, though, if only because every time I had to put it away, I REALLY wanted to pick it back up again and read on. 
 Juliette fights back, that's for sure, but she's not like most dystopian YA heroes. She is broken. She's a little strange and that reflects in the way the book is written, which I really liked. All right, yes, the romance is a little cheesy and it went a little fast (I feel like it always does in these kinds of books) but it didn't really bother me. It was also very sweet and both main characters were relatively realistic and easy to relate to, which definitely helped. Over the course of the story, more is slowly revealed about Juliette and Adam's lives, rather than that information being given all at once, which kept things interesting if only because you want to know more about what happened to them in the past and how they became the people they are at the start of SHATTER ME. 
 The story itself was good and well-paced; I wasn't bored for a moment, but I also didn't feel like it went too fast and the ending was open enough to keep the reader curious about the next book, but not so open that I found myself yelling at the book in my hands (as was the case with books from a couple of other series or trilogies), for which I personally at least was grateful. The villain is repulsive. I do have some suspicions about what might happen to him that I hope will not come true, because that would be a little cliche, but so far he's been intriguing and definitely gave me the creeps. (Although I did think that he was middle-aged for a while at the beginning of the book; he definitely does not act like a nineteen-year-old.) 
 I wasn't as impressed or drawn in as I have been by some other books or series in the past, but I'm hoping that will change as the series progresses. For now, it's enough that I really liked this book and I will move on to DESTROY ME right away to see what is going to become of the characters I just left behind.

What to say, what to say..... 
 I only got to page 37. No, that would be a lie. I skipped some pages. I honestly and truly wanted to give this book a chance, I kept reading past the first page. And the first chapter...... And a little ....bit....more.....after I read some positive reviews. (That's not a lie, I was ready to put it down with one star couldn't care less and have a couldn't care less about it attitude.) With the positive reviews came the reading more and the flippant attitude turned into hate. 
 The part that irked me the most was the writing. The sentences are all choppy. And short. And they spoke with bad grammar. In published works, when I read, I expect decent grammar and sentence structure, so I was greatly disappointed to the point that I couldn't read on. It was done this way on purpose, to create imagery and a sense of realism, to make it as if the character herself is telling the story, I get it. But if the main character is completely against school and the education system and hates writing and reading, it is uncharacteristic of her to be WRITING A BOOK. It is reflected in the bad grammar and awful sentence structure, because it wouldn't be able to get published otherwise. This could have been written by a dedicated grade four-er. 
 In the description: "Burdened by such grim knowledge [her seeing the dated of people's deaths], Jem avoids relationships. Until she meets Spider, another outsider, and takes a chance." One, there is nothing on Jem avoiding relationships. One sentence on how she doesn't like to be with people, and the next moment, and I mean the next moment, the audience meets Spider and she's hanging out with him. What I mean by next moment is, PAGE 2. *clears throat* Would you like a sample? I will provide one, regardless. "That's why I was pissed off when I got to my favorite haunt down by the canal and found someone had got there before me. If it had just been a stranger, some old dosser or junkie. I'd have gone somewhere else, easy, but, just my luck, it was one of the other kids from Mr. McNulty's "special" class: the restless, gangly, mouthy one they call Spider." Ahh yes, character development at its finest. And what is this chance that she is taking, as description entails? Befriending Spider? Oh, such a huge step up. What puzzles me about the 'starting of this friendship' is why. Didn't Jem say that she doesn't like relationships because they "always leave"? And with her special ability, the /spoiler/ death date of the dude is in three months. /end/ Which makes no sense. 
 Lets get to the heart of why I picked this book up in the first place. The special power that Jem has. It is very popular to have the protagonist with a power of any story despise their own power. And especially because Jem has to deal with a power that deals with death, she is portrayed as someone that would do better without it. The whole "avoiding people's eyes" thing makes you think that she's the one that in actually causing their death, when in fact she can only see the date of their death. Seeing the date of death should not have that much of emotional trauma. And she doesn't use her power at all. It was disappointing to read. 
 Not impressed with the first couple pages. I even pushed for some more, but there is a limit. I want a strong heroine, and Jem doesn't seem like the type to provide one. I, also, couldn't relate with her one bit. What really got to me was her view of school. Buddy, if you don't apply yourself, no one is going to fucking notice. If you don't want to learn, no one is going to fucking care and want to force you. If you don't want it, no one is going to push you. But then don't fucking whine about how awful people treat you because you don't care about it. Don't make them out to be a villain, when they're trying to get you to realize that you're fucking scum and you should do something about it because no one is going to do that fucking something for you. 
 I'm sorry, it really bothered me. (*<*,) 
 Will not recommend to anyone if I can't bear to read the first couple pages. The good cover is a lie, it's purpose being to draw in suckers for good covers, aka me. And don't listen to the description, read the first couple pages and decide for yourself. Please don't spend money on it before you've had a taste. Thank-you.

 "Why is straight the default? Everyone should have to declare one way or another, and it shouldn't be this big awkward thing whether you're straight, gay, bi, or whatever. I'm just saying." 
 Basically: In between being blackmailed and hiding his sexuality, it's proving difficult for Simon Spiers to figure out who his mysterious email pen-pal is in Becky Albertalli's Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda. 
 As far as Simon Spiers is concerned, the only people who need to be worried about his sexuality are him and his email pen-pal, Blue. But when another student finds out his secret and uses it to blackmail him, Simon has to figure out how to avoid being publicly outed to the whole school--and his family--while also protecting Blue's identity. Oh, and he still has to make time for the school musical rehearsals. Junior year just got a lot more complicated and as someone who hates change, Simon is having a hard time adjusting. 
 Simon is one of the most realistic contemporary YA characters we've ever encountered. He's a stickler for proper grammar, but occasionally suffers from an embarrassing autocorrect (we feel you, Simon). With his love of Harry Potter and fondness for Oreos, he's pretty much our idea of a great BFF. He's sweet and stubborn and funny and introspective, and, unlike a lot of YA characters who have eyes for only one person, just because he's "in love" with the mysterious Blue, it doesn't stop him from checking out other guys in his class (how many of us have given someone the ol' once-over even if we're with someone else?). 
 The rest of the characters are just as quirky and diverse, from Simon's reality-show loving parents who make watching The Bachelorette a sport, to his sisters--politically correct Alice and quiet but talented Nora. His core group of friends, Abby, Nick, and Leah, also have their own mini side plots. The supporting cast of Simon is interesting enough to keep us reading, even if we're mostly impatient to discover Blue's identity. If you're paying attention, you can guess who he is, but their flirty emails and the final reveal are still smiling-until-your-cheeks-hurt satisfying. 
 Albertalli's debut is a convincing portrait of a young man, written with such a strong voice we almost forgot Simon isn't real. It's very much a character-driven novel, but Simon is so engaging, it makes the fairly simple plot easy to swallow, and we loved getting to know the students of Creekwood High. 
 In the end: Read it! Albertalli's witty prose will have you equal parts snickering and smiling foolishly. And, though it's already been optioned for a movie, there's something special about reading Simon and Blue's adorable emails for yourself.

The Good 
 Some of the "minor" characters had a lot of growth here. Isana, in particular, gets several truly kick-ass moments. I love how Butcher found a way to really play with her strengths by making her into a diplomat/emissary to a new culture. From now on, I am mentally referring to her as "Peace Chief Isana". 
 We get to know Antillus Raucus, the father of both Maximus and Crassus, and he shares some insights into the circumstances around the death of Tavi's father. Lord Aquitaine isn't an entirely bad guy -- who knew? 
 We finally (finally, FINALLY) get to see the Ice Men! Love what I see so far, I just wish we'd gotten to spend some more time with them. The Canim continue to shine, of course (I'd say that Canim political maneuvering is far more interesting than the naked power plays back in Alera). 
 The Bad 
 Not a lot of growth for our hero in this installment. Tavi has reached a sort of zenith militarily -- his men love him, the Cane respect him, he gets to be really smart and kick ass. His plans are fun to watch unfold, but unlike the last two installments, there were no real personal challenges for him to overcome. Very disappointing, really. 
 Also, this book spends a ton of time with the Count and Countess of Calderon. I've never been a huge fan of Amara, and found myself reading through her parts as quickly as possible to get back to Isana or Tavi. 
 The Ugly 
 The Vord are better in this book, but are still far less interesting than the other races of the world. Something about their naked, single-minded purpose leaves little to the imagination. They're just going to kill you, in the most efficient manner possible. At least they're smart about it. 
 The Verdict 
 An entertaining installment in a fairly excellent series, but not an earthshaking one (well, aside from the literal earthshaking during the major battles). I hope that Butcher can find something to really challenge Tavi with in the last book. It's great to see him kicking ass, but it doesn't leave much room for reader investment.

Wild Born (Spirit Animals #1), Brandon Mull (Scholastic) 
 call your animal 
 diverse cultures and plot-lines 
 for the young at heart 
 Brandon Mull kicks off Scholastic's newest fantasy series aimed squarely at "middle grade readers" (aged 8-14, because, seriously, even big kids enjoy an epic, yet accessible fantasy). It's in the same vein as Deltora Quest, but has the advantage of being written by different authors, including Maggie Steifvater (#2), Garth Nix and Sean Williams (#3) and Shannon Hale (#4). This presents different interpretations of the main characters and world-wide events. 
 The first book introduces readers to an alternate psuedo-Earth called Erdas, with key continents mirroring our own, including: Eura (Europe), Nilo (Africa), Zhong (China), Amaya (America), Oceanus and the Hundred Isles (Pacific and South-East Asia), Stetriol (Australia?) and Arctica (Arctic). There are four main characters, each drawn from a different continent and a distinct culture. There is Conor: a shepherd from a classic medieval-style Eura; Abeke: an accomplished hunter (but bit of an outcast) from the drought-affected Nilo; Meiling: a very accomplished leader and warrior, as well as the daughter of a general in Zhong; and Rollan: an orphan from the frontier towns of Amaya. 
 The chapters alternate through each of the characters, which is a standard approach, but works well and allows each of the four characters to become rounded and an important part of this epic story. Each child (yes, they're 11 years old) has a spirit animal bonded to them, and these animals are actually ancient Gods/Great Beasts. Instead of a single Chosen One, we've got four! 
 Instead of repeating the same origin stories, Mull manages to slowly introduce a major world-wide threat as he introduces the characters. By the time Rollan is introduced, the reader already knows a major war has broken out in Zhong and also threatens Nilo. He manages to keep the momentum throughout the story, and presumably into the next book. 
 In addition to a fast-paced and fairly descriptive story, the Spirit Animals series also includes a companion website where readers can answer questions to discover their own spirit animal before going on adventures of their own. 
 [7.5/10.0]

** spoiler alert ** 
 Look, we didn't spend ten short stories about Simon's time at Shadowhunter Academy for him NOT to Ascend. As a reader, I was totally cool with Simon struggling with his doubts and going on a walkabout or whatever, then turning up and Ascending, nbd, because that's what it's all been about. It's OK that it isn't surprising, because that's the point. It's his journey of self-discovery. 
 So it's because Simon's Ascension isn't surprising that George's sudden death is shocking. George's death is completely unnecessary to the story. Simon already mused about the death of so many friends and family, and just as he has his entire memory restored, George dies in front of him. Painfully. Is it...to show that Simon can't have nice things? Because we've read all the other Shadowhunter stories, and it's a theme we already know. The only reason for George to die is to not have to write his character into Simon's changed life in subsequent books. That's such a rookie move. 
 I'm not upset about his death on an emotional level, I'm upset about his death because it doesn't serve the story, and if it doesn't serve the story, and it doesn't serve the readers (who would surely clamor for his safety), the only person left is the author. Assuming she actually liked George as a character as much as the rest of us did, the only reason to kill him is to get rid of him quickly, and quickly and painfully to cause shock. It's shocking only to be shocking, does literally nothing to further the story, and feels like a big "f*ck you" to readers who have invested time and effort into all these stories. I was cool with just following the arc of Simon's development, I didn't need this emotional bait-and-switch as some kind of brutal, misconceived "payoff". Had I known the series would end without the use of any writing craft, I would have reconsidered starting it at all.

Sara Wolf combines hilarious humor and witty dialogue for a story that had me constantly alternating between rolling on the floor laughing and sitting on the edge of my seat waiting to see what would happen next. 
 I'm desperate for friends, not socially suicidal. There's a fine, pathetic line between the two and I'm toeing it like a ballet dancer at her first recital.

 "No. Unlike you, I have a life to attend to. I can't afford to waste my time arguing the fine points of what makes you an idiot." 
 Isis is a walking contradiction. Her self-esteem is 10 notches below sea level yet she speaks with confidence, snark, and self-deprecating witticism that keeps even the most popular kids in school engaged. She has a heart of gold and will do anything, including punching a guy and making his life hell, to protect someone she cares about. She's convinced she will never, ever experience love or intimate relationships personally, but even in her lowest moments she fights to stay positive and strong. She is observant, smart, and can run circles around most of the kids her age. 
 Jack is an enigma. No one knows him. He is the ice prince of the school and refuses to lower himself to even acknowledge others at his school, yet everyone wants to know him, be with him. Something about Isis forces him to fight back and engage when he's accustomed to blocking it all out. They are equals in intelligence and observation. He is a mystery in so many ways. A knight in shining armor for a girl named Sophia, the reader can tell there might be a heart buried under all that ice but he also has a dark past that hints at danger and violence. My favorite thing about Jack was that he wasn't just the typical jerk and as soon as you got to know him, you saw his cold personality hid a well-kept secret and a heart of gold. He is committed to his role as asshole/ice prince and doesn't deviate - it will truly take someone special to cross the Grand Canyon that is the defensive moat around his heart. 
 Most importantly, Isis can't take another heartbreak, so no matter how intriguing Jack might be, I was so terrified to see her get hurt again. Not all secrets are revealed in the first book in the Vicious series and certainly not all wounds are mended and I am in giddy anticipation of SAVAGE DELIGHT! 
 LOVELY VICIOUS is a great book for anyone who likes a strong heroine who won't let anyone silence her. I can't imagine anyone not falling in love with Isis' incredible personality and witty, snarky humor.

I could go into detail about the parallel storylines, the timeframes, and the relationship dynamics featured here, but it doesn't change the devastating portrait of a woman who grew up broken, unbelieved, invalidated, and judged. After all, broken people are at times the most difficult. But I for one really liked her character and was less impressed with the behavior and thought-processes of those around her. Ms. Knoll's incorporation of realistic fiction, suspense, mystery, and complexity make this novel incredibly engaging from start to finish. Speaking of finishes, I must note that I was expecting a big twist or mind-boggling revelation at the end (likely due to the fanfare), but this wasn't the case. I did, however, leave my reading experience extremely satisfied with a feeling of hopefulness for TifAni. Instead of a gasp, I ended with a smile, and as long as TifAni was smiling too, that was OK with me :)

 "He saw me at my stray-dog lowest and still he stood behind me, did everything he could to help me. He imagined the future I could have before I even wanted it for myself, and he was the one to push me toward it. That's faith. Growing up I thought faith was about believing Jesus died for us and that if I held on to that, I'd get to meet him when I died too. But faith doesn't mean that to me anymore. Now it means someone seeing something in you that you don't and not giving up until you see it too."

 The characters are amazing. Of course the reader ends up loving the protagonists: Cormoran Strike and Robin Ellacott, but Rowling's talent also shines through strongly in all her supporting and side characters. She did an amazing job at crafting living, breathing characters that leapt off of the page. I could easily visualize all these people. 
 Strike is such a mensch - I love reading about good men, strong men, men I want to snuggle with. :) Strike was very attractive to me - although I WAS disappointed in him when he chose to make a poor sexual decision near the end of the novel. 6'3", chubby, a bit grumpy, damn good at his job, with past military experience, smart, funny - wow. Knock me over with a feather. What a hottie. :) I also loved the way he tackled the case - he was very thorough and hardworking. He reminded me a bit of another P.I. I adore - Robert B. Parker's Spenser. 
 Robin Ellacott - I liked this character too, although she is engaged to a jackass. I never understand why sane, well-adjusted women in novels end up dating/engaged to/married to jerks. I just don't get it. Matthew is one of those guys that is jealous of her boss. You know, what people nowadays describe as "alpha," this attitude of "no other man gets to talk with you/see you/be in the same room with you but me" which is often (in romance novels) portrayed as strong and "alpha" but in reality is weak-ass. Being so insecure in your worth as a man and so insecure in the love of your woman that you feel threatened by any other male who gets near her is weak as hell. For some reason Robin puts up with this crap, along with comments about how "childlike and naive" she is and Matthew feeling like he has a right to tell her what jobs she can and can't have. What a jerk. 
 Okay. Bad taste in males aside, Robin is innovative, clever, shows initiative, and has a secret inner yearning to be a P.I. She is a perfect match for Cormoran - who gives her the praise that she is sorely lacking from her fiance. And it's not like Cormoran Strike is praising her because he wants to get into her panties, he really genuinely thinks she's amazing. Contrast that with what she has to put up with at home and I cannot understand why she doesn't leave that jackass. Not 'leave him to have a relationship with Cormoran' - just leave him period. 
 The mystery is excellent, it slowly comes together and it is fun to piece it together alongside Strike. I felt like it really worked and was very clever. This book is 455 pages and I didn't feel like any of it was superfluous. It was well-crafted, and didn't go down the paths I expected it to go, especially with confrontations. Oftentimes I thought two people were going to hash it out, and the book would take a different turn - it was exciting and kept me guessing. 
 The writing is wonderful, Rowling has a great way with words. I loved the descriptions, the vocabulary, people's little quirks, - all of it. Very well-written. 
 Rowling also does a good job of tackling race, racism, and the benefits and drawbacks of being biracial - three things that I was surprised she decided to take head-on, but she ended up pulling it off admirably. 
 Another thing I want to note is that while she gives Cormoran a disability, but a disability that he can 'pass' with. That is to say, no one ever HAS to know he has a prosthetic leg unless he WANTS them to know. This allows Rowling to have a disabled character but also allows her to not really have to deal with characters reacting to his disability. A cop-out? I don't know, you decide. I thought it was fine, but other people might have a different take on it. 
 Overall this was a very vibrant and satisfying mystery, full of colorful characters. I thoroughly enjoyed it and definitely plan to read SILKWORM soon. 
 P.S. I did not choose to read this because Rowling wrote it - it had been on my to-read list before she was revealed. If anything, finding out it was Rowling made me a bit hesitant to pick this up. 
 P.P.S. I could NOT get used to characters in the book referring to the paparazzi as "paps." Every single time I read the word "paps" I thought about Pap smears. So that was not exactly what I wanted and initially left me very confused. I don't know if this is a British thing, or what? ???

Going into this reread, I feared that this book wouldn't be everything my rose-tinted memories professed it to be. It was, after all, one of my first exposures to adult literature and epic fantasy, and I've read a great many good books since then. Luckily, this book held up better than I could have hoped. 
 First, let's admit that this isn't a perfect book. Then again, I doubt such a thing exists. Out of plot, character, setting, and prose, Sanderson is definitely the most deficient in the prose category. His writing rarely sings to you the lush, fat melodies that tickle your inner ear. But he always delivers on plot, and in this book more than most, he delivers very hard on setting. 
 There are so many minute details that make the world come to life. We can start by marveling at the very existence of the Shattered Plains, then extend that to warfare on them, the existence of bridgemen, and chasm duty, and we still haven't glanced at the surface of what this world is. The parsh people, the histories, the myths, the varied cities and cultures, the storms and stormlight, the flora and fauna, the Shards, the grander cosmology hinted at. So many things that invest this world with a vibrance and an originality I've never encountered elsewhere. 
 One thing I heavily admire about the POV characters is that there's always more than one mystery going on. You have the general mystery of the day-to-day plot, i.e. what's going to happen next, but then you have grander, deeper mysteries scratching below the surface. For example, Kaladin Surface: everyone around him dies, struggles with the absolution of apathy; Deeper: what is happening with Syl and stormlight? Shallan has her family and mission, but she also has these weird things with patterns for heads that appear in her drawings. And so forth. 
 I always learn something new about how I can improve my writing when I read Sanderson, and particularly when I read Stormlight Archive. As I said, it's not a perfect book. Some parts were too slow (especially some of the flashbacks). But this book deserves nothing less than five stars.

When Edie, new to the job, accidentally leaves a patient's arm unrestrained and in his delirium, he pulls out his ventalator and subsequently dies, Edie is compelled to find the mysterious 'Anna', the name whispered with the patient's last dying breath. Add in the mysterious 'Shadows', and the nebulous vampire hierarchy and you get a confusing mishmash. 
 There are already a couple of more books out in this series, so obviously someone liked this book more than me. I won't be bothering with the rest of the series however.

Emerson Cole began to see people that weren't actually there right before her parents passed away. She seems like any other teen girl, but really she has just learned to keep her visitors a secret from her family and friends. She lives with her brother and his wife who both seem to easily accept Emerson's affliction. Even going so far as to recruit people claiming they can help her, but unfortunately they are just frauds. Then Em's brother hires Michael who works for the secretive organization called The Hourglass. Emerson feels like she finally found someone who can truly understand and help her. Em is just the beginning of what I loved about Hourglass. This book starred such an array of well-developed characters and relationships. Even though I loved all the amazing characters, the aspect I appreciated most about this book was the dialogue. This author has a writing style that is uniquely her own. I can't even think of an author who is similar. It gives her a definite edge that makes her writing stand out among other authors in this genre. AND it isn't dumb downed! I can definitely see this series appealing to teen and adult readers alike.

They both bring something special to the table. I'd be hard pressed to choose a favorite. For the reader who is anti love triangle, please don't let the mention of two boys scare you off. This book doesn't go the expected route when it comes to the romantic relationships. Yet another reason I love this book! The angst was practically nonexistent. 
 Hourglass is a delicious mix of romantic and sci-fi elements. The plot was fast paced and packed with twists and turns. The dialogue was witty and smart. Talk about a page-turner! I am madly in love with everything this author has created. I don't think a series, let alone author debut, has ever impressed me more. This is really two books, so I offer two reviews: 
 The Stranger Beside Me: Ted Bundy the Shocking Inside Story 
 When Ann Rule is focused on her memories of Ted Bundy, when she is really giving us a look at a serial killer from the perspective of someone who knew and liked him before his guilt was revealed, her book is an impressive (and I am guessing singular) piece of true crime writing. 
 The case she makes in the original book (there are numerous addendums as times changed and new developments arose) is about as close to the truth about serial killers as I think anyone has ever dared to write. Eventually, years later, she changes her tune and joins the ranks of those who believe serial killers are incapable of loving or caring and comes very close to suggesting Bundy was pure evil, but early on in the book she makes a very different and, to my mind, more compelling and frightening case. She suggests that, actually, Bundy was a good man in many facets of his life. She cites lives he saved, care and attention he lavished on her and others (which had no discernible motive beyond friendship), and excerpts from personal letters that seemed -- even out full context -- to be, at least at times, from a decent man like any decent man one might meet. I think he probably was all those things, and also, at the same time, one of the worst serial killers of the 20th century. I don't buy the psychologists and psychiatrists who say killers can't love or care, and I think the idea that they can't, that they are only liars, that they are pure evil, makes them vastly more dangerous and our world a whole lot scarier. I think Ann Rule had it right her first time through. Ted Bundy was good and evil. And the good that was there, that was really, truly, genuinely there, made it easier for him to bury and hide the evil from everyone around him. Sadly, though, we seem to need to believe in the pure evil because then we know that we and the people we know and love could never be one of those murderous strangers. It helps us sleep at night. But in this one book, Ann Rule was trying to keep us awake. 
 The Stranger Beside Me: Ann Rule the Shocking Rise to Fame 
 This book, the book in which Ann Rule charts her rise to a level of notoriety through the killings of Ted Bundy, is nowhere near as interesting as the other book, but it is somewhat disturbing all the same. It is the hypocrisy that makes it so. Rule avoids talking directly about the personal things that made her and Ted friends for so long, yet she talks about them indirectly every time she talks about herself. She is narcissistic, she desires fame, she is driven to succeed, she likes to pass judgement on those around her, she considers herself an expert when it comes to serial killers, she glories in her writing career, and she never misses an opportunity to drop names or trumpet her achievements. And all of these are things she criticizes Bundy for time and time again. She is oblivious to the hypocrisy, and there are times when her intrusion into the tale she is telling -- intrusions that have less and less to do with the case and more to do with her success -- is just too great a distraction. Yet all of this can be forgiven because of the other book she wrote alongside this one. That book mitigates this.

Dan Choan's Stay Awake: Stories is a collection unlike any I've read. Although the stories are in many ways horrifying - featuring suicide, attempted murder, ghosts, a haunted house, and a two-headed baby - they tend to resemble psychological thrillers more than gothic horror or classic horror. Choan is wonderful at creating vivid characters, and their nuanced treatment lends these tales their power. I found the book strangely compelling. 
 That said, the book left much to be desired. In the first place, the stories are not very different from each other. Moods, motifs, and even plot points reappear in multiple tales. After a while, they almost sound the same. More importantly, the stories do not depict the dark inner thoughts of normal, everyday people who struggle to overcome the challenges of daily life (although Choan certainly could have written such a collection). Instead, these characters - these endlessly fascinating, likeable, pitiable, memorable characters - are people in extraordinary, borderline supernatural situations. And that doesn't work so well because the characters, so central to Choan's character-driven style, have become what they are because of plot, and the plots in this book are dreadful. Sometimes, not enough details are given about a character's backstory for the reader even to know who killed whom! (And since suicidal/murderous parents, prescient children, and magical, lovesick fortune tellers are probably not the norm for most of Choan's readers, the bare bones, at least, are essential.) Worse, the stories lack endings. It's as though the last four pages of each story are missing, and the end comes just before the reader would understand what's happening. I know that the minimalist style can be an art form, but I'm not a huge fan of minimalism to begin with, and it just doesn't fit too well here. 
 I understand, of course, what this collection is trying to do. I realize that one of the main ideas behind it involves getting into a character's mind at a given moment, and I know that by minimizing plot, the emotional developments are emphasized. However, the plots are too weird to allow the characters to work and too unfinished to stand alone. This collection is too middle-of-the-road to do anything well. It might have been a good group of horror stories, or a very well-written bunch of character studies. It remains a gripping book, morbidly fascinating in its own way, but it never really goes anywhere. It tries for a noir-ish psychological-thriller-feel, but it doesn't quite pull it off.

"Finn said art isn't about drawing or painting the perfect bowl of soup. It's about ideas. And you, he said, have enough good ideas to last a lifetime." 
 June has a special relationship with her Uncle Finn. Finn is a famous painter who lives in an apartment in New York. June has always had a hard time fitting in with her family and peers. Finn offers her an escape filled with culture, exploration, and understanding. He accepts her for who she is and indulges all of her quirks and curiosities. 
 The year is 1987 and June's world is beginning to change. Finn has been diagnosed with a mysterious illness. Her parents, both accountants, are in the thick of tax season and spend little time at home. Mom has been very muted about Finn's illness. June is only allowed to visit him during weekly trips with her mother and sister. She knows little about AIDs, but June sees the debilitating effect it is having on her beloved uncle. After weeks of deterioration, Finn finally succumbs to his illness. 
 June is devastated. The only person who truly loved her for who she was is dead. Mom seems eager to put the whole ordeal behind them. While the rest of her family seems keen to leave the memory of Finn in the past, June wants to know more. Who was the strange man at Finn's funeral that had Mom so upset? Did that man really kill her uncle? And what has become of Finn's apartment and possessions? 
 In Tell the Wolves I'm Home, author Carol Rifka Brunt presents a deeply moving coming of age story about love, loss, and acceptance. By having fourteen-year-old June narrate the novel, the author makes the heavy topics a bit more palatable. We feel every emotion of June as she discovers the cruelty and ignorance that surrounded the AIDs crisis. At its heart, Tell the Wolves I'm Home is a coming of age story that manages to weave larger themes into its foundation. From the very first page, the book captured my emotions and imagination. Tell the Wolves I'm Home is a stunning debut novel that will have you contemplating its layers long after the final page.

 As a fan of Historical Romances I've read quite a few of them, but not one was like The Duchess War, and I appreciate anything that stands out in this lot of overused tropes and cliches that modern literature is swamped with. I'm referring to stories of rakish heroes whose love for the virginal heroine turns out to be some sort of renaissance of their souls and they completely change into loyal, loving husbands, but who still can rock the heroine's world in the sheets like nobody's business. I mean there is simply no appeal in a hero who say, is a decent enough human being and is a little inexperienced in bed or even a virgin. Right? Well, that's the case with Robert, and I don't care what your prejudices are, he had me utterly charmed. I liked him from the start, how he was sort of awkward in company, especially Minnie's. He even admits it, which instead of making him sound like a loser, makes him adorable and attractive and irresistible. 
 Minnie was... undeserving of Robert. And I'm not saying it only because I'm biased. I am not convinced of her love toward him. She had some of her own issues, which made her reluctant to accept his advances, and later on proposal, but she was way too cold, way too reserved even by end of the book, when they said their I love you's. Her behavior made me think that her emotions for Robert only go as far as lust. 
 The side characters were fun, the story is pretty much fast paced with minor plot holes and the writing is okay. All in all, The Duchess War is definitely a must read for HR and romance fans alike, especially for those who'd like to read a different story from what they're used to.

For a long time, I avoided dystopian books because I was afraid there were all going to be like the Hunger Games. I do see a recurring theme in these kinds of books, but other than that- there is no similarity at all. 
 Divergent is a very good book. It was very engrossing and hard to put down. It never bored me for a single second; never seemed cheesy or forced. The writing style was very interesting and the characters really draw you in. The first couple of pages kind of sounded like Hunger Games, but then it was nothing like it. Tris/Beatrice is a very tough girl. I admire her a lot. She seems to be the most sensible character of YA genre probably. I don't know how her character develops in the next book, but I have high expectations now. Veronica Roth is my new favorite author. She has the talent to suck you in her story, leave you wanting for more and give you enough to satisfy you at the same time. 
 I also loved the character of Four/Tobias. He is the perfect kind of guy I would go for. He is tough and gentle at the same time. He is smart and a very skilled fighter. He can almost scare you at times. I loved his vulnerabilities and soft side. The romance between him and Tris was predictable but it didn't seem forced. They are kind of the same people underneath and that is why they are drawn to each other. I just didn't like his name- Four. But it does give him a tough exterior because it is such a different kind of nickname. I really want his and Tris's romance to stay intact in the second book but I am sure that is not going to happen. Almost always- the girl and the guy have to be forced apart in the second books of trilogies. 
 I wasn't expecting the last 50 pages of the book the way it turned out. This book sounds like an actual science fiction novel than a chick lit genre. The simulation concept was pretty amazing. It made me want to go out in the fear landscape and see what it is like to experience your fears firsthand. The scene where Tris makes Four face his fears was one of the best scenes of the entire book. I just loved the tension and passion between them. 
 The supporitng characters don't add much to the story, but there were well written. I loved Christina and Will. Peter, Al, Molly and others were cliche bad guys but they were rather harsh bullies. I am happy with the outcome they got. I was pretty devastated while reading the loss of Tris's parents. That was probably the only part I didn't like. It was too much happening at once altogether. But then, the writer gave the main character something worth fighting for. There's no better reason to rebel than to want to avenge your parents' death. I am not sure where Caleb's character goes from here on. I am expecting Peter to turn out to be good and Marcus being evil all over again. 
 All in all- a great book and a great imagination. Veronica Roth did a fabulous job with everything and there isn't much I have to criticize about. She tells us a sensible story.
