Brief summary: The Emperor has been murdered, and his three young adult children are now embroiled in a plot where it is almost impossible to discern who is friend or foe. The novel is told from the point of view of each child. Adare, the oldest daughter who serves as the Minister of Finance in the capital, Valyn, the middle child and youngest son who is training to be a fierce Kettral warrior, and Kaden, the new Emperor who has been training with monks for eight years in a distant mountain range. 
 The Emperor's Blades was recommended to me by a friend. I tend to get excited about a book, and then completely forget about it for months, or years, and meander back to it before slowly reading and never getting through it because I have the attention span of a gnat these days. It took me about three months to finish this book, quick for me, despite it dragging and fucking dragging. 
 But first, the good stuff. The prose in this novel is beautiful. It is not overwritten and purple, but it has just enough exposition to paint an image in your mind, and just enough narrative to keep you entertained because the point of view of each main character is quite engaging. The characters are interesting, and not just the MCs. The side characters in this novel really shine, and sometimes they outshine the MCs. In Valyn's arc, I am particularly fond of Gwenna and The Flea, and in Kaden's arc, I loved Akiil and Tan. These characters are very well drawn, and their history and backstories are evident in their actions, speech, and body language. 
 If it were not for the characters, I would have been unable to keep plodding through the first 75% of the book. Adare gets little pagetime, and Valyn and Kaden spend the bulk of the book going through various forms of training. Valyn's storyline circles around a mystery with a somewhat obvious end, and I'm not 100% sold on the method of training given the end result, but the banter between the cadets was great, and I genuinely enjoyed being in Valyn's head (with the exception of the continuous use of fantasy-cursing. personal pet peeve. it's just as bad as him saying fuck every other word. I don't care if it's the name of a made up god.) 
 Kaden's training is often dull, and he is dealing with his own mystery but it's often ignored so he can do tedious things to learn abstract skills while Tan bitches him out. If not for Kaden's reluctance and inner sass, and Akiil livening things up, I would have skimmed most of his parts even though Kaden is my favorite character. I can think of a number of side plots that would have made this arc more interesting, but they were not put in and the monk training was kept pure until the last 25% of the book where things picked up at a pace that finally allowed me to read straight through to the end. 
 The ending was fantastic and worth the journey. I can't wait for the second book. 
 However, the real issue with this book is the female characters. I'm sure exactly no one is surprised to see this in a fantasy book, because fantasy books tend to do a huge disservice to female characters in general, but here it felt unnecessary. There were several female characters with a lot of page time in Valyn's arc, but even Gwenna (my favorite) was often shown as being more brawn and quick temper than brain, and the focus was on her body more often than felt necessary. That was the case for all of the female cadets. I don't know how many times Valyn checked out the shape of their breasts in their uniforms, but it felt like a lot. The main female character in Valyn's arc was Ha Lin, and I found her hardly bearable. Too grouchy, too ruled by emotion, sometimes irrational, and it was strange because she didn't start out that way. Why the female cadets had to be consistently grouchy, overbearing, or void of personality, is a mystery to me. There was plenty of good stuff to work with in order to give them a more nuanced role. 
 The biggest issue I have is with Adare. She is the most intelligent of the siblings and spends the book surrounded by enemies, but she has a handful of chapters in around 45, and is under-utilized in a way that was very unfair. She also made such a novice mistake at the end that I was left cringing. Once again, it was unnecessary to write her into such a position when her trust could have been given to a traitor in more creative ways. She turned into an annoying cliche. I am being deliberately vague so as not to spoil, and it's hard. 
 It's clear that this book was more about 1) exposing the plot and 2) allowing these young adults to come of age and go through hardships and betrayal to better handle what's coming down the road. In that way, the book worked for me. If you told me these three would be running an empire at the start of the book, I would have said no way. Now, I feel they stand more of a chance and have picked up a lot of useful skills along the way. It was a tedious journey, but the arcs were probably necessary just so all of the development is effectively and believably built in. 
 That being said, as much as I would love to give this book 5 or even 4.5 stars, I can't do it. A number of issues knocked it down a peg, for some people probably more than one peg, but I enjoyed it enough to stick to a solid 4 star rating.

I enjoyed most of this book a lot more than I enjoyed re-reading the previous two, but for reasons that are pretty specific to me. For one thing, I was reading Mastiff for the first time, so it was more suspenseful. For another thing, I had the same reaction to (view spoiler)[Farmer (hide spoiler)] as I did a long time ago to (view spoiler)[Numair (hide spoiler)] in the Immortals quartet, i.e. (view spoiler)[I developed a ginormous crush on him right along with the protagonist (hide spoiler)]. That was fun, and I was very happy to learn that Pierce's writing can still make me feel that way, but I know this kind of response really depends on the individual reader. 
 There were two plot points that blunted my enjoyment, although one only pinched briefly, and the other was so late in the book that it didn't spoil most of my reading. 
 I found it unnecessarily emotionally manipulative when [spoiler, but also possible trigger warning] (view spoiler)[the scent hound Achoo (probably my favorite character!) was mortally wounded in a battle, but Pounce used his magic to heal her at the last second. I think maybe Pierce did this because (a) we needed a reminder that the characters' quest was really dangerous, and (b) she wanted a good reason for Pounce to have to leave Beka's life eventually. (He wasn't supposed to interfere in the world so much, so the gods punished him with temporary banishment.) I was glad that Achoo didn't die after all, because killing off an important dog character is the cheapest authorial trick ever and I would have spent the rest of the book crying and being furious at Pierce. But I'm annoyed at her for nearly going there, too. She didn't have to do that; there were other ways to send Pounce away, and I knew the quest was dangerous. (hide spoiler)] 
 The other thing, that happens much later in the book, is something that at least one other Goodreads reviewer has also objected to. (view spoiler)[We find out, nearly at the end of the quest, that Tunstall has become a traitor. This comes nearly out of nowhere. I say "nearly" because there is foreshadowing, but frankly I think Pierce made a very clumsy job of it. Beka suspects that there is a traitor among the party, but none of the signs that suggest this to her seemed at all convincing to me. Maybe if I re-read the book I would find they held together better, but at the time, everything seemed insignificant and inconclusive -- especially given that there are so many mages involved, and Beka doesn't understand or even notice much of what the enemy mages are up to; as far as I can tell, their activity could have explained everything strange that Beka interprets as betrayal. 
 There's also some characterization of Tunstall that I don't remember appearing in the previous books -- that he has some narrow ideas about appropriate masculinity. After the revelation of his treason we find out that these ideas contributed to his motives. This seemed pretty pasted-on to me. From Terrier, I understood that Tunstall was complicated but totally honest and loyal. When Beka described Tunstall's ideas about men at the beginning of Mastiff, I thought, approvingly, that we were just getting an even fuller idea of his character, which included some flaws. Now this seems cheap, because I suspect it was just to set the reader up to distrust him. (hide spoiler)] 
 I find that I don't have anything more profound to say about the trilogy as a whole now that I've finished it. I began reading it now because I was curious what Pierce would say, on a deeper level, about societal disorder and state-sponsored violence. It turns out she doesn't really say anything. The viewpoint character is a Provost's Guard -- a policewoman -- who is loyal to the Provost and to the monarch. She sees corruption within the Guard and notices problems in the government, but is not the kind of person who would contemplate any radical changes; she simply wants the people in power to have good motives and be effective. She makes the logical connections between poverty and crime, approves actions that ameliorate poverty, and disapproves of rich people who waste resources that others need, but a revolutionary thought would never cross her mind. (There is actually a rebellion in Mastiff. The rebels are nobles and mages who resent the current monarch for taxing them for the sake of the rest of the people. This change in taxation, which Beka supports, does apparently seem radical to the rebels, but to Beka it's simply the wise action of a responsible ruler.) 
 I think if Mastiff had been more like the previous two books, with Beka working in a third criminal investigation, in order to raise the stakes Pierce might have needed to deal more deeply with things like police corruption. But the situation in Mastiff is different, and the big thematic problem, if there is one, is slavery (legal in Tortall during this series, though not in the later, earlier-written Tortall books). And, well, an author today has their work cut out to write fictional slavery as thought-provoking. From Pierce's dedication and afterword it seems she was thinking of modern forms of slavery like sexual trafficking, which are very serious problems that demand thought and attention and action -- but the slavery in these books isn't illegal trafficking, it's a state-sanctioned, socially established sector of the economy. I would be very surprised ifMastiff inspired any new thoughts about slavery for any of Pierce's readers. Not that it needs to be thought-provoking -- it's an exciting story and I liked it for that. But I think Pierce could have done more with this series.

I've taken a while between finishing this book and actually sitting down to write the review. Mind you, I don't write reviews for every book that I read, but I certainly will for ones that induce a complex emotional / intellectual response. 
 I had a hard time knowing what to think after reading this, and it was only after some extended discussion with a good friend of mine (yes, you, Caitlin :-) ) that I really was able to articulate my feelings. This book has some really cool elements that I love. As many of my friends know, world building is extremely important to me as a reader, and I think that Johnson executes this aspect of her novel well. There are interesting and thought-provoking details that she adds--the fact that Palmares Tres is a gigantic pyramid, the caste system that lives within the city, the idea that art could be constructed entirely of light-were all really fun to devour. I understood the parallels that she was trying to make with a lot of these elements, and the contrast between ancient and futuristic concepts was well thought out. However, my biggest issue with Johnson's story, which ultimately was its downfall to me, was that it felt like Johnson was just exploring the world that she created for the sake of exploration. The elements that she created did not connect for me to form a complex and homogenous story. So much of what she wrote appeared to be exactly how the protagonists executed their art--art for the sake of it. So many of her devices to influence plot seemed arbitrary and random, which was confusing for me. It seemed like the plot was aimlessly wandering, and didn't have a coherent overall message. Perhaps I missed some key components as a reader, but because an overall concept was lost on me, I couldn't embrace the idea entirely. 
 That said, Johnson's writing style is beautiful, and her themes and ideas were really powerful and interesting. I really enjoyed imagining the city of Palmares Tres as Johnson whisked me away with her words. 
 Overall, 2.5 stars. Johnson's world was beautiful, but the themes didn't connect and pull through to make a cohesive story that I could believe.

I feel like I should start this review with a disclaimer: I don't do well with series. For one, my memory is just awful so if I don't read them right in a row I have a hard time remembering what is happening or why I should care. I also just lose interest over time, possibly related to that memory issue, but also I think because series tend to meander. There's nothing wrong with side plots and secondary characters and philosophical musings, but I think series tend more than single volumes to get caught up and sunk by too many details. 
 This is an issue, I think, that Saga is facing. I've felt for the last two volumes like there were too many irrelevant side plots and characters; at the same time, these books manage to feel more like an outline than like actual stories. They're hitting all of the plot points - girl is kidnapped, family goes on rescue mission, family finds girl - but it doesn't feel earned. In general, this volume kind of felt like filler - like he's just trying to quickly close out previous storylines to move onto something new and exciting. I might have an easier time with that were I reading the issues as they came out, rather than waiting for the collections. It was rough to wait so long for this, and to ultimately feel like nothing really happened. (A strange feeling for sure, since a lot happened re: Hazel reuniting with her parents. But that reunion came so fast that I didn't feel like I should care that it happened. Then again, I absolutely teared up when Marko and Hazel were reunited. Vaughan is a great writer and Staples is a great artist - they knew how to make that scene hit. But I still don't feel like it was earned, and I kind of resent the emotional payoff without any real build-up.) 
 I don't know quite how to explain my problems here. Like, do I just think that these stories should be longer? Maybe. Maybe this book shouldn't have opened with a time jump that skipped Hazel and her grandmother's experience in the detainment camp, Alana and Marko getting back together, and the kid Robot whose name I've already forgotten growing up. And - I get the sense that this is going to be the story of Hazel's entire life. That's a LOT of ground to cover, and BKV can't include everything. I get it! I just find myself questioning what he's including and what he's leaving out. Was the reporter side plot really necessary to this story? Did we need to see Marko's pseudo-adultery friend again? And I generally like the Will, but his presence here felt so unnecessary! 
 This volume also made me question the world building here, some. I see what BKV's doing, drawing these parallels between homophobia or transphobia and inter-species relationships, but I don't necessarily like it. This volume really brought it to the forefront, which means that it also brought to the forefront the fact that BKV has imagined an entire UNIVERSE of different species which all apparently follow completely human, heteronormative relationship patterns. Like - every species is divided into males and females, every species expects males and females to shack up together but most of the universe has gotten over its inherent homophobia - great? That's all you got, man? I know that authors have been using sci-fi to talk about human rights issues for decades, and to do that you have to, to some extent, force human social expectations on alien societies. At the same time, I feel like it would be more progressive to just straight up write societies where gender and sexuality aren't a binary. I mean, you've got an entire universe to work with! 
 Anyway, I don't know. I still enjoyed reading this. His dialogue is great, her art is a pleasure. I'm just a little disappointed that it's not as solid as the first few books in the series. I also know that I tend to feel this way about series in general (like, I'm pretty sure the middle of Y: The Last Man lagged for me too) so I'm going to stick it out. Here's hoping the next one has a little more going on.

This is an amazing trilogy set in one of the most unique, fantastical world that I, an avid fantasy reader, have ever encountered. A blend of past, present, and future, in an alternate universe, the world building is the first thing that pulled me into this beautiful series. Right from the start, there are so many questions that you're dying to have answered. The thing is, at the end of both Incarnate and Asunder, readers had even larger lists of questions than when they started. Finally, in Infinite, we're given answers to every. single. question! 
 Beyond all the answers that add to the world-building, there's also a lot more world-exploring! Ana is no longer in the city, but venturing out in search of all these answers. Thus far we've learned a lot about the world, but being immersed in this world made it so much more interesting and exciting. Dragons in theory are terrifying enough, but being face to face with one is another entirely. 
 I especially loved the romance in this book, because it build so well on the previous books. Ana and Sam's relationship is slow and steady, something rarely found in YA. And more than that, I love the fact that there's a sort of authenticity to their relationship. It doesn't feel shallow like most romances I encounter. It's realistic and complicated and sweet. They have amazing chemistry and they are completely devoted, but they still have problems which they work through. 
 I love the symbolism in this series. First butterflies, then roses, and now phoenix feathers. Phoenixes are symbolic of rebirth, which is a large part of this series. Phoenixes also play a super important (secret!) role in the entire series, which is explained finally in this book. Music also has an important place in these books, and as a musician, I love how beautifully it is woven into the actual plot, as well as the role it plays thematically. 
 An epic conclusion to a fantastical series, Infinite delivers on every front and leaves readers satisfied.

This book had some flaws, but the tone and the prose were so solid I was willing to ignore them. It's beautifully written, giving a sense from the very beginning of everything protagonist Alana has at stake: her love of ships, her family, her ability to work and live in a body that is slowly betraying her, her love of ships. I mentioned ships both first and last because the book itself is most vibrant when talking about starships and living "in the black" or "in the big quiet." They're lovely images, full of weight. When the same passionate language is used for another character not long after Alana meets her, it felt sudden. 
 Things I liked: the prose, the seamless integration of hand-wavium into the story's high-tech world, the forthright looks at class and disability and sexuality and personhood. Alana's disability is an important part of who she is, and permeates the plot as well: it doesn't disappear when it's inconvenient. Race and sexuality don't seem to be issues in the world we are given, but there is no white straight default. I appreciate that. I like that there is no shame or doubt regarding Alana's sexuality. I like that we're given a world that includes women and men and both and neither, in which most of the main characters are competent women because why not? 
 Spoilers in the things-that-didn't quite work for me: (view spoiler)[Everybody was a little too attractive for me. Alana fell for the captain SO quickly, and I didn't feel enough reason for her to call it love beyond physical attraction. The destruction of the world her parents were on felt abrupt: we were told it was important to Alana only in the seconds before it was gone. Her sister felt like a caricature for the first half of the book. The way Slip set Alana up at the beginning felt more manipulative than necessary given the relationship among crew members. Alana forgave some pretty awful behavior fairly easily. I'm not a romance reader, generally, but the romance in this was well integrated. It would have been even slighter if Alana wasn't such a processor, giving us her emotional state at every step. (hide spoiler)] 
 All of that said, I couldn't put the book down once I started it. I was willing to put up with those flaws for a solid space adventure with three-dimensional, diverse characters.
As with most anthologies, there were some stories I liked better than others, but the collection overall was an interesting and enjoyable read.

This book is compulsively readable. 
 Many years ago, I studied fairy tales as scholar. I have left that phase of my career behind, but I am still fascinated by a well-told retelling of a classic tale. 
 Rhiannon Thomas has proven herself to be a gifted and creative writer in this imagining of what happens when Beauty wakes up. The Princess Aurora was cursed with sleep by the witch Celestine--no one knows why. Her family keeps her "safe" by locking her in a tower throughout her childhood, but the curse finds her regardless. And this is where Thomas' story strays from the older tellings. In Thomas' story, Aurora is the only one to sleep. Her parents, her castle, her kingdom--all of them are unaffected by the curse and their lives continue--until they die. "Unaffected," though, does not mean that the curse does not change their lives. Aurora's sleep eventually leads to political unrest and a series of new families on the throne. 
 Upon waking, Aurora is thrust into a narrative (their Sleeping Beauty legend) that she did not expect and did not embrace. Everyone wants to shape her into being a part of a story that will make them happy, but her own happiness is ignored. 
 What can she do to shape her own destiny when so many forces want to tell her that it's already been written?

 I appreciate this book so much. It truly is a treasure. The words themselves are lyrical, full of raw emotion, and the gorgeous, gorgeous illustrations by the talented Jim Kay capture the wildness and sorrow that only true grief and loss can bring. 
 A Monster Calls is about facing what frightens you, accepting what's been lost, and letting go of what cannot be changed. The characters of Conor, his mother, his grandmother, and the monster itself bring to life not only their vibrant personalities, but also their emotions and responses to heartache in a way that is so wonderful, powerful and important to remember. 
 This book is so real. Part of being human means having to bear terrible loss. A Monster Calls reminds us that it's okay to hurt. It's okay to wish. All that matters is that we let go.

**Spoilers throughout review** 
 Wow, I must say, after the original "Soulless", this one is definitely my fave book in the series. I mean, c'mon- an action-packed steampunk romance with bisexual werewolves and pregnant preternaturals, all on top of political conspiracy and a suffragette sister. There is nothing about this book that I do not love and/or actively seek out in reading material. 
 "Heartless" begins some months after "Blameless" left off, with an extremelty pregnant Alexia Maccon trying to solve the mystery of a ghost telling her that there is a plot out to kill the queen. Being Alexia, she has to get down to the bottom of it, eight months pregnant be damned! She eventually finds out that there may be some connection to the murder plot against the queen brewed by the Kingair pack (her husband's original pack) some twenty years ago, and even more shocking, her father Alessandro might be involved. Alexia is an extremely harried woman- she must also deal with an unsettled new pack member (poor Biffy), the fact that she must let Lord Akeldama adopt her future child for the sake of her and the child's lives, and her friend Madame Lefoux's crazy octomaton contraption that just can't mean anything good for anyone. To top it all off, she is just so dang hungry ALL THE TIME! Poor girl can't catch a break. 
 I loved the insight into Professor Lyall's background, since he is one of my favorite characters. It almost made me cry when Alexia found out that the love of his life was her father, because it mirrors her relationship with Conall- a preternatural and a werewolf, one who lives forever and one who is unquestionably mortal. I know this is a light and humorous series, but I thought that was such a well-written part, and it really shows how good Carriger is at making us love and feel for her characters. 
 I also love how Alexia got everything done, solved every problem, and landed on her ass a few times, all while pregnant. It is a rare literary example of a woman who is her own person and has her own problems and issues while still being a mother, and how woman are not made of glass when they're pregnant. I think Alexia would be a kick-ass mom- a little strict, not overly affectionate, but fiercely protective and always loads of adventure. 
 Loved this installment, took me about two days to read. I'm starting the last one and I will cry buckets when this series is over!

Judging from other reviews, this is one of those marmite books, that you'll either love, or hate. Luckily for me I'm in the 'LOVED IT' group. 
 New Crobuzon is an immense city which is both filthily squallid and amazingly vibrant. Filled with a fantastic plethora of people and cultures. Artists and Scientist, Thieves and politicians (often the same thing), rich and poor, bug-people, cactus-plant-people, bird-people, generic humans, steampunk cyborgs (called re-made) and countless other wierd and awful things. 
 Issac Dan der Grimmnebulin is a sort of free-lance Scientist, who picks up an intriguing new client. A Garuda (bird-person) called Yagharek, who commissions Isaac to give him back the power of flight. Isaac throws himself into the scientific task, spurred on by three things; A love of impossible problems, the fascinating mysterious character of Yagharek himself, and a ton of money. (Yeh that would probably get me too). 
 Whilst investigating many different scientific options, Isaac comes into possession of a strange rainbow coloured caterpillar that refuses to eat anything but a psychotropic drug called 'dream-shit'. And with these two set-ups for the main plot line.. how could things ever NOT become interesting? 
 Big thanks to Nancy for recommending this book to me; I got completely hooked into this book. It took me a week to get through - it's fairly massive, and a bit tough to get into a first - but well worth the effort involved. 
 All the characters were brilliant and detailed, but my absolute favourite was Yagharek, the wingless Garuda. he's such a mystery in the beginning. And I found myself rushing through inbetween sections (as interesting as they were), hurrying to his next appearance and then reading voraciously for any hint and suggestion as to his background. Why and how did he lose his wings? What crime would be so great as to fit that punishment? Why do I have a crush on a fictional bird-person? These things kept me up at night until I closed the last page of the book. 
 I can't say the book didn't have it's flaws. The one thing that did bother me, was the the concept of the bug-people. (The other races I could actually accept). But the bug people.. the problem for me was that in this race, the females have a human female body, but their head is a bug. And the males are just a bug (no human parts). Most of the story was much of the same: this guy calls Bish, tells him to do something, Bish does it, then the guy calls Bish with another thing to do, ad infinitum. It got really annoying and it made the book drag. Not a good feeling to have when the book you're reading is 400 pages... 
 2) I didn't connect with any of the characters. I'm not sure what it was, but something was missing from this book; it didn't have that Melina Marchetta spark that makes her books so special. Yeah this book had A LOT of characters, but I don't think that's why I couldn't connect with any of them. Almost all of Melina's books have a lot of characters--some might even say too many--but that never stopped me from feeling for them. Their quality was not sacrificed because of the fact that they were amidst a bunch of other characters. My issue with this book is more so about the quality of the characters rather than their quantity. I just didn't feel like I knew any of them. I'd read these emotional scenes and I would feel...nothing. Intellectually I recognized oh, this is an emotional scene, I should be feeling something but emotionally I was like eh. And it guts me to know that because Melina's emotional scenes always wreck me. I know what she's capable of, and it felt like she didn't quite deliver it in this book. 
 That's really all I have to say about this. I didn't love it, I didn't hate it. It's been less than a day since I finished it and honestly, there isn't a single scene from it that stands out in my mind. It was just meh. 
 Gonna be anxiously waiting for Melina's next books though. However long it takes. (Hopefully not that long though. I need more Melina Marchetta in my life. Desperately.)

Fever gives us a wider view into what our world has come to, that Wither only gave us a peek in. But in this new dangerous world, nothing is as it seems, and Rhine's situation goes from bad to worse and has very few bright spots in between. With their life span on the line, Rhine is determined as ever to reach her brother and the safety of their home, before her life comes to an end at age 20. 
 Where females only live to 20 and males to 25, this dystopian world isn't one I would want to be a part of. However, Lauren's writing is just as wonderful and pristine as the first book. 
 There were a few times I didn't want to read this book. Not because it was bad writing....far from that actually.  I am very determined to finish this series, because while the series can be a downer, it is also very beautiful. I can only imagine what Sever might bring.

In urban fantasy, human beings are usually the pathetic losers - we don't get any cool supernatural powers that witches, werewolves or vampires get, and we're usually depicted as ineffectual racists. At best, we're just oblivious. 
 Kim Harrison is among the few authors to tackle the subject with any real depth. "A Perfect Blood" is a smart, witty, fast-paced book where a small but clever cabal of humans humans are the enemy. While the plot gets a little bogged down in Rachel's woes as a new demon, the main plot is tense, taut, and genuinely scary at times. 
 Rachel is furiously treading water in the government bureaucracy when an old, powerful vampire (via a young one named Nina) offers her a deal -- if she helps solve a bizarre crime, he will arrange for her to be declared "alive" again. 
 But the crime is more than merely strange: a young man who was ritually murdered, and partly transformed into a hideous beast-man. Even worse, he's not the first. Rachel realizes that someone was trying to transform him into a demon. And the perpetrators seem to be HAPA (Humans Against Paranormals Association), a hate group that wants to destroy all Inderlanders, and is now using magic to do it. 
 And since Rachel's demon blood makes her a huge blinking target, she begins worrying about the people she cares for -- and what will happen if she finally removes the elven bracelet. But soon she begins to realize that has members hidden in the IS and/or FIB -- and everyone around her might have their own agenda. To keep herself and her friends safe, she might have to trust 
 I honestly have developed a leetle pet peeve at how humans are depicted in urban fantasy -- usually it's as frothing racists who have no chance against the overpowered supernaturals, but for some reason they're able to oppress the poor Metaphorical Minorities. Ugh. 
 "A Perfect Blood" is one of the few that DOESN'T annoy me. It's tightly written, burning with dark intensity and filled with taut action scenes and some genuinely scary foes. The scariness of HAPA is not just that they're fanatics using magic, but that they're SMART. And, well, that the authorities don't want to acknowledge that they exist. 
 With such an intense plot, Kim Harrison spends a lot of time weaving dark plot threads and spidery twists into the story. But she also includes some of her trademark wit and humor (Jenks' stormy love life with Belle) and some touching moments (Rachel has Kisten's pool table refelted), and some genuinely suspenseful mysteries (who is Felix?). The one downside is that for some chapters, the HAPA crisis gets shoved on the back burner so Trent and Rachel can deal with her demon problems. 
 Rachel spends most of this book being crippled by her fears and her denial of her new demon nature -- and she won't be able to trounce HAPA unless she overcomes them both. And her relationship with Trent is growing by leaps and bounds. While she still doesn't fully trust him, Rachel is starting to see that the stately elf is not the monster she once thought he was, and that he might feel more than friendship for her. It's actually rather cute, in a Lizzie-and-Darcy way. 
 "A Perfect Blood" isn't quite perfect, but it's close enough to be one of the best books in Kim Harrison's series yet. It's dark and intense, but threaded liberally with humor and a tinge of romance.

My first experience of this book came from my friend, who read me the funniest quotes from later books in the series during a lazy afternoon reading session. Of course, it took me a while to get around to the start of the series myself. In many ways, I loved what I found. In other ways, I didn't. 
 My absolute favourite thing about Just One Damned Thing After Another is how much it takes its premise and runs, leaping and bounding and gibbering, into the sunset. Time-travelling historians working out of a secret university building, hopping around time, blowing things up, and fangirling way too hard as their lifelone passions come to life in front of them. It has its own unique madcap energy, much like academia itself, and narrator Max's enthusiam was a massive part of what kept me glued to the pages. I personally have little interest in technobabble, so some of the "science, whee!" was a little lost on me - but I am a humanities student at heart, and not even my soul can remain unmoved by the delightfully nerdy details of a pack of equally nerdy nerds doing nerd things. 
 But the good times were not to last, and something emerged from the scenery with all the elegance of a drunk apatosaurus to plonk its irresponsibly massive feet in the middle of my fun. Romance. The kind that comes with sex. Way too much sex. 
 I never have, and never will, see how a romantic subplot could ever be as interesting as time-travelling historians going back in time to watch dinosaurs, or observe the raising of cathedrals, or rescue the library of Alexandria. Sadly, Max does, and while I liked her character well enough I grew less and less engaged as more of her life turned into a series of "who wants to have sex with me and who do I want to have sex with oh golly gee whizz isn't this man handsome/interesting/creepy". It felt immature, it felt forced, and I was never happier than when Max and her love interest were having a tiff and/or separated by a rampaging t-rex so we could get back to the fun stuff. 
 I've a minor quibble or two about pacing - I feel like the book should have stopped a little sooner, or perhaps done a little trimming in its latter half to help the ending feel less flabby - and an element or two that comes seemingly out of nowhere and jars with the pretty-realistic-all-considered setting, but I had enough fun with the whole thing that it didn't dampen my spirits. It wasn't quite what I was expecting, but it was clever and original and fun and I'm willing to let a lot of things slide for a book that can get me genuinely excited about a slightly burnt pinecone. So, despite a personal distaste for one major element, Just One Damned Thing After Another isn't getting away without a thumbs up from me.

 Larry 'Doc' Sportello is a private investigator in LA in 1969, and he's also a damn dirty hippie who smokes dope constantly. Doc gets a visit from his old girlfriend Shasta who has been seeing married and wealthy Mickey Wolfman. Wolfman's wife and her boyfriend want Shasta to help them with a scam to get Mickey committed to an asylum, but Shasta feels guilty and wants Doc to help Mickey out. 
 Doc no sooner gets started than he gets blamed for a murder by his arch enemy LAPD Detective Bigfoot Bjornsen who has nothing but contempt for hippies. Mickey and Shasta have vanished, and while Doc tries to wrap his foggy brains around these developments, he's also approached by another woman who claims that her boyfriend, a saxophone player in a surf band that supposedly died of an overdose, is still alive. 
 The Crying of Lot 49 is the only other Pynchon I've read, and this one has the same kind of hazy vast conspiracy lurking in the background . And like that one, I was left kind of liking the book in a general sort of way while thinking that Pynchon is just fucking with me on some level. There's a lot going on in here in terms of information and secrets with a friend of Doc's feeding him info he's getting from the first primitive form of the Internet. 
 The spacey and affable Doc makes for a unique main character to guide us through a noirish but laid back landscape, but it was Bigfoot Bjornsen with his constant stream of anti-hippie comments that I found the most enjoyable. 'Cause much like Bigfoot and Eric Cartman, I am also a hippie hater. 
 I get why Pynchon is worshipped as such a post-modern master, but there's just something about his style that isn't engaging me at the gut level.

 This is a crossover retelling of Sleeping Beauty and Snow White. Two fairy tales that I know of but am not too overly fond of. Slowly but surely I'm starting to despise all things "damsel in distress" and so I was a little apprehensive going into this. BUT LET ME TELL YOU ... MY FEARS WERE ILL-FOUNDED. Instead of two damsels we have severall badass female characters who kick ass, are clever and sassy and independant and who fuck shit up! It was very refreshing and I'd rather read Gaiman's tale to my kids than the original two (my imaginary kids, that is...)! 
 So the premise of this book reminded me a little bit of Gaiman's Sandman (a body of work that seems to overshadow all of his works but well THE SANDMAN IS JUST THAT BRILLIANT, READ IT!) because there is a sleeping sickness in the lands. And it's spreading fast. Sleeping Beauty is locked into her tower and no hero managed to get past the roses and give her a good peck on the mouth. When Snow White hears of this, she fears for her people (and *coughs* also sees an excellent opportunity to delay her shitty wedding to some shitty king) and sets out to free Sleeping Beauty. 
 This is a tale about bravery and doing the right thing. About being strong and finding what makes you happy. To take your own freedom and just to be a badass lady! 
 Chris Riddell's illustrations are STUNNING and accompany this tale beautifully.

IQ "Saba used to say there was a difference between bravery and courage. Bravery was doing something dangerous without thinking. Courage was walking into danger, knowing full well the risks." Willem, pg. 133

The strength of this story lie in the travel narratives, the journey aspect as Willem travels from Europe to Mexico to India and meets the classic people who will change his perspective and impact his journey. The author has an infectious love of travel that happily comes through the novel and makes it even more enjoyable. I also like this book for avoiding sappiness, it is about a romance but it is not about finding a romance. Rather, the story used the romance as a jumping off point and then expanded to become a story about family and fate vs. luck, acting and double happiness. I like that it did more than just have two characters fall in love and be in love (I still agree with Willem that there is a difference). 
 Like the first book, the sequel does have a plodding nature but unlike JUST ONE DAY while the part where Willem is moping around Amsterdam isn't nearly as frustrating, it still didn't really keep my interest. I focused more on the details of life in Amsterdam than what Willem was going through with his friends and girls. Also as much as I liked the bits about Mexico, it seemed pretty unnecessary. It takes the story so long to get going, my sister flew through the first book and couldn't even finish this one because she grew bored. But again, I am impressed at the efforts Willem goes through to find Allyson (although I do think these books should be read fairly close together because I did not remember a lot of secondary characters or details such as what happened to the postcards Willem wrote Allyson and left with Celine) based on the little knowledge he had about her and his simple lifestyle. Willem is 21 and I hope authors continue to focus on college-aged or true 'young adults' because their stories are fascinating and it's more believable when they act independently (as opposed to in actual YA). This is a different kind of romance and travel tale and I am appreciative of that fact, Willem's family has a great backstory and it is a surprisingly complex book.

Meanwhile, she has Ella making them breakfast every morning, cleaning the house, and basically being her slave for whatever she wants. Ella has dreams to attend ExcelsiCon, the convention her dad founded, and entering the cosplay contest. Ella can't stand that they are casting teen heartthrob, Darien Freeman, in the role of Carmindor, her favorite character. She angrily posts about it on her blog, unknowing that it would go viral and be read by none other than Darien Freeman. Darien tries to call and back out of attending the ExcelsiCon event, but ends up reaching Ella's phone instead. The continue texting, unknowing who the other really is. 
 I thought this one was super sweet. Maybe a little too sweet at times, but definitely what I needed after reading a super angsty book right before this one. There are a lot of fairytale retellings out right now, but I thought this was a great modern retelling. There were a few really cheesy parts, but overall I really enjoyed it. I loved the banter and dorkiness between Elle and Darien through text messaging. 
 Elle never had too many friends growing up, so I loved when her and Sage became friends. Sage is an awesome secondary character. I honestly think she made the story for me. She always had Elle's back and didn't make any excuses for the way she was. 
 I enjoyed Darien's character a lot too. He was afraid to let anyone close to him after being burned by a friendship before. He is also unfairly judged by a lot of people, Elle included, because they see him as nothing but a teen heartthrob when he's really just as much of a superfan of Starfield as everyone else. Both Elle and Darien did frustrate me with the way they let people walk all over them though. Darien with his dad/manager, and Elle with her stepmother and sister. I was glad when I finally got to "see" them both stick up for themselves a little more. 
 If you are looking for a really sweet, Cinderella retelling then this may be the book for you, especially if you have a dorky side too. This one was a touch too sweet/cheesy for me but the characters won me out in the end and I ended up enjoying it a lot.

"I remained steady and still until I had every last person's attention. Then the door opened for the final time that morning and she stepped into my classroom. 
 Late. 
 I looked at her--she looked at me. 
 My ending, staring right at me from the very beginning." 
 Addison Lancaster is doing her best to be perfect in everything she does. One thing she doesn't want to do is to be late for her first day in her high school senior year. But then she gets tied up in her morning activities that she did not expect that she would have a new teacher. 
 One look at the new teacher makes Addison's tickticktock stop. 
 Greyson McKendrick never wanted to be imprisoned to the four corners of the room. Having been told that his father has been diagnosed with cancer, he came back from a long, soulful vacation and became the new teacher of his hometown. He never expected that the student of his will crumble all logic and ethics, that has been taught by his father, to dust. 
 "Life is full of ironies, because with him, I'd never felt more alive." 
 Addison and Greyson embarks on a forbidden affair. Greyson battles between the logic his brain is saying with what his heart is trying to tell him. He can't have a relationship with his student because it is illegal. But he does it anyway since he has never felt more... at peace with Addison. 
 But Greyson is the only that sees Addison behind all those perfection she has covered. 
 "How could it be that the only semblance of peace for me was with someone I wasn't allowed to have?" 
 And then they get caught. 
 Everything that Addison is trying to push away and forget comes crashing back to her. 
 Greyson is gone. 
 Then, she breaks. 
 "I'd done it and would do everything all over again just for a moment with her. For her smile, her laughter, and the way she looked at me with absolute trust in her eyes." 
 Amazing. Simply amazing. 
 I myself didn't notice that one was a student and one was the teacher. Addison was wise beyond her years that made her older in my eyes. 
 What was so gut-wrenching in this story was Addison. She was starved for affection. She wanted her parents and her little brother. But that accident made her whole family different. And made her so hungry for someone's affection. I wanted to hug because almost throughout all the pages she wanted someone to love her even though she isn't really perfect. So when she met Grayson, she has never felt more alive, loved...and free. 
 I wasn't much into Greyson's character even though he has his POV in the story. It was really Addison who tugged my heart. And their relationship, too. But more on Addison though. lol 
 I do understand why Greyson doesn't want to pursue the direction of their relationship. Even though I am not an authority, I do see it. Yes, it maybe because of their age, their status and their position they are in but love is love. 
 Love transcends anything, even Heaven and Hell (kinda read that in some book but I don't remember which one). I think that's the beauty of love. It may defy logic and science but it does explain somethings we don't understand because the answer might be love. 
 You may call me illogical, romantic or dumb but I do believe that love may pose as the answer. Just don't answer in Math that the product, sum or whatever is love. You might as well call yourself...inappropriately unknowledgeable on the said lesson. 
 Yep. But if you do that though, I don't mind. 
 After you then. 
 "Was this what love was supposed to be like? An emotion that made you want to willingly give up everything for another--and how much was I willing to give?" 
 I really do love and appreciate this kind of story. It makes me feel so depressed and appreciative at the end. Weird, but true. 
 I think you should really add this up in your TBR list. And then READ. IT. NOW. 
 Seriously.

The Optimist's Daughter: Eudora Welty's Celebration of Life and Memory 
 "But the guilt of outliving those you love is justly to be borne, she thought. Outliving is something we do to them. The fantasies of dying could be no stranger than the fantasies of living. Surviving is perhaps the strangest fantasy of them all."--Laurel McKelva Hand 
 It is bittersweet to write about this little gem. It comes with no frills, no literary allusions, no photographs. 
 My mother died on February 1, 2012. She gave me this book for Christmas, 1973. I was twenty-one, had never lost a loved one, nor even a close friend. I had nothing ahead of me but the future. Memory was reserved for college examinations. And mine was very good. 
 But over the passage of time, as we all have, or all will, we will view memory with different eyes. There will be less plates to place on the dinner table. There will be fewer birthdays to celebrate, a package or two less to wrap at Christmas. I attend more funerals these days. 
 Welty portrays the classic Southern funeral with perfection. Everything is there. The exaggerated and loud voices nervously chatting up the good qualities of the deceased. The tables heavily laden with hams, vegetables, casseroles. The odor of flowers. The subsequent emptiness, and the loneliness. 
 I know Laurel. We could walk hand in hand. I imagine we could talk for hours about love and the loss of it. Some may find her too prim, too reserved. But perhaps tears are better shed in privacy, as opposed to Fay's widow's breakdown, perfectly timed and very public, though I suppose there is a place for that, if the feelings are true. 
 Welty puts this story together in layer upon layer as carefully as my grandmother put together a coconut cake at Christmas. Laurel's past is slowly disclosed. The meaning of the group of bride's maids becomes clear only well into the story. Laurel is a war widow. Her husband shook hands with a Kamikaze in the Pacific. She still dreams of him. She has remained a widow by choice. 
 But now she has suffered loss for the third time. Her mother, her husband, her father. But she was an optimist's daughter. 
 Her father, Judge McKelva, had weathered the death of Becky, Laurel's mother. In his seventies, he married Fay, younger than his daughter, and he weathered that marriage, though Fay did not have the intelligence of his wife or daughter, nor have his place in society. She was young and someone to protect, a factor never to be underestimated in any man. Perhaps he did not see her love of the material, her coarseness, her shallowness, or vulgarity. But he moved forward where Laurel did not. 
 I can't put my hands on that Christmas gift from years ago. It is packed somewhere among the many books boxed away along with photograph albums of three generations. But I will find it. Each day I look at all those boxes, and with few exceptions I say, "No, not today." But I will find it. And when I do, I will read that gift from a Christmas so long ago. 
 As Miss Welty said, 
 "It is memory that is the somnambulist. It will come back in its wounds from across the world...calling us by our names and demanding its rightful tears. It will never be impervious. The memory can hurt, time and again--but in that may lie its final mercy. As long as it's vulnerable to the living moment, it lives for us, and while it lives, and while we are able, we can give it up its due." 
 For my Mother, Ann Sullivan, August 27, 1935-February 1, 2012

 I could get a lot of hate for this, but I am not a big fan of John Green. His writing style is not one I'm drawn to. In saying that, there is no denial that he is a very talented author. He can understand the human mind and human emotions very well, which is what makes his writing so interesting to many. 
 He's stories are always very real and down to earth; he does not sugarcoat the truth of life. 
 What drew me to this particular book were the chapter titles. It started with so many days before, counted down, and ended with so many days after. 
 The very first question that comes to my mind is; before what? 
 That is the question that made me read on. 
 Miles is obsessed with last words. Like many of John Green's deep and intellectual quirks he gives to his characters, this one that took me a little while to understand. Seriously, don't even get me started on the metaphor thing in The Fault in Our Stars. 
 The point is, when I realized why such an idea would even exist in a book like this, I liked it. It really got me thinking about people's last words. Though that's not really the point of this book's plot. I actually couldn't narrow down the point of this book's plot, seeing as there were so many issues jammed into it. 
 When Miles meets Alaska, he falls for her pretty much instantly. I really couldn't see this as any more of a typical school boy crush; his reasoning for liking her starts with the fact that she is hot, and her outfit probably doesn't do anything but ramp this up three notches. 
 He then is led to believe she is awesome because she reads a lot. Nothing wrong with that, of course. 
 To me, Alaska didn't really stand out to me in a good way. Everything about her was rebellious and flirtatious, to the point she was really bordering the line of her loyalty towards her actual boyfriend, and you'd think she was a goddess the way everyone went on about her. 
 Of course, she has her reasons for her behavior, as any decent character would. 
 Along with these two characters, there were a handful of other characters in the book who were similarly rebellious, and it all blended together so much that I can't even remember their names except for The Colonial. 
 As Miles and Alaska grow closer, and the countdown grows closer, I start to make guesses at what might happen when it reaches zero. This is what really caught me off guard about this book, as my suspicions were going the right way when they proceeded to kiss. But then I realized, and a wave of horror hit me, when a drunk Alaska got into a car and drove away. 
 That's when I knew this book wasn't going to have a happy ending. 
 The first day after began, and Alaska was dead. 
 The book can be split into two in a sense; the first part dealing with normal teenage issues and new friendships with the possibility of love. The second half focuses on grief and coping with it, as well as trying to determine what caused Alaska to run off that night. As a result, this book sort of becomes a romance story plus a mystery novel. 
 Because of these factors, the book both flows well, and also doesn't. It's got a smooth plotline, guided by the countdown, but the issues and messages in the book are choppy and all over the place. 
 Miles, with his obsession with last words, really stabs you in the heart in 'part two' of this book. We realize very quickly that he never learned Alaska's last words, and he never would. Of any person's last words he could have heard, I think he would have wanted to hear hers most. 
 It's obvious that Miles and Alaska had feelings for each other in this book, and that was the part that was supposed to make you cry. The reason I did not cry is because of the fact that their relationship wasn't really written well. It consisted of cheesy romance lines and thoughts of Alaska's hot body, and there was barely anything emotionally deep to tie these two together. Alaska's death was the blow that was meant to cripple readers. I fully understood what Green was attempting to do here, but it didn't work for me. 
 Before I finish, I will just reiterate that this is one of John Green's books that I did enjoy. I'll never be head over heels about his writing, or feel that it has the power to rip my heart out of my chest like it does to others, but I can acknowledge a decent plot line and creative twist when I see one. I did enjoy the 'last words' concept of this book, as well as the question as to what each chapter was before.

I definitely liked the beginning, as the idea of finally answering a major question of the setting drew me in, and the potential for an exciting quest was something to look forward to. It started to feel as if there were one or two too many viewpoint characters, as often the narrative has something exciting happen and then takes a while to get back to it. Most of the characters are interesting, and given at least a bit of development, but I admit I didn't really like experiencing the point of view of one of the villains. It was nice to be following the leader of the Druids as a viewpoint character, though. The plot took a while to get off the ground, as there was a fair bit more build-up to the quest than I liked, especially given the other stuff interspersed with it. Also a lot of the plot elements feel like retreads of plotlines from earlier novels in the series. Nonetheless, it was fun to return to this world, and by the end of the book I feel as if things are going to start moving at a faster, more exciting pace. Especially given the cliffhanger ending. Also, this was definitely an improvement over The Measure of the Magic. So I'm definitely going to read the next book in the trilogy pretty soon, though I'm not quite as enthused about it as I was expecting to be.

Originally posted at SmexyBooks-http://smexybooks.com/2016/03/review-... 
 Joint Review: Sheena and Tori 
 Favorite Quote: "Look at the situation we're in! She has a clipboard!" 
 Tori: Jace Berisha's life wasn't all that grand, being the wife of a sociopathic religious cult leader, but she never expected him to kill her. When she is granted near immortality by the goddess Freya, she grabs hold with both hands. Of course, being able to exact revenge on her murderous husband is a bonus. Working with the Crows to prevent the coming of Ragnarok, Jace finally has the life she always wanted and an outlet for her anger issues. 
 But something wicked is coming. 
 An ancient goddess, bent on vengeance, is cutting a bloody swipe through humanity and her goal is the Crows. In order to save the world and themselves, the Crows will have to join forces with their greatest enemies, the Protectors, a clan built for the sole purpose of killing Crows. Luckily for all of them, Protector Danski Eriksen is a lover, not a fighter. And the woman he wants to love up on? The one and only Jace. 
 Crazy clans? 
 Check! 
 Unstoppable gods? 
 Check! 
 Annoying pets? 
 Check! 
 Let the games begin. 
 Anything Shelly Laurenston writes is pure, unadulterated fun. The queen of humorous paranormal romances continues to keep her title with her latest series-Call of the Crows. The Undoing is the second installment in this action packed, laugh out loud, sexy as sin series based on Norse mythology. Set in the present, Laurenston creates a world brimming with supernaturally enhanced warriors who have been enlisted in the fight to save the world from complete annihilation. Each one is offered near immortality at their death with the condition they must serve the god or goddess who gave them their second life until their final death. Some are chosen due to their heritage while others are chosen for their skills. What you end up with is a melting pot of obnoxious, arrogant, loud, petty, narcissistic, trouble making death bringers who can't stand one another and will leave you gasping for air as they wack, stab, and beat their way to victory. 
 "Is there something psychologically wrong with you?" 
 The Undoing starts off with a BANG. We learn exactly how Jace Berisha became a Crow which is foreshadow for what's to come. Now a full-fledged member of the Crows, the introverted Jace spends her days hiding from the more obnoxious clan members who want her to "socialize" and playing with her puppy, Lev. Her nights are spent drenched in blood and kicking arse as she and her fellow Crows carry out their missions. When one mission to recover their Goddess's bracelet goes horribly wrong, Jace finds herself being saved by a very sexy Protector. 
 Danski (Ski) Ericson and his fellow Protectors were sent to retrieve some priceless books by their God but they never expected to walk into a murder of crows. With bodies and parts flying, he is more than a little pleased he finally gets to spend some time with the lovely and reserved Jace. When he learns the books are in a language none of his brethren can read, he hurries over to the Crow mansion and offers Jace a job as one of her talents is knowing multiple languages. After being told no numerous times, Jace finally accepts the job to get away from the Crows and a love affair is born 
 LOLOL 
 No, it's not but soon will be. 
 I loved this installment. Filled with Laurenston's trademark humor and snark, we get a ringside seat to the romance of two warring clan members while the tsunami of a storyline expands the world and the arc while building an intriguing conflict. New and old faces offer more background towards the coming war while the interfering clans keep you in tears. 
 "KERA!" 
 "WHAT?" 
 "Get Brodie to drop that squirrel!" 
 "Oh my God. It's got the plague or something, right?" 
 "It's...it's not just a squirrel." 
 "What?" 
 So Sheena, what did you think of The Undoing? 
 Sheena: Tori, I love this series and Laurenston's hilarious writing style so much, that any and all romance is just icing on the cake. I get so engrossed in the zany Crow bickering and larger than life personalities that this world of Gods and warrior clans fighting to prepare for- and stave off Ragnarok, is more than enough to captivate. That being said, I was supremely satisfied with the hot Viking sex. 
 Jace is a berserker with a cause. Her character sang to me because for the love of the gods, she is not overly shy, she just wants to be left the eff alone and avoid small talk. I have far less traumatic reasons for hating small talk in comparison to Jace, however, I found myself fighting giggles whenever her introvert-ness was confronted. Ski was handsome enough. Present enough, kind enough and pretty much served his purpose. For all intents and purposes, this was all about the Crows. Ski was more of a prop. Never really got to know him. Even so, his lack of development did not really bother me. So many rich characters vied for my attention that Ski's "meh" ness did not really register. When he wasn't slowly finessing his way into Jace's favor, he was engaging in a series of standoffs with book one's hero, Vig, that nearly busted my gut. Besides Jace, the Crows and the most outrageous house party I've ever seen, highlights of the story included a Protector called Bear and his tenuously brokered affinity for Jace's dog, Lev. I loved Bear. He is a brutal, alpha warrior with a sweetly crass streak that made his character really pop! The Protector's are seriously studious, owl-like warriors who fancy themselves above the fray- until they are knee deep in it, of course. Heh! 
 Tori: Sheena, I'm pretty sure Jace is my fictional sister from another mother. I too despise small talk and have some, err, anger issues, am shy, and prefer books to people. While I have never gone as far as hiding in a cupboard (or biting off someone's nose), I have walked away while someone was in mid-sentence, peeked around doorways to avoid talking to anyone, and pretended I didn't hear someone calling my name as I ran away. Jace's awkwardness resonated in me and I adored her. I found her backstory fascinating. OMG her grandmother. (I died). Jace had good reasons for her actions and I can't help but hope we met more of her relatives in future installments. I have to agree with you about Ski. I liked him because he was the one for Jace. Laurenston created him as a foil, a grounding agent for Jace and we never learn his backstory or gain any real feeling for him as an individual. Not like we got for Vig in book one. But he gets the job done between, over, under, beside the sheets so yeah... VIKING SEX FOR THE WIN!! 
 Shenna: I did not think it possible, yet I very much so enjoyed The Undoing even more than it's predecessor, The Unleashing. I could not get enough of the snarknado tendencies of these Crows! Amsel, Chloe, Kera, and the whole gang come together as often as they clash and fight- always proving that Crows stick together, no matter what against any enemy or threat of any kind. It was heartwarming and emotional to see how they looked after Jace, the obligatory sisterly warnings they gave to Ski when he expressed his interest in her, and the downright deadly defense when it came to protecting her from her own blood. No matter the threat, these girls stick together! 
 Tori: The Undoing was phenom. While I enjoyed The Unleashing, The Undoing went into expands on the world with stronger details, with more humor, stronger elements, and a better balance between the arc and the subplots. The teasing, pranks, and snippets of violence between the clans and each other as is the almost homicidal need to protect one of their own is part of what makes Laurenston's books so funny. They are predestined to mess with each other and Lord is it hilarious. Their motto is literally 'love hurts.' The Crows are the ultimate girl gang gone wild. I was almost hysterical watching the the party unfold and & Cleo's ex husband...my stomach hurt from laughing by the time I was done reading. 
 "Since this is my party, shouldn't I have a say in who gets to come?" 
 "It's a party in your honor. No one said it was your party." 
 The whole character base is a is the literary equivalent of taking LSD. Bear and his OCD tendencies was a story all on it's own. In fact, each of the Protectors all had this calm, cool, anti-social vibe going on that when they did associate with the Crows and other clans, you were shocked by how devious they were. So much goodness in here. 
 "What did you do?" 
 "Just smiled pleasantly." 
 "Always instigating. You're almost as bad as Erin." 
 Shenna: The Undoing boasts vibrantly colorful supporting characters and hysterical interpersonal struggles within the clan factions. These clan run-ins occur in conjunction with Jace's personal journey which all ties into a race to stop a demon from prematurely setting off events to bring the great battle before its time. Ultimately, The Undoing had me utterly ugly laughing, akin to the "ugly cry" but far more embarrassing and less voluntary. 
 The broader story arc got a little too fantasy-crazy for me but, hey, I never let a little envelope pushing get in between me and a good story, so I am in it for the long haul for The Call of Crows series. I am already eager to get my hands on information for book three. More Bear...and Viking sex please. Said everyone- ever! Ca-cawww!!!! 
 Tori: Indeed. There wasn't one single character who didn't make a lasting impression on me and leave me wanting more. I myself enjoyed the arc and main conflict. It was 'out there' but all her plot lines are and I couldn't imagine them any other way. I think Laureston does an excellent job of expanding upon it from book one and giving it just enough zaniness to keep me wide-eyed without leaving me eye rolling and wondering about the logistics. 
 The Call of the Crows series is a definite must read for fans of humorous, outrageous, over the top PNR that overflows with colorful storylines, insane characters who refuse to act normal, and sexy adult romances that aren't hampered by emo drama or baggage. 
 Sheena Grade: A 
 Tori Grade: A

In What's Left of Me Kat Zhang introduces us to a really interesting concept: people being born with two souls in one body, where the norm is that after a couple of years, one of the souls vanishes and the dominant one takes over. A sort of natural selection. But what if the soul doesn't vanish? Eva didn't vanish and she and Addie are still together. Eva is the 'recessive' soul, Addie controls their body. It was pretty awesome how Kat Zhang managed to make Eva a lively character, even when for the most part she couldn't actually DO much of anything. She was a vibrant personality without much of a voice heard by anyone other than Addie. 
 And while I felt like I knew Eva, I never felt the same way about Addie. Which is kinda weird, cause most of Eva's life and thoughts revolve around Addie. I sometimes didn't very much like Addie and I'm not even really sure why. I get that she was grasping for control of their situation, but sometimes I wanted to shake her really badly. 
 This may be out of context for those not having read the book, I don't want to give anything away, but I felt really bad for them and the whole situation with their parents and their brother, and if I'd been them I'd have felt SO betrayed. I know it was an impossible choice, but seriously, I felt like her parents should have done something. 
 The institution is REALLY CREEPY. Seriously, it's kinda scary what people can do under the name of 'helping' people. It was sort of like the creepy experiments that went on during World War II. And while I felt like I should have been on the edge of my seat reading about it and not being able to stop myself turning the pages, I wasn't. I was kinda sitting and waiting for them to actually DO something. 
 So I'm kinda in the middle out this book. I thought the concept was really cool and original and I did like reading it, but I never felt that connection that makes me want to READ until I just can't read no more, you know? 
 Though I will probably pick up the second book because I do think hybrids are pretty interesting. 
 My rating: 3 stars

Full review at Smart Bitches, Trashy Books 
 Ascension features a protagonist (named Alana) who is a black woman who is also a lesbian, and who struggles with chronic pain. She also a spaceship engineer who dreams of sailing the stars. I truly could not ask for more from life than a heroine with these specific characteristics. By page 18, I was in love. The rest of the book was something of a disappointment, but boy did I adore Alana. 
 I love that this romance features women, not just in a romantic way, but also as crewmates and family members. There's only one man on the ship and he's part wolf, so that's a thing. I actually got all the way through the book before I realized that in the entire book there are only two male characters, and one barely shows up. I appreciated that this felt so natural - as common as if I read a book entirely populated by guys but with one token chick. I especially enjoyed the portrayal of a contentious yet ultimately loving relationship between sisters. Incidentally, the book is also unusual in that it is accepting of a poly relationship and presents that as a viable Happy Ever After option. 
 Unfortunately, neither the plot nor the characters, other than Alana and her sister, Nova, gelled for me. This was especially a problem when it came to the romance between Tev and Alana. I liked the idea of Tev, the polyamorous lesbian ship captain with a prothetic leg, but she never became more than a cool idea. As much as I like the idea of this character, I need her to act like a person who happens to have all those characteristics, not a paper doll that says "Alana's Fantasy Woman. 
 Basically, this book has every possible idea that can appeal to me (including a Firefly vibe with the crew of misfits who tiptoe on the edge of the law), but it falls flat in the execution. I still have my eye on the next book, because I feel like if all these pieces were ever to come together in artistic harmony I'd be the happiest woman on earth. But at the moment, this book has great representation in a lot of ways - of women, of people with disabilities, of people who are lesbian or bisexual, of open relationships, of people of color - but it doesn't pull them together into something that feels like an organic story with organic characters. I want to give this an A for effort, a diverse cast, and a great cover, but I have to give it a C+ for the final product. 
 - Carrie S.

A lot of this book was insights I already knew, or at least already sort of instinctually "got"--what counts as real food vs. what doesn't, why the Costco buying mentality sucks when it comes to food, how monoculture is bad for everything, and so forth. So while it wasn't always teaching me anything new, it was good to feel vindicated. And there are all too many people who *don't* know these insights, so they ought to read this and get healthier.
