I'll be the first to say that I'm the biggest wimp. I hate all horror movies and books. If you like horror, then I won't mind if you completely disregard this review. This book isn't strictly horror, but it has the slasher-movie feel to it. Maybe that's why I never really got into it. It wasn't that it was too scary- I just got tired of waiting for something to jump out of the shadows. 
 The writing was full of suspense. I never knew what was going to happen next, although I had a feeling it would be something bad. The author seems to be in a habit of repeating herself over and over again. There is quite a bit of cursing which I shuddered at occasionally, (I don't curse) but other than that, I didn't mind the style. 
 Dru got on my nerves every now and then. Her tough girl attitude sometimes felt a little forced. Then again, how would I know how it feels to be chased by a zombie? Nonetheless, I had a hard time connecting with her. That is probably because I'm not anything like her. Sometimes I wished she would just say what she was thinking. By covering up her feelings with rough language, Dru often comes across as unemotional. Still, I have to admit, it was pretty awesome to see the lead girl take control and kick some monster booty. :) 
 I would recommend this book if you're looking for a book that will keep you on the edge of your seat. Now, if your looking for a Twilight spin-off or another supernatural romance, I would advise you to steer clear. I wasn't planning on looking into the sequels, but after I read the ending, I am interested to know what happens next. Maybe I'll read Betrayals sometime.

I am a masochist for going through this beautiful, mental torture. Seriously, it was mentally exhausting, which is why it took me three days to read it. But at the end of the day, it was so worth it. 
 Going into the story, after reading the summary, I thought it was about a girl cutting herself (I was right about that one), and set in high school -- she was bullied, and met with friends and support group that helped through it. But the most important thing was, the main character herself worked to get through whatever things that she had to go through. But meh, I was wrong. The book was much more than that. It was a coming of age book, and self-discovery, in a way. 
 There was so much hype surrounding this book, and I tried not to keep my expectations so high, in case I was disappointed. But it turned out I didn't have to worry about that at all. The book was well-written, and it was so beautiful, and realistic. I felt like I was there too, experiencing all the clusterfuck that Charlie had to go through. I felt so damn sad reading it, that when I am not ugly sobbing, it left me feeling choked as I read page after page. 
 To sum it up, if you need a book, a realistic, well-written and beautiful story that will make you cry so hard, this is your book. If you want a book that tells you that only YOU can change your life, that you can ask for help, but it's only if you make the effort that your life will change, well, then this is your book. I think fans of Aristotle and Dante Discovers the Secrets of the Universe by Benjamin Alire Saenz, Fans of the Impossible Life by Kate Scelsa, Every Exquisite Thing by Matthew Quick, and Am I Normal Yet by Holly Bourne would really enjoy this book. 
 I bet you're wondering why, when none of the books I've listed out involved cutting. Well, they have something else in common. And it's not the mental illness issue. It's about making the readers feel like everything's going to get ugly when the shit hits the fan with all the clusterfuck, and the despair, and everything gets worse before it gets better. That is what these books have in common, and that is why I think they'll enjoy reading Girl In Pieces. 
 I rate this book 5/5 stars.

This series. You love it. You hate it. You love to hate it. People are all over the place with it. And I can be too. It's one I love overall but some books are hit or miss. This one...definitely a hit. I really did not care for the prior book and was nervous about starting Dead Ice but within a few pages that nervousness started turning to excitement because I could see that old Anita from earlier in the series peeking out and that...was freaking awesome. I've missed her! 
 There's a lot happening in Dead Ice but I think overall there was a great balance between the heat and the paranormal. Way more balance than recent books have had. There's romance and lust. There's a little skin time (but not overly much--only 2-3 scenes in a near 600 page book). There's some zombie raising and some police consultation work as well. Relationship woes and advances as well and some metaphysical woo-woo to top it all off. It's pretty much 600 pages of non stop action in one form or another and while that can be exhausting it can also be exhilarating. It edged towards the latter for me and I really could not put this book down. 
 While it wasn't perfect--there was a little bit of repetition happening--it was a great read and a lot of fun watching Anita spending time in all of the different aspects of her world. Dealing with a difficult police case involving zombie porn/slaves that really glecked me out while she encountered with difficult detectives, old acquaintances and just not knowing what was happening with the logistics of the case. Dealing with her actual job of raising zombies and her powers escalating--there were some crazy moments and again with the glecking me out. There was a bit of gore and ick in this one. Not complaining about that though. lol And finally dealing with the many varied men and women in her life and making permanent commitments to some, cutting others lose, struggling with power plays, unexpected metaphysical hotspots and adding in new members to keep everyone happy and content. It was a lot to keep both Anita and me on our toes watching the three parts of her life weave in and out of each other. 
 The heat...was interesting. Compared to previous books this one was incredibly tame. There were a couple sex scenes but they were very tame and for the most part only one on one action. While there was some sexual tension and lots of relationship changes throughout the book the actual heat and sex too a backseat instead of being front and center. What was there was hot though. 
 Overall, I was really pleased with Dead Ice. It was nice seeing the series not get back to it's roots entirely but start to show some of it's old flare and what made it so special. I'm very much interested to see how a few of the somewhat open threads of the storyline will progress in the next one. Here's hoping Hamilton keeps it up and the next has that same taste of the original Anita who was so badass.

I've seen the miniseries version of this multiple times, so I figured I should probably read the actual book. Though many of the secondary characters are flawed through singular characteristic traits, I took the "big picture" route and viewed them as part of the whole story and focused on how they aided Margaret's evolution throughout. The miniseries version was pretty true to the book--the biggest change I can think of was the ending, but each version works for the story. The book version was a softer, more private finish (as befits Mr. Thornton & Margaret) but the film version was just as romantic. I read reviews that compared this story to Jane Austen, only more political, and I do agree to an extent. However, I'm pretty sure Mr. Thornton has trumped Mr. Darcy on my list of handsome brooding fictional men. :p

I'm not sure how exactly to describe Saving June. I think it defies being pigeon holed into one particular genre. It's a story about grief, despair and death. However, it's also a story about joy, discovery and living. Then just to defy description again, Saving June is a hilarious road trip adventure filled with a nostalgic nod to the power of music to change and heal a fractured soul. 
 "He took his pain and turned it into something beautiful. Into something that people connect to. And that's what good music does. It speaks to you. It changes you." Jake speaking about Eric Clapton's Tears in Heaven. 
 Harper's older sister June commits suicide leaving Harper shattered. June was always the perfect over achieving sister, at least in Harper's eyes, and now she wonders what signs she missed, regrets her last words spoken to June and wonders what her place in her broken family is. 
 While Harper's divorced parents are arguing over how to split June's ashes, she hatches a plan to grant June one last wish. June's dream was always to go to California. Harper, her best friend Laney and a mysterious boy named Jake take June's urn and embark on a road trip to take June to her final destination and discover truths about themselves along the way. 
 This is where this review gets dicey for me. There are things I adored about Saving June. I mean really LOVE! The prose is beautiful. Harrington is a truly gifted writer. I read the book in under 8 hours, I was fully engrossed. 
 However.....the characters were all fairly selfish. Harper stole her sister's ashes. I could never shake that fact. I deliberately had to shove that in the back of mind so I didn't think of how agonizing it must have been for her mother to have not only lost one daughter, but to also lose the choice of how to dispose of her ashes PLUS have your only remaining daughter missing with only a note and a "trust me" to go on. 
 Laney the best friend is described as a free spirit, always looking for adventure, willing to skinny dip with total strangers, and having random hook ups. She's an incredible and loyal best friend that I liked a lot but OMG how I worried about her safety. There is nothing fun about getting trashed on Tequila and swimming naked in the ocean at night with two other total strangers when you are 16 years old. 
 As Jake says: "A bunch of drunk kids skinny-dipping in the middle of the night. That'll end well." 
 I'm not sure if it's my age (46) or something else. I think these things do happen and I was not a perfect teenager....at all... but I felt these kids were engaged in some pretty dangerous behaviors. I know I was just supposed to go with the free spirit - this is a fun road trip, coming of age, adventure of a lifetime feeling but I just couldn't relax about it and have fun as I think the author intended. I do want to point out that lessons are learned and there are a few consequences but for the most part these kids lucked out. 
 Jake is a really nice, quirky guy who is REALLY into music. Mostly old. Meaning I'm old because it was all the music I grew up with. The Rolling Stones, ABBA, Tom Waite, The Doors.... Just put on a song and Jake Tolan will tell the story behind the song and the artist. Consider him your personal VH1 Behind the Music narrator. I think this was my favorite part of the book. He's incredibly patient with Harper (even when he's snapping at her) and has his own reasons for wanting to be on this trip. His connection to June is kept vague for much of the book. I enjoyed his relationship with Harper and Laney. He called them out on their bullshit even though he needs to be called out on occasion too (which Harper does quite well). 
 There were tone shifts throughout the book that threw me a bit also. I would be reading a philosophical debate about the existence of God and then the next scene would be about going Fridgehenge at a dump. Sometimes it worked, sometimes it didn't. 
 Saving June was one of those really unique reading experiences for me. I loved all the characters, yet I was horrified by some of their behavior. I felt the ending was way too neat and tidy but I finished the book with a wide smile on my face. 
 Much as the book defies description, so does my reaction to reading it. 
 Yeah - I know that doesn't make much sense or help you decide if you want to read it or not but that's how I felt. I will say three of my blogger friends put Saving June on their top reads for the year if that helps. 
 My final thought after I put the book down was to run to listen to music for hours non stop. I tweeted this: "Saving June by Hannah Harrington makes me want to listen to every song ever written and have Jake Tolan explain every one of them to me." 
 Rating: 2 out of 4 or wait.....4 out of 4?? (My blog rating system) I just don't know....I'm still thinking about it.....I felt a jumble of emotions when I finished.

I forgot how much I loathe Dolores Umbridge. Rowling does a really, really good job of making her evil and making me want to punch her in the face.

 3. I'm getting tired of the need Harry has to explain is past adventures in his inner monologue. Who is going to say, "I think I'll go read one of those Potter books... I think I'll start with.... Book... 5. Wait? What is going on? What is this... Mirror of Erised thing everyone keeps talking about?" 
 4. *Spoiler* The whole plot of Book 5 is Voldemort getting Harry into the Department of Mysteries so that he (Harry) can retrieve the prophesy because you can ONLY remove prophecies that are about you... except if you smash the shelf that the prophesy is sitting on and it falls down. Then you can remove as many as you want, thus nullifying the whole point of the book. 
 Aside from that, it's great.

Amazing book! I can't say enough good things about it. I like good science fiction, but I definitely relish when good science makes the fiction feel real. As an engineer myself, and as someone who has respected science ever since I was introduced to it, I have to admit that this book talks to me in very different levels. At first, it's a wonderful story: a sort-of "Robinson Crusoe meets Mars" kind of novel. I think that, as humans, we relate very easily to stories about survival. I can't imagine a better setting than a planet we've only dreamt of visiting. 
 I've heard some people complaining about the amount of calculations, physics and chemistry references throughout the book, but as a nerdy geek, that has always appealed to me. I couldn't avoid thinking about what would I have done in his place. It's a difficult question, because I'm no botanist, and have not been trained for a space voyage, but I liked his resourcefulness, the pure essence of any engineer: knowledge and applied ideas. 
 I loved how the story jumped from Mars to NASA, and back again to the astronauts, willing to give their lives in the name of science and humanity. I loved that it is about the natural sense we all humans have to eventually try to help others in distress. 
 I'm amazed at the amount of research this book must've had in its writing. I read the author wrote a program to calculate the orbits of the space crafts around Mars to be as much scientifically accurate as possible. I honor him for that. 
 The only thing that was a bit left behind, was the background story of the main character. There are times when the author describes the private lives, love affairs, yearnings and dreams of much of the astronauts, but I think he leaves Mark Watney behind, and he is, at the end of the day, the character we all want to survive. A bit of more empathy would have served the purpose. Other than that, I loved it, from the first sentence to the end. I highly recommend it to any engineer, botanist, chemist, physicist, mathematician, astronomer, or science enthusiast out there.

Old-school fans of the WARDen, rejoice! The author who brought us into a gritty world of vampires and their slayers, shitkickers, glymera, The Pit, needing, and the like is getting back to her roots with the new Black Dagger Brotherhood Legacy series. The main series--Black Dagger Brotherhood--has transitioned into more of a family saga with numerous players than the straightforward paranormal romance it captivated us with early in the series. 
 The Legacy series focuses on new recruits for the Brotherhood. In J.R. Ward's Blood Kiss, the new couple features two students in the BDB training program. Paradise is one of two women in the program. She's part of the glymeria, but finds their focus trivial after the terror the society has experienced of late. She wants only to do something to help her people. She doesn't have combat training, but has an iron will. Her focus on life away from glymeria rules isn't the same as Marissa's story. We have a woman who knows what she wants here, and her moving toward the Brotherhood isn't a result of the stifling rules. 
 Craeg doesn't descend from nobility. Actually, he has huge issues with the "ruling" class. His father died in the raids, while working for one of those families. He joins the training program with nothing else to lose. He wants to learn how to protect the vampires, sure, but he also wants vengeance. His steadfast focus makes him a hell of a match for Paradise. 
 Neither of these two wants to be caught up in bonding scents and the distraction of lust, but isn't that how it always goes? Both are very much tied to one another, but fight it. Craeg gets caught in the moment with Paradise often, and then pushes her away when the lust-fueled haze dissipates. For her part, Paradise is naive when it comes to the other sex. It isn't that she doesn't know guys, but she hasn't had any experience. She needs a few meddling friends to put her and Craeg together in order to see the chemistry is really there. 
 And, hot damn, is it there. The intensity of the scenes between Craeg and Paradise in Blood Kiss may be liable to melt e-reader screens and singe paperback pages. J.R. Ward has again created a couple that craves one another and fights it because they're stubborn. Except that inherent frustration only makes every interaction burn brighter. Sure, Paradise's blindness to Craeg's feelings can make you want to intervene like any good friend, but every moment between those two is palpable, purposeful, and will positively leave you needing more. 
 Just like Craeg and Paradise. 
 Blood Kiss will certainly sate fans of the early Black Dagger Brotherhood novels, but it also splits plot time with ongoing threads with Butch and Marissa and vampire societal issues that work whether you're up-to-date on the series or not.

I was provided an ARC via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. 
 Macey is very smart, she's the best student at school and is apparently very beautiful too but she doesn't know it because no one sees her since she's the best friend of the school's sex god, Cam. 
 But prom is around the corner and she really wants a date with someone who cares, who loves her. 
 Enter the list. 
 Since she's so smart, she decides to make a list of tropes to get her perfect boyfriend out of her favorite author romance novels... 
 I was expecting a sort of Kasie West contemporary or something like Jennifer Echols Superlative series... 
 But no. 
 Disappointed doesn't begin to cover what I felt. 
 First of all, the list: 
 Wendi Cooper's Guide to Catching a Man 
 1. Every man loves a damsel in distress 
 2. A lady worth having is hard to catch 
 3. If a man wanted a parrot, he'd buy the bird 
 4. Men love to compete against each other 
 5. If Men Aren't Working for You, Try Batting for the Other Team 
 6. A Makeover is the Way to a Man's Heart 
 7. Every Good Romance Starts in the Bedroom 
 8. Arranged Dating -It's Still a Thing 
 9. Date Your Best Friend's Sibling 
 10. Fake Your Way to Love 
 I mean the sexism in this is astounding. 
 Macey needs a new favorite author.... 
 Also, there's nothing I hate more than a character calling themselves smart and everyone calling them smart but that it never shows in how they act. Well this was a textbook case. 
 Or a character that is called a bookworm but is never reading... 
 There was so much sexism in this book... Slutshaming and also this kinda thing: 
 "So, if a girl said a guy was bothering her, would that bring out your protective instincts?" I blurted as soon as I sat down in my usual seat. "Hello to you, too." Cam smirked. "Why are guys supposed to have protective instincts?" Teagan blinked, looking up from a piece of a motherboard he was tinkering with. "Because it's their job to protect women." I nodded indignantly. 
 I mean... She's so smart! 
 Now onto the LGBT+ representation... 
 First : 
 "I'm not a lesbian. I'm undecided." 
 "Same thing." He waved her off. 
 I don't think I need to comment on this.... It speaks for itself. 
 Then, Macey decides to ask this girl, Neyland out: 
 "So, um, Neyland, would you be interested in going out this Friday? Maybe catch a movie or something?" 
 There, I'd said it. My heart was doing the cha cha in my chest. Then she laughed. 
 My face flushed hot as embarrassment weighted down in my stomach. "Um, what's so funny?" 
 She waved me off as she wiped a tear from her eye. 
 "I'm sorry. I don't mean to laugh at you, but you're so straight, you couldn't be gay if you wanted to." 
 Anger replaced embarrassment. "What the hell does that mean?" 
 "The first day I met you, my straight-dar said you were not one of us." 
 "Straight-dar?" 
 "Yeah, the internal indicator that tells me if someone is straight or gay," she said between laughs. "I'm sorry. I know I should get control of myself." 
 It took her several deep breaths before she regained her composure. 
 "If you were gay, I'd totally date you, but you're not." 
 This makes me so angry. Besides the fact that you cannot tell people what their sexuality is, there's more sexualities than gay or straight............... 
 And finally, after Macey follows some guy in a basement, he starts commenting on her clothes and then: 
 He shrugged and stuffed his hands into the front of his pressed khaki pants. "I'm merely stating the truth. You are definitely a dress and cardigan type. Very simple and classy. I will give props to whoever did your hair, though. The lightened color really makes your eyes sparkle." 
 Oh. My anger quickly subsided. It made sense now. 
 Yep. Thanks to that supersmart brain of hers, she just figured out he was gay. I'm not even gonna start explaining why that's not ok. 
 I hated all the characters. I already went over the main one (stupid, sexist, etc..) but now, her best friend, Cam. 
 I mean Macey keeps telling us what a great friend he is. 
 And that's true. Such a good friend who keeps asking her to break up with every girl he hooks up with for him... 
 I couldn't stand him. 
 It was also filled with cliches and I do mean FILLED. 
 To me, it's only quality was how short it was.............

Hm.

 And honestly, although Grace is not as stupid as Bella, how stupid was this: 
 "This, Sam and me, this was my real life. The life where I went to school and waited up for my parents and listened to Rachel vent about her siblings - that felt like a pale dream in comparison. Those were just things I had done while waiting for Sam."

Then we jump back and forth between four different POVs from the group we met in chapter three, with no mention of who the hell we met in chapters one and two or what the hell they're doing. It's like the first two chapters were a completely different story. For all I know, it actually was. 
 Anyway, I can't figure out what I'm reading or follow what's going on. Even when we're introduced to the main characters mentioned in the blurb, we're not really spending any time with them. Instead, it's all about the secondary characters. And so I'm just bored with it. It's not interesting enough to keep me going and it's too confusing to make me want to try.

I don't even know how to describe this book. It is SO amazing. The Program takes you on an emotional rollercoaster. 
 It takes place in three parts. Which I thought was brilliant. 
 The book begins by introducing us to world that Sloane and James live in. Teen suicide is an epidemic and considered more of a spreading disease, like a virus that can spread from teen to teen. It can hit without warning and so each day students must fill out a form to say if they are anxious or depressed. If they are deemed depressed they go into The Program where their memories are erased and they are given a blank slate in order to be happy. 
 Sloane and James are dealing with the suicide of her brother. James was his best friend. Neither are allowed to fully grieve and must pretend everything is okay, but it's not. Putting on a happy face each day takes it tole. 
 Sloane and James are madly in love and cling to each other to survive. 
 I don't want to say too much more and ruin the book for anyone, actually I erased this review three times thinking I gave away too much. 
 The Program is wonderfully written and you feel the fear and sadness of Sloane. I found myself crying for no reason several times. And then I was laughing out loud. 
 Everything comes full circle with people from the past and characters changing and evolving. It was brilliant. Absolutely brilliant. 
 I absolutely cannot wait for April when the second book comes out. And I would love to see a novella with Michael Realm. Please, oh please! That would be incredible!

A classic of the noir genre, thus all characters are hard-boiled, cynical, and just don't care, guzzling booze, with a cigarette in the mouth and guns in the holsters. There is not much detecting, Spade keeps stumbling onto things that send him running. The story is good, the conclusion is surprising, the action well-paced. 
 But the characters are sooooo dated. I think at this point of my life I just don't tolerate misogynistic assholes very well. Spade is full of condescension towards every female - they irritate him unless he needs them. To be fair, he bullies men just as much, be it police, criminals or his own friends. He doesn't give a rat's ass about his partner, or his partner's wife, whom he f*cks but otherwise can't stand. The other female is a manipulative bitch who gets her way with sex. 
 Yeah, I know it is noir. But it is downright stupid. The characters are caricatures. If you picked a fight all the time, you would not survive very long in the underworld. We are not supposed to like Spade, but we do supposed to have a reluctant admiration - but all I see is an arrogant, bullying idiot. 
 Marlowe did not have the same reaction from me, so maybe it is not me - maybe it is Hammet.

This was different from what I expected. Part of it I think is because most YA Paranormal I read tends to have romance as well and usually as a strong part of the storyline. This didn't. This was definitely more interested in exploring Mia's new surroundings, her family and the world she was now thrust in as a Demon Catcher. 
 I felt most enthralled in this book when Mia would go into lengthy descriptions or discussions about Milan and the history therein. Beyer's attention to detail whether discussing the everyday mannerisms of the Della Torre family or the horrors that Italian Jews faced during World War II had the same dedicated feeling. Beyer obviously felt deeply for her subject matter and that shines throughout her writing. 
 Of less interest to me was the actual demon hunting. When I hear 'demon hunting' I immediately think of either Buffy or the Winchester brothers--butt kicking heroes who attacked the vicious citizens of the Underworld with sword, fire and crossbow. I did not think bells. Or candles. The demon hunting part was anti-climatic and not quite as tense as I think Beyer wanted. Interesting at first, but anti-climatic.

Anansi Boys is loosely related to American Gods, but each book stands alone and tells an independent story. The main connection is that Anansi is one of the gods we meet in American Gods, often referred to as Mr. Nancy. 
 Anansi himself doesn't really show up in Anansi Boys all that much, but he's referred to a great deal and several stories are told about him. Our main character is Charlie, Anansi's son, who is quite ordinary, shy, and easily intimidated. At the beginning of the book, we read about Charlie's childhood and the things his father Anansi did to embarrass him. Before long, we catch up to Charlie as he's living his adult life, which is quite an ordinary life. Then, of course, something happens, and Charlie's life starts to get pretty strange and not very pleasant. 
 Charlie was a funny and interesting character. He starts off kind of spineless, and I was afraid he would get annoying, but he slowly started to get more assertive. The story was interesting. Between the blatant foreshadowing and the hints, I can't say anything about the story was terribly surprising, but it held my interest. Toward the end, I thought some things happened that stretched the boundaries of credibility, even considering the subject matter. I was really enjoying the book up to a point, but I started feeling a little less enthusiastic by the end. 
 This had a very different tone than American Gods. I enjoyed both books, but for different reasons. By comparison, I thought American Gods was darker, meatier, and more serious. Anansi Boys was lighter, hilariously funny at times, and sometimes downright silly. I couldn't really say which one I liked best. During the first half of this book, I would have said I liked Anansi Boys better. Now that I've finished it, I'm leaning toward American Gods.

This book made me feel so warm and nostalgic for all the magic fantasy novels I read in middle school. The fantasy and nature elements of this world especially reminded me of Tamora Pierce or Shannon Hale. It's a very intuitive, poetic, and sensual kind of magic, a real pleasure to immerse yourself in imagining. The world-building is also so sensual and rich. I wanted to stay in this world a while and really get to know all its nooks and crannies. More importantly, I felt like this world was fleshed out enough for me to sense that it HAD nooks and crannies. It felt vast and historied and altogether lovely. 
 At the same time, the conflict was complex and seemingly overwhelming. The pacing kept me glued to the page. I genuinely cared about the village and the villagers' predicament as well as Agnieszka's personal predicament. 
 The rapid growth of Agnieszka's skill in magic was almost too easy, making her something of a Mary Sue, but I didn't even care because it was a lot of fun anyway. It's kind of like watching a superhero movie--you don't care that Spider-Man suddenly has powers; you just sit back and enjoy it. 
 I have three complaints about this book. 
 1. Several characters seriously needed to be fleshed out more. (Agnieszka's BFF, Kasia, is at the top of my list. She's so central to the plot, and in an emotion-driven way, but... who IS she? Kind of a flat character.) 
 2. The solution to the major conflict of the novel felt a bit too easy given how big of a problem it seemed to be. 
 3. The most forced hetero romance ever between (view spoiler)[Sarkan (hide spoiler)] and Agnieszka. OH MY GOD. I have so many problems with this ship. 
 My feelings about it can basically be summed up as follows: 
 Ugggggghhhhhh no. No no no nonono. 
 Detailed, mildly spoiler-y reasons below the cut. 
 (view spoiler)[FIRST of all, Sarkan is a serial kidnapper. For decades and decades, he's been taking a girl every ten years from Agnieszka's village to keep isolated in his tower for his own comfort. The book implies that because he doesn't rape these girls and because he's a pillar of the community, it's really not that bad of a thing to do to them. Meanwhile, these girls' families live in dread of the Choosing. They don't want to lose their daughters to him, and the daughters don't want to go, either. Sarkan even admits that's largely the point: he wants a maid who can't walk out on him if she wants to. Basically he wants a live-in slave. He turns his girl-of-the-decade into someone powerless to give consent or take it away. It's not rape, as it's not sexual, but it's still a life-altering theft of these girls' autonomy for his own enjoyment. This dark side of Sarkan is a cool plot element and drew me into the story (so many Beauty and the Beast vibes!), and I can appreciate that it made the story a whole lot more interesting. I don't mind that there's a character in this book who acts like this, but it did strike a serious blow to any possibility of me seeing him in a romantic light, and it bugged me that it doesn't feel like Agnieszka/the author was ultimately that bothered by the fact that he's been doing this awful thing. 
 It's later revealed that part of why he takes the girls is also to help him save the village from the Woods by drawing on their connection to the land or whatever, but... okay, even if he does need a villager to live in his tower, he could go about it in a less creepy and controlling way. He could ask for a volunteer (any sex, any age) to help him instead of taking a girl away from her life and her family against her will. 
 So yeah, Sarkan has kidnapped Agnieszka, making whatever relationship that develops between them in the months that follow already iffy. There's a big power difference and some consent issues just from that. Hell, when he grabs her from her village and hauls her to his tower, she's terrified of him. He takes her to the kitchen on the first day and she's legit afraid that he's going to burn her alive in the fireplace. Great start to a relationship, that. 
 Also, Sarkan just sucks as a human being. He insults Agnieszka repeatedly and unnecessarily. Then he also starts magically draining her energy without her consent on a daily basis, to the point where she literally has to crawl away from him across the floor while he watches and fails to give a shit. Meanwhile, she's cut off from her home, her best friend, and her family, so she's lonely, homesick, and bored. Living with him is pretty terrible for her, and he's never even a little bit remorseful or apologetic about that. Before Sarkan realizes Agnieszka is a powerful witch, he's verbally and physically abusive and doesn't value her at all as a person. He acts like she's the scum beneath his shoe and a thorn in his side, and he clearly doesn't give a shit how she feels about anything. 
 Worst of all, one evening Sarkan hosts a male guest (I won't say who b/c spoiler) who decides he's going to rape Agnieszka for political reasons. Now, at this point Agnieszka is a prisoner in Sarkan's tower; she's only there because he took her and locked her up there, so I feel like Sarkan has a responsibility to care for her. Plus, he's her lord; he's supposed to protect the people of the valley in general. Instead, Sarkan KNOWS this attempt at rape is happening and could stop it, but he's okay with it for diplomatic reasons. When Agnieszka defends herself (by herself) against her rapist, only then does Sarkan FINALLY come to intervene, and not because he's at all upset with the rapist. Instead, he's exasperated with Agnieszka for not lying there passively and taking one for the team. He insults her some more at this point for good measure. And his solution to the problem (the problem being that the rapist failed to rape her because she fought back, so the rapist is going to be upset)? He implants a detailed false memory of him successfully raping her in the rapist's mind to make him think that he succeeded, which was so squicky. The whole situation felt gross, but especially Sarkan's attitude throughout it all. 
 Sarkan never apologizes for any of this stuff, by the way, in case you were wondering. 
 Perhaps it's not surprising that Agnieszka gets a little, ahem, worked up from the intimacy of magical collaboration with Sarkan, especially given that he's the only guy she's interacted with for who knows how long (not counting Rape Dude). Even so, from start to finish, there's zero chemistry between Sarkan and Agnieszka. Sarkan is a valuable ally, but I had trouble understanding what either of them saw in the other beyond a growing professional respect for each other as fellow magic-wielders. 
 Oh, and did I mention he's over 150 years old and she's a teenager? Because I feel like that's an important detail. If he didn't magically look like a 20-year-old, I bet you she would be looking for someone her own age instead. When he points it out to her, though, she just laughs it off like he's being silly for worrying about it. This romance is like Twilight 2.0, except that at least there, Bella thought Edward was a fellow student her own age as she was falling for him. The power dynamic in this book is in some ways even creepier than Twilight because Agnieszka KNOWS going into it that Sarkan is an old man, and their relationship dynamic at the time of their first kiss is somewhere between master/servant and teacher/student. 
 Also... why was there a sex scene? Just, why? What did that add to the story? 
 P.S. I was EXTREMELY disappointed that Sarkan ("the Dragon") can't actually transform into a real live dragon. I was hoping for some dragons and I got none. False advertising!! (hide spoiler)]

DH and I are going to Ireland next year, so I thought I would read some fiction set there just to get a taste of the culture, writing, etc. What a novel to start with! 
 As a child, Dublin Detective Rob Ryan was the only witness (and surviving victim) of a crime that claimed his two best friends. Too bad he remembers only a few bits and pieces of it. Now, 20 years later, a girl has been sexually assaulted and murdered in the same remote place--are the crimes connected? It's up to Ryan and his partner Cassie to comb through the threads to uncover the truth. Along the way, we get class differences, city politics, archaeology, and psychological twists and turns. 
 I have to admit I didn't see the end(s) coming, although I did figure out one small piece of it. In this debut novel, French does a wonderful job of capturing both places and times, past and present, and her characters are flawed and believable. Highly recommended, but be in a good emotional place when you read it--that's all I'm going to say.

I love a good Beauty and the Beast story --and this one delivered in every way. My only complaint is that it's over. 
 Sidonie's sister Roberta has amassed an enormous gambling debt and the man she owes it to, is her husband's greatest enemy, Jonas Merrick. There is no way Roberta will be able to pay back the money, so Jonas agrees to let her repay him in trade. What better way to get revenge on his horrible cousin, than to cuckold him? 
 The thing is, Roberta's husband is violently abusive and if he were catch wind of any of this, Roberta's life could be forfeit. So Sidonie agrees to take her place in Merrick's bed. When she arrives at the castle, she is expecting a monster. After all, Merrick is horribly scarred and must be a brute to have put her sister in such a position. But she finds that she barely notices his scars. In fact, she is even drawn to him, and he, to her. 
 Merrick doesn't force Sidonie into his bed. Instead, he makes a deal with her. She'll give him one week to seduce her. It will be her choice whether they make love. And from there begins a seduction that is only partly of the flesh. Because while Sidonie does fall captive to his body, she also ends up connecting to the broken, lonely man within. 
 The development of the story was a bit predictable, but I absolutely 100% did not care. I loved watching their journey. Merrick is so damaged both physically and emotionally. He has been branded a bastard, which has ostracized him, and Roberta's horrible husband --his cousin-- has the title that should have been his. The peerage rejects him, but he holds himself away as well, refusing to let them hurt him. Yet he falls so hard for Sidonie and her innocence, her goodness. He begins to feel his broken heart growing whole again --and I just wanted to climb inside the book and give him a hug. 
 I liked Sidonie. She is practical and loyal. And she has to make some tough choices, with one that you know is going to come back and bite her when it comes out. When it all comes crashing down, it's hard to bear, but it's riveting. I couldn't put it down. 
 Anna Campbell gave me two main characters I truly cared about and a villain easy to hate. The plot was interesting. And the sex was just right. It was hot and plentiful, but it never overshadowed the story. I just... loved it. 
 Rating: A

The book is awesome. My only real complaint is that the ending is a sheer cliff. 
 So we've got Kvothe here, telling his story in three days to a scribe. At first I thought this book would be it, but turns out this is only the first day of the three. There is no real climax yet in Kvothe's story, no ending, it doesn't really go towards anything; this first book is about his early life and "adventures", just a basis for the story to continue on. 
 It's very good though. I don't have a lot of experience with fantasy, so maybe that's why I think it's so great. Towards the end, however, I was waiting for some goal, some enemy or big event or something. About a hundred pages were left when I realized that it wouldn't happen, so it was a little bit disappointing. I could compare it to a TV series: this first book wasn't the first season of a series, but a first episode. 
 I'll go on to the second novel soon, and I hope the ending will be a bit more satisfying there.

Definitely recommended.

Girl Lost by Nazarea Andrews is the first book in the Neverland Lost series. 
 What happens when you can't trust your own mind? When everyone that loves you believes you to be crazy. Gwen has spent years trying to rationalize the "boy". Why she sees him, how he always manages to be there when she needs him most. 
 When she starts school at Northern she meets Peter. The similarities between him and how she remembers the "boy" are uncanny. Peter is how she would picture the "boy" looking as he grew up. 
 But is getting close to him going to cause her to relapse into her crazy space or help her heal? 
 A very twisted turn on the story of Peter Pan, Wendy, and Neverland. I loved it and am excited to read the next part of the story in Forever Found.

Passionate and brutally honest, Ta-Nehisi Coates holds nothing back and reveals his deepest fears for the coming generations of black and other non-white Americans. He is eloquent, lucid, and at times overwhelming, but, above all, his words resound with heartfelt sentiment and truth. 
 He discusses many contemporary tragedies - of children killed in a manner that continues the tragic dominance over black bodies in America - and vividly conveys, from his own and other experiences, the fear that rules the minds of all who live in such a segregated world. 
 He helps answer many questions, of black youth and black movements, and hints at a palpable futility of many nonviolent efforts toward equal civil rights for all. One gets a clear sense of a sentiment that nothing can and will change - for generations to come. He offers no false hope and instead hopes only to lead his own son to consciousness through his work. 
 An intense but easy read, highly recommended.

 An extremely impressive debut novel! Imagine if Ellen Kushner's 'Riverside' novels were set in an analogue of 1920's Germany?

 The story involves spies and double agents at a popular decadent nightclub; and the complexities and betrayals spawned by the intersection of inclination and obligation. I didn't find any of the characters to be sympathetic - but they were all interesting.

Amid nepotism, corruption, party politics, murder and hedonism, Xiaolong introduces the party's rising star Inspector Chen who often quotes poems from Tang dynasty and writes his own on the side. 
 What starts off as a routine murder mystery slowly morphs to a study of 90s China, Shanghai specifically. Through the eyes of Chen readers view the cramped living spaces, common cooking area, crawling traffic, living situations of ordinary government workers, pride and adoration of a Chinese housewife and life in general. Xiaolong takes his time in unwinding the murder as he first opens the city to (non-Chinese) readers and gives a taste of Shanghai. 
 In fact it becomes clear who the killer is somewhere in the middle of the book. Xiaolong shows no sense of urgency in solving the case as he moves his characters in a pace similar to what would have happened in the 90s. It makes the experience all the more fascinating as we struggle to move things ahead just like Inspector Chen and his assistant Yu. 
 The novel is set couple of years after the infamous Tiananmen Square protests which shows an evolving China. The narration begins right when the changes are set to motion and the officials are trying to deal with repercussions of decisions made in previous few decades. 
 This isn't a book that's meant to be read in one sitting. The liberal use of old Chinese poetry draws parallels to the narration and makes the atmosphere heavy. The words linger for several pages, just like Jasmine tea that many of these characters seem to enjoy.

In North America's severely depressing future all the outlying districts of the Capitol must participate every year in the Hunger Games. In order to do so they must supply one boy and one girl between the ages of twelve and eighteen (known as tributes) who will enter the arena and fight until only one is left standing. It's purpose? To keep the districts in line and serve as a constant reminder of who's really in charge. This year for the Everdeen family the unthinkable happens, twelve year old Prim gets picked to go to the Games. In an act of desperation and sisterly love, her sixteen year old sister, Katniss volunteers to take her place. And so begins a horrific nightmare for Katniss (and her co-tribute Peeta) as she does everything that she can to stay alive. 
 Browsing through the bookstore the other day I came across the Hunger Games and thought that it was about time I see what all the fuss was about. Now I totally understand. The adventures of Katniss and Peeta and their struggles in the Hunger Games are addictive! This book is pure action, just when you think it's slowing down a bit (so you can process the craziness that's just happened) it throws you through another loop. Katniss and Peeta are perfect co-characters. They play off one another's strengths and weaknesses and you can't help but fall in love with them. Katniss is tough and a survivor. You want to root for her and her incredible ingenuity and bravery. Peeta is caring and thoughtful. He is the perfect ying to her yang. 
 This review was really easy to write because put simply, I loved this book. It keeps you guessing, its entertaining, the characters are great and the story is perfect, not intertwined with filler to make it longer. If you're a fan of dystopian fiction or adventure stories check this book out. Make sure you pick up the second at the same time though because you will want to read it right away!
Pretty enjoyable, had me mulling and musing over perception, senses and how we define reality.
lol I love snicket's commentary in this one. Another enjoyable instalment of the series!

I debated whether to give this 4 or 5 stars, but I can't think of a single thing I didn't enjoy about this book. I'm so glad I decided to read it, as I was hesitant due to the length. Loved Alma's life story, each of the different stages of her life were so interesting, and even her father's youth and background were fun to learn about. I learned more about botany, Tahiti, moss, and botanical drawing than I ever expected to, and I enjoyed it. I loved that she didn't get everything she wanted in life, but she still had a long, fulfilling, interesting life. I also enjoyed the long span of history that her life (and her father's life) covered. 
 Excellent audio narration, the voices and accents were all perfect.

These books are just so much fun. The prose style is nothing special, but the pacing is great. This second book was better than the first because there's more consistency in and development of the characters. It's hard even to put my finger on why I'm enjoying the series so much - it just feels light and engaging, charming, suspenseful, and dreamy. (I have to say, I also really like the cover designs.)

Eh. I'm not a huge fan of Sarah Dessen's writing style, but I decided to give Lock and Key a try anyway. I'm not dissapointed, exactly, but I don't think it was very good like others seem to. Something that bothered me exteremely, though I don't really know why? She used the word "flat" to describe how something was said way too often. Like I said, I don't know why but for some reason it just got on my nerves. Every time I saw it I seemed to cringe. Just one of those things. Anyway, I wouldn't necessarily recommend the book to anyone, but I don't think it was awful. I could relate a little to Ruby and the other characters were great, but I think it could have been improved upon.

I anticipated this book for literally years after DFW's heartbreaking suicide, and wasn't disappointed. 
 I don't recommend this as a first DFW book, because it's long, and tedious -- on purpose. The book chronicles the histories and current lives of a group of IRS agents. It spends a lot of time discussing boredom and going in-depth into the bureaucratic ins and outs and laws of taxes. The point of this, from what I understand, is not to harm or confuse the reader, but to bring the reader in so they can experience the tedium the characters suffer firsthand. Which sounds like it sucks, but there are trademark DFW chapters, most notably the back-stories and portions that entirely unattributed conversations, that are laugh-out loud brilliant. Nerdy, and immersive, and a wonderful conclusion to DFW's work.

Holy hell. Did that just happen? What.the.effity.eff. That book blew my tiny mind... 
 I will not go into details about this book. I can't. My mind is mush and my heart is sore. I need to recover. I will just tell you to start with book #1 - Blood Warrior, #2 Half Black Soul & #3 The Rise. 
 "Everything that has a life must lose it eventually. What matters is that it was a life worth living." 
 ..."Is it Kayden? Is it worth living?" 
 Kayden tilted my chin up with his fingers and kissed my lips, and the answer to my question was evident to me in his touch. "Oh yes, my Warrior," he said, his golden eyes burning into my own. "I really think it is." ~ Conversation between Alexa (Sun Warrior) & her Libra - Kayden 
 If you've read my reviews of books 1 to 3 you know for me this series is freaking EPIC. The final installent was no different. I had tears of laughter, and of grief. 
 From the prologue. 'In the end, we all die. This is not of question. Inarguable. No mystery lies here. The mystery dwells in two questions: How long will our story be, and what will be left in the pages?' to the last sentence on the last page 'And with her note in my pocket and her love in my heart, I am able to live.' 
 There were time where I literally had to set the book down and convince myself to keep going and rip off the bandaid really quick. It was that intense. 
 'Waiting to be attacked. Waiting to attack. Running. Fighting. Hurting. In that moment it seemed to be such a pitiful existence; an existence in vain.' 
 The ending, FMD. My face is puffy. My pillow is soggy. And my clothes are wet from the salty tears that poured down my cheeks, throat and onto my shirt. It was more insane than my wildest dreams and yet the heart break and sobs doesn't mean Ms Gordon could have done it any different. Where others would have copped out, she followed the course that was mapped & followed through on what we were all praying would never come to pass. 
 'How is one broken thing supposed to fix another? 
 With love. 
 Yes, love. That was what I was fighting for. That was what I was living for. And maybe, not so tragically, that was what I would die for.' 
 One word, genius. She writes a monster and the blackness in ones soul as if she has lived it and love as if she has plenty. Bravo Ms Gordon... 
 "My love for you," I whispered, "may very well be the greatest thing that this world has ever known, and because of it, the story of my life will be eternally beautiful." ~ Alexa to Nell 
 I can't wait to read about this girl we met. Bring on Shooting Stars! 
 'A chick that looked as kick ass as this, I may have liked if given the opportunity. But her next words said that there would be no such opportunity. ~ Alexa thinks as she meets Surah

I've waited a long time for the latest three christine Feehan books and they didn't disappoint. They changed what was becoming repetitive which was understandable by this point (this is book 26) and she introduced the lycans. She also had the dragonseeker women and they are my favorite's in this series. 
 So with an all new direction and with all the other Carpathians joining in it made this book and the 2 presiding novels worth reading to any fans who were getting a bit tired of the dark series. The werewolves were good and the werewolf/Carpathian cross an exciting new addition.

If you grew up reading the fantastic Lioness Quartet by Tamora Pierce like I did, then this series is sure to reignite your love of fantastical worlds and badass heroines. The series follows Karigan as she traverses across Sacoridia as one of the King's Green Riders, couriers of the Kings most important messages and letters. Gifted with the ability to disappear through time and space, she saves the King and Sacoridia numerous times with both skill and ingenuity as we as readers learn more about this strange land. 
 Britain does a fantastic job building this world, and as the series progresses she peels more and more layers back, revealing a land long torn apart by the various races that call it home. 
 Lovers of the Song of Ice and Fire will enjoy the political intrigue that is interlaced with magic and mystery. These novels do a good job balancing love plotlines and magic, with neither outweighing the other. While some of the scenes almost tend to weigh in on cheesy, with many of the characters painfully falling on the "too perfect" side of the spectrum, none of which having any endearing flaws, I still find myself rooting for these characters. 
 While the first two books are amazing and keep you hooked with every page, the third and fourth books are not as successful at keeping the reader gripped to the pages. The first two books also move much faster, covering more time in much fewer pages, while for the last two books Britain uses much more descriptive detail, making most scenes rather arduous to read. While still interesting to read, the last two books tend to curb your appetite for more of Sacoridia. The next book, Mirror Sight, is schedule to be released sometime this year, and I hope Britain "makes up for lost time" with it, creating a much more fluid and gripping read than The High King's Tomb and Blackveil. *fingers crossed* 
 Overall, if you're looking for a good series to tuck your face in and fall in love with, despite some flaws, The Green Rider series will perfectly suffice, if not exceed your expectations.

This book was a blur of Telar, IIC, the Array, the Cradle and the Lens, and demons and the devil himself! But I read most of it in one sitting, so at least it kept me interested. This book is a continuation of the previous, in which nothing got resolved. In this one, finally!! Things get taken care of! The good guys triumph and the bad guys lose! 
 Or do they? 
 There is leftover plot for the next book but at least there's a sense of conclusion from the main storylines. And I see the shadow of a love story brewing there too. So I read on...

I don't even know what to say, I am that blown away. 
 I love this series. I re-read all the books in preparation for the release of the final book. 
 For kicks and giggles, I checked my iBooks library at 12:03AM on Monday morning to see if my pre-order had arrived, and it did, so I started reading. I think I started crying in chapter two or three and cried off and on all that day while reading. Everything from quiet tears to put the book down and sob, ugly crying. 
 Ms. Halle has completed the journey of Dex and Perry beautifully. The final adventure is very heartbreaking, terrifying, and above all, satisfying. Do I want more, yes I do, but the series doesn't need more books. I just don't want to let these amazing characters go. So, I'm going to go through and re-read again. Starting at the beginning, letting myself be swept away by these amazing books. 
 I recommend Experiment in Terror all the time and I don't know if people are put off because they are Paranormal Romance. If you are put off because of that, please don't be. The main characters are not otherworldly. They are ghost hunters, and can be best described (by Ms. Halle herself) as a sort of Mulder and Sculley. The first book is still FREE on iTunes, so pick it up and try it. You will be HOOKED! 
 Darkhouse, here I come again.

This could have been a great book if someone didn't come up with the splendid idea to insert an enormous cliffhanger! That really REALLY sucks Katy! If someone had told me about it beforehand I definitely wouldn't have started reading this until the second book had also been released. 
 It's also completely unnecessary in my opinion. It's a romance novel. Come on. 
 Super frustrating. When I look back on this book in a couple months all I'll remember if the abrupt and unsatisfactory ending. 
 The story itself was quite alright, very predictable, but that's to be expected in this genre. 
 My recommendation: Do not read until you can read the second book right after.

When I found out that the premise of the book is about a matchmaker and a divorce lawyer, I knew I need to read it. I'm always game for a romantic comedy to lighten up my day. Too much angst is bad for my well-being. 
 Slade Montgomery is a divorce lawyer, cocky, overbearing and cynical to love in general. After going through his own divorce and witnessing his little sister, Jane spiraling to the deep end after being dump, he no longer believe in happily ever after. 
 "Romantic love is just a mirage - a glass of ice-cold Coca-Cola in the middle of the desert. You stumble and reach to quench the thirst, then find the glass vanishes right through your fingers." 
 That was Slade's idea of love. Although he came off as such a tough lawyer, he had a soft side when it came to his sister's welfare. Best brother ever, 
 "Are you still upset over your breakup? We can go slash his tires, get drunk, and watch chick flick movies." 
 When he found out that Jane had sign up to Kinnection's matchmaking program, all he can think of is Jane will be getting hurt again by some scumbag, while getting con by these so-called matchmaker. He decided to sign up himself to spy on his sister and prove that Kinnection is nothing but a scam. 
 Kate Seymour the co-owner of Kinnection along with her best buddies, Kennedy and Arilyn. She inherited a special gift that can help her match two soul mates that are meant to be together. Yet, her own love life is miserable with Robert, her rescued dog as company. When she met the insufferable Slade who had a total opposite beliefs with her, she felt a spark that she can't denied. 
 The first half of the book was a romcom at its best. Kate let Slade to sign up with them as long as he is open and willing to accept their advice in this matchmaking process. There were so many hilarious lines, mostly from Slade, when Kate tried to coach him on how to date for a long term relationship, instead of a one night stand. 
 "Sex is a way we can find out if we're both compatible. This isn't Victorian England, for God's sake!" 
 Who knew matchmaking can be such a tedious process, 
 "Relationships aren't all fluff and fun. Is tough work." 
 "At least you're preparing them to be strong when the divorce happens." 
 Slade stated down on how his ideal woman should be. But it seems like what he want was everything opposite from what Kate is. Due to Kate's gift, whenever they touch, there was an instant spark that can light up the city. Slade was so drawn to her and Kate keep telling herself the man was all wrong for her. She can't be with someone who don't believe in love. 
 "Big Ivy school doesn't impress me. Even blonde cheerleaders can get into law school there." 
 "If you're even trying to cite Legally Blonde to me, I will sue you. I barely made it out of that place alive, and I can assure you, there were no sorority girls there." 
 I just love Slade, he came off really domineering, know what he wants and grab it. The internal sexual frustration they both experience was borderline paranormal, I can't help but snickered. I guess Kate read too much Black Dagger Brotherhood. 
 "I need to change your intake form. Seems there's a bit of dom in you." 
 "Funny, lately I've been feeling like the slave in this relationship." 
 When Slade had to acknowledge that Kate needs more than what he can provide her, things turn ugly between them. Kate believes in HEA, Slade believe in divorce. I think they both should compromise a little and meet each other half way. 
 Love the little side story and possible love triangle between Kate's friend, Gen and her Dr. McDreamy and Wolfe. Sounds like something interesting is going down there and can't wait for their story. Kennedy and Arilyn also provided so much needed girl power to have Kate's back whenever she needed. 
 I took away 1 star for the back and forth between Kate and Slade at the second half of the story. I wish they would just stop over thinking and accept what fate brought them. And the ending was too abrupt for my liking. I usually prefer at least the last 20% to have some lovey dovey scene. Love that cute epilogue, though. Quite an unique touch. 
 "I'm not looking for forever. But I am looking for someday."
This was well-written, but after not really liking Just One Day or Just One Year, this was more just closure than something I really liked reading.

Wow! 
 Happily ever after doesn't mean a lifetime of perfection. I don't think anyone believes that happily ever after means there are no unhappy days, even unhappy years. It means loving forever, despite all the many reasons it's easier not to. 
 There is this movie with Robin Williams, "What dreams may come". You most likely remember it. Chris loses his children, his life and suddenly he is in heaven and he is not happy because his wife is somehow in hell, lost in her crazy mind. And he tries to find her, he keeps looking for her because heaven without his only love equals personal hell. He knows that she exists, he knows that she is real and she needs his help because he simply believes this fact: 
 What's true in our minds is true, whether some people know it or not. 
 And he finds her. 
 You may ask, 'why is this relevant to this book?' 
 Well, this book is not what you think it is. This book is basically a journey to the human mind. 
 Yes, it is romance. 
 Yes, it talks about pure love and commitment. 
 Yes, it is about two people who have fallen in love. 
 Yes, there is happily ever after. 
 But nothing is what is seems. 
 But nobody is who you think he/she is. 
 But there are twists and turns that they may make you gasp "WTF" many times. 
 When the main male character from the book says to Lily: 
 If you go away, then I'll come and find you, even if it means I have to get lost for a while, too 
 , 
 I think I was crying harder than the first time I watched the Robin Williams' movie and there was this scene when he finds his broken wife and tells her: Annie, I'm here babe, I still exist. 
 Please, be open-minded when you start this book!

4.5

 Overall I liked the characters and the original story idea. It was a nice quick read :)

"Fate has plans for us all," Inej said quietly. "And sometimes fate needs a little assistance." 
 LEIGH BARDUGO YOU BEAUTIFUL QUEEN. I honestly think I'm going to have to rank this a tiny bit behind ACOMAF on my favorites list for 2016. This kind of book is what should set the bar for all future YA fantasy. There was an amazing plot, great writing and world building, and the characters were both memorable and realistic (well I honestly pretend they're older than they are, but overall). 
 "I can't believe we broke out of the Ice Court but we're trapped in our own town," Wylan said. It didn't seem right. 
 Going into this, I wasn't quite sure what to expect. There aren't many YA fantasy duologies out there and because the first book packed so much intense action and plotting, I really wasn't sure how everything was going to be wrapped up in just one more book. I'm almost glad it was, though. Don't get me wrong--would I love to see an entire series with all of these goons? Hell yeah I would. But sometimes I feel like when a plot this outrageous with characters of this magnitude gets stretched out, things go wrong. Without spoiling anything, I'll tell you that this book did not disappoint me in any way. I laughed, I gasped, I cried. This book will make you feel and it won't be easily forgotten and I think that's extremely important. 
 "I would come for you," he said, and when he saw the wary look she shot him, he said it again. "I would come for you. And if I couldn't walk, I'd crawl to you, and no matter how broken we were, we'd fight our way out together--knives drawn, pistols blazing. Because that's what we do. We never stop fighting." 
 This books picks up pretty shortly after the first. Everyone is scrambling to gather information about where Inej is on the DL since they have pretty much been booted out of their own city. 
 *Spoilers Ahead* 
 I was sooooo glad to see that Nina was still surviving her brush with parem and was super surprised that they got Inej back so fast. I mean...I didn't doubt their abilities but I just was initially surprised that Bardugo had it happen so fast. In the end though I see why it did happen as it did. They needed that encounter with Van Eck right away because it played into later schemes. 
 "Calm down, Matthias." 
 "Perhaps I'll write a story about insatiable Ravkans who like to get drunk and take their clothes off and make unseemly advances toward hapless Fjerdans." 
 "Now that sounds like a party." Matthias shook his head, but she could see a smile tugging at his lips. She decided to push the advantage. "We could play," she murmured, quietly enough so that no one around them could hear. 
 "We most certainly could not." 
 "At one point he bathes her." 
 Matthias' steps faltered. "Why would he--" 
 "She's tied up, so he has to." 
 "Be silent." 
 "Already giving orders. That's very barbarian of you. Or we could mix it up. I'll be the barbarian and you can be the princess. But you'll have to do a lot more sighing and trembling and biting your lip." 
 "How about I bite your lip?" 
 "Now you're getting the hang of it, Helvar." 
 Ohhhhh the schemes. You know you are reading a good book when you just sit there and are so fully immersed you think more along the lines of "wow Kaz is so fucking smart, how does he think of everything?" when really it's Bardugo! HOW DOES SHE DO IT. I swear her and Maas must get together and trade their craziest scheming ideas. Whatever the case...I WAS STILL SURPRISED AT EVERY TURN. And as a sequel and final book in a series should be, everything was so much bigger, better, and more complex. Gahhhhh it was insane. Like this isn't exactly a light hearted book that can be read over and over again when you have spare time but I guarantee you I will be re-reading for many years to come. 
 Jesper leaned in and said, quietly enough that no one else could hear, "I can read to him." "He has a very soothing baritone," added Wylan, and then the guards were hauling his father down the aisle. 
 Ships: I WILL GO DOWN WITH EVERY SINGLE ONE OF THESE SHIPS OMG. The ending with Kaz and Inej=pure gold, when Jesper and Wylan FINALLY KISS=pure gold, every single fucking thing with Nina and Matthias= PURE FUCKING GOLD. And even though my heart is heavy and I am mourning for Matthais, I was prepared for one of them dying. Did I think it was going to be him? No. Did I bawl my eyes out? Embarrassingly so, yes. I will cherish every moment they had together though, especially the scene where they were on their way to the Ravkan embassy. Sigh...damn you Bardugo. (Can we also talk about how adorable it was when Jesper's dad told Wylan he was rooting for them because Wylan is good for his son??!? I melted) 
 Like it or not, Ketterdam--brutal, dirty, hopeless Ketterdam--had become her home. And she would defend it. She knew its rooftops the way she knew the squeaky stairs of the Slat, the way she knew the cobblestones and alleys of the Stave. She knew every inch of this city like a map of her heart. 
 Finally, for the King and Queen of Ketterdam. Kaz and Inej. I came to the conclusion toward the end of the book that if Six of Crows was mainly Kaz's book, that this one was for Inej. She was missing, and she was rescued and we got to see how essential she was in the group. We got to see more of her flashbacks and her internal struggles which made my heart ache for her. While I don't think her and Kaz will ever have anywhere close to a traditional relationship, that ending was so satisfying. I honestly thought that it just wasn't going to happen for them. But it did and it was wonderful AND HE HELD HER HAND AND HELD HER AND FOUND HER FUCKING PARENTS OMGGGGGGG. These two...are so, so special to me. I am so glad to have read about them. 
 Kaz as a whole is probably one of the most complex characters that I have ever read about. I think that Bardugo is just really good at writing anti-heroes. There were a few times that the reader is let to believe that Kaz has done something extra horrible but then come to find that he actually didn't and just made the whole thing up for some reason. Outwardly he doesn't show affection, doesn't really get close in with the crew and only seems to want fame and fortune. He slips though from time to time. His moral compass is decidedly gray. I actually really liked the conversation that he and Inej had towards the end about how he thought she wanted to make him out as a good man and the hero of Ketterdam and she told him she just wanted him to be himself. He was fine with him being a little nasty as long as it meant that he used his reputation to get the especially horrible people out of their city. I actually am glad, too, that he wasn't just magically healed with it came to touching Inej. He tried, but it obviously was still bothering him. That's how real world is though. People who have experienced that level of psychological trauma don't just become healed when they fall in love. It wouldnl't have been right for either one of them. Though I did appreciate the hopeful openness of it all. Inej would fight for him but let him heal on his own and I really respected that. 
 Free. To live as she wished. To seek forgiveness for her sins. To pursue her purpose. Would she miss this place? This crowded mess of a city she'd come to know so well, that had somehow become her home? She felt certain she would. So tonight, she would perform for her city, for the citizens of Ketterdam, even if they did not know to applaud. 
 Finally--I don't know about any of you guys, but towards the end I was starting to get really worried that while the scheme with Van Eck would be completed...that the conflict with jurda parem would not. I was kind of right..but..it was okay for now. I mean the book still was wrapped up and felt like a conclusion to me--I didn't feel that anything was lacking. BUT. I have a theory. Jurda parem is a really big deal in the Grisha world...and while Kuwei won't be selling out the recipe, that still doesn't mean things are over. The Shu still have some and they have those modified people that are supreme warriors. That isn't just going to go away. I think that if Bardugo is willing to stick around in this world, that a series with Nikolai will continue with that threat. AND I NEED IT SO BAD. I hope that that comes to be a real thing. If not though, I will be fully satisfied with this beautiful series and its characters that she has already given us. They will be in my heart for a very long time.

Honestly I'm torn on how to rate this. But mostly I am just befuddled as to how this storyline possibly warrants multiple books. If this was one and done - it would have been a fun read. As it is - it feels like the story's being dragged out because a trilogy is expected these days. I wish it wasn't. This premise is fun and I enjoyed reading much of it.

This one is my favorit! 
 Zsadist, i love you!!

As usual, Diana Wynne Jones' imagination runs rampant, giving us a fun adventure with lots of amazing ideas packed in. I want to know what a butter pie tastes like, more than anything, but all of it was interesting and had me trying to puzzle it all out. 
 It wasn't surprising in any way, to me anyway, because it somehow seemed very typical of Diana Wynne Jones. But it was fun, and hooked me in well. 
 Not my favourite of her books so far, but that would be difficult to decide anyway...

I'm giving The King 5 stars, not because it was the best book I've ever read, but because J. R. Ward gets so many things right with this installment. I haven't been as enthralled with the last 5 books as I was with the first 6, but The King was a pleasant reminder of why I love this series and story. 
 The main storyline is of course, The King. Wrath's throne is in jeopardy. He drifting apart from his wife and he's been retreating into himself. I was reminded of the Wrath from Dark Lover, the last purebred vampire we all fell in love with back at the start of the series. 
 Beth wants a baby and Wrath's reasons for not wanting a child are presented to the reader in a series of flashbacks that explain quite a bit about why he feels that way. Beth is just as feisty with Wrath as she's always been, and it took me back to what I love in this series. 
 The subplots of Assail and Sola, Trez and iAm (I'm starting to get interested here after 12 books) and Xcor and Layla all kept from crowding the center stage for the most part, while moving these stories forward. I like drug-addicted Assail and his feelings for Sola and I'm curious to see how that will end up, although I could care less about the drug dealing stuff. And I thought there was some humor associated with Xcor in this that made me smile a little, although someone needs to find a way to get some sense into Layla. But I didn't find the way that J. R. Ward cuts to another storyline as annoying in this book as in the previous installment. 
 What I loved the most about The King was the beautiful character arc we get to see with Wrath. I loved seeing where he started and what sort of ruler he chose to be. It was just lovely, but made me feel also like this book was an ending of sorts.

I was a little disappointed by this one. I really wanted to love it. I enjoyed the southern elements (talking about the city and the culture), but I found that the story and the characters fell flat for me.

 I seriously love Kristen Ashley, and always love everything she writes. Kaleidoscope is no different, and therein lies the problem. It's not a big problem, definitely not a problem that would keep me from reading anything she writes, down to and possibly including her grocery list. Although all of her books feature different characters, most of the hot & uber-alphas are interchangeable. I like the way they talk and don't want that to change, I just wish there were more distinction between them. Like I said, a very small annoyance that I may have never paid much attention to if it hadn't been pointed out.

I really hated most of this book. It's very slow and the plot doesn't feel like a serious plot. I kept waiting for the plot/conflict to become clear. I did like the last 20-30% of the book, but the first 70% was a chore to get through. Very long and slow and a lot of recapping what happened in previous books, well past the standard 30-50 pages of exposition. 
 I'm glad to have finished this book and it felt like it took me an eternity to get through. The date listed as my start date is incorrect, I started this a couple of weeks before. It probably took me a solid 3 weeks to read this, where the first two books in the series each took me a couple of days. Plain Kate is a plainly wonderful, dark fairytale about a girl and her cat. 
 The setting is based on Slavic mythology and feels like the middle ages. It's a time of superstition and witch hunting. Whoever sticks out from the norm, by his looks or by an enormous talent, easily becomes the target of accusation and must fear for his life. Main character Kate is exactly this kind of easy scapegoat, she looks different and is a highly skilled carver. With her father dies all the protection she had, she loses everything and can only run ... and run some more as she encounters one blow of fate after the other. 
 Plain Kate is indeed a dark, sad story. The atmosphere reminded me of Kino's Journey, while quite different stories per se, they both are a journey to the darkest depths of the human soul. The humans in Plain Kate are selfish, unjust and cruel. They accuse whoever they can find. They trample the weak, to ease their own fears. But there is always also a tiny ray of light, one person who does not judge, one who helps, that restores your faith in humankind, if only a little. 
 The writing is very strong, the characters have distinct voices and grow as the story progresses. Kate, especially, is a wonderful main character. She has a particular, impressive way of standing up for herself and I liked the way she was conflicted at the end, about sacrificing something she loves in order to save a bunch of strangers, who kill so-called witches. Very realistic. Of course, Taggle is also an awesome character. His sense of humor helps lighten the overall dark mood a bit. 
 Plain Kate is a book that can really make you think and will leave a lasting impression. It is smart, profound, well-researched and well written. This is the kind of YA novel (according to the author's homepage it is YA) I want to see more of. Highly recommended for everybody, unless you are looking for a light and fun read, because Plain Kate will most likely make you at least a bit sad.
