 I... I am not alright. 
 I was not alright when i finished A Darker Shade of Magic, I was not alright while I was waiting for this book, and I am most certainly not alright with waiting a full year (at least!!) until getting the third book in this emotional roller coaster of an incredible series. 
 I hate you, V.E. Schwab. But I would also gladly sell my soul to you for even a glimpse at that next book. Please. 
 Right. The beginning. Where in the world do I start. 
 The Characters 
 Kell was definitely my favorite character in this book, but Lila, Rhy, and Alucard were all right behind him. The character development in A Gathering of Shadows is absolutely incredible, and by the middle of the book, I wanted to simultaneously hug all of them and go on wild, cutthroat adventures with them as well. Still, I have a certain thing for badass red-haired magicians with a chip on their shoulder and a name starting with K (*cough* I'm still waiting for Kvothe's next adventure, Rothfuss), and his fragility along with his occasional bouts of darkness in this book was exactly what I was craving for in his character, not that I didn't love him in aDSoM as well. His relationship with Rhy, too, is the perfect bromance and all the more perfect with the angst on both sides of their new, special...bond. I mean: 
 Rhy tugged the folded piece of fabric from his pocket, and handed it over. The cloth was red, and when he unfolded it, he saw an image of a rose in black and white. 
 "How subtle," said Kell tonelessly. 
 "You could at least pretend to be grateful." 
 "And you couldn't have picked something a little more...I don't know...imposing? A serpent? A great beast? A bird of prey?" 
 "A bloody handprint?" retorted Rhy. "Oh, what about a glowing black eye?" 
 Kell glowered. 
 "You're right," continued Rhy, "I should have just drawn a frowning face. But then everyone would know it's you." 
 How can you not love those two? And speaking of pairs with Rhy... (view spoiler)[ I didn't think I'd find something I shipped as much as Lila/Kell, but oh my god that scene with Rhy and Alucard. I was reading the book in public, and I'm pretty sure I visibly swooned. So if you saw me, just know that I was reading a steamy scene between (former, and hopefully future) gay lovers <3 (hide spoiler)] Rhy had a soft part in my heart from the last book, but dear god did he take that soft part with his flirtatious ways and rip it apart with his angst. Every bit of it was sweet, painful, and absolutely incredible. I swear, V.E. Schwab is drawing these scenes straight out of my character fantasies. 
 Moooving on before this review passes the character limit, let's talk about Lila. 
 Thief, Pirate, Man, Magician, Lila is badass no matter what mask she puts on. I didn't dislike her in aDSoM, but she wasn't incredibly dear to me. In this book, she was the tough as nails female mc so many books these days are so severely lacking. 
 "No," said Lila in decisive, if broken, Arnesian. "I don't share beds-" 
 "Tac?" teased Vasry, dropping his chest on the floor. "Surely we can work something ou-" 
 "-because I have a habit of stabbing people in my sleep," she finished coolly. 
 Vasry had the decency to pale a little. 
 Her POV did a lot more to help me understand her in this book than it did the last one, and all that character development sets her at a solid #2 on my favorite characters of aGoS list. Even though I loved all of them. Don't tell me who to love, I can hug them all if I want to. (nevermind the fact that none of them are real) 
 And I don't think I need to say anything about Lila/Kell. They're perfect, their relationship is perfect, the slow burn is as wonderful as a slow burn can be. 
 Plot 
 As some other reviewers have said, the first 40-60% or so of this book is a little slow, but personally, I thought the slow pacing suited the book well. But when the action hits, oh boy does it hit. You can physically feel the tension building, and I felt physical pain when it all hit the fan. And of course, even more of it when it left us with nothing but that cliffhanger. 
 The Element Games were wonderful, and really introduced the reader more to the world and what magic is capable of. Also plenty of badass Kell, badass Lila, and badass fighting in general. In floating arenas. As I said, wonderful. 
 Still, there were a few things I had issues with. I was a bit disappointed at the (view spoiler)[ abruptness of the ending, though I understand why it came to that. Kell going with Okja straight out of the blue felt very abrupt to me, and even if he wasn't in a very sound state of mind, it doesn't sound like something he would do considering he's never seen her before and she's clearly there for nefarious purposes. I have to say though, poor Holland. For an antagonist, I really can't stop feeling sorry for him when his sole desire is just to have a mind of his own and fix the only world he's ever called home. (hide spoiler)] In the end, I really did feel like I'd been reading 509 pages of buildup for a giant climax to occur in the next book, albeit incredibly well written and engaging buildup. Hence the 4 star rating, despite really /really/ enjoying the book. 
 Overall, if you love badass yet dark and flaw-filled characters that will crawl their ways into your heart and make a mess of it, gorgeous writing and descriptions of a world that will take your breath away, pirates, magic, and cats, pick this book up right away. Well, A Darker Shade of Magic first if you haven't read that, but if you haven't, where have you been? It was an emotional ride from start to finish, and I'll be clinging to it until the next book finally comes out. 
 And you know, attempting to drown my feelings about that cliffhanger in chocolate. That too.

 Marie Antoinette, Serial Killer was one of my most highly anticipated fall books and I was so excited when I got approved for an e-ARC through Netgalley. I couldn't wait to get started on it. Unfortunately, Marie Antoinette, Serial Killer didn't live up to my expectations.

I received an ARC of this book from NetGalley in exchange for my unbiased opinion. 
 The Girls is the story of Evie (now in middle age) looking back at herself as a 14-year-old girl in 1969, getting drawn in to a cult because of how much she admired and wanted the attention of one of the girls in it, Suzanne. Evie's parents are recently divorced, her dad now living with his girlfriend and her mom mostly absent as she tries to win the affections of a new boyfriend; this leaves Evie with almost no parental guidance for her summer before high school. After Evie and her best friend get in a fight, Evie has nothing to fill her time until she meets Suzanne and is invited to start spending time at The Ranch. There, Evie quickly falls into a lifestyle it's hard to imagine any 14-year-old should (drugs, sex) or would want to (eating half rotten food, a general lack of hygiene) take part in. 
 The story itself was extremely disturbing at times. However, it was very well written. My main complaint is that while I like the idea of Evie looking back as an adult at her time with the cult, the parts of the story that took place in the present took me out of the story. I didn't feel like Julian and Sasha added anything to the story.

 The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald is one book that requires no introduction. Considered to be the pinnacle of American Literature, it is an ode to the America of the Roaring 20's or the 'Jazz Age' as Fitzgerald called it. The book has influenced generations of readers since its first publication in 1925 and continues to be groundwork for modern American literature. 
 It is narrated by the ever so amiable protagonist Nick Carraway, a young and thoughtful man from 'West Egg' who moves to the east to make it on his own. Nick begins his tale by informing the reader of a little bit of his own history. He also mentions how he is inclined to reserve all judgements when interacting with someone and hence strange people are attracted to him and end up confiding in him. This gives us a sense of foreboding of how the strange new peoplehe is introduced to, within the time frame of the novel, are also drawn to him. 
 On moving to East egg, Nick reconnects with his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom Buchanan. Daisy and Tom are dissatisfied with their marriage but are still tied together by their mutual love for decadence and gaiety. Daisy is described as quite the beauty with a charismatic albeit careless air about her while Tom is a victim of one of the most derisive remarks ever made in American Literature: 
 "Her husband - one of those men who reach such an acute limited excellence at twenty-one that everything afterward savors of anti-climax." 
 What sets the story in motion is Nick's increasing curiosity about his wealthy and mysterious neighbour, Jay Gatsby, the eponymous hero of the novel. Gatsby has a reputation that reaches far and wide and has stories told about him in varying degrees of gossip, in spite of the fact that not many people have personally interacted with him. After a breezy mention in a conversation at Daisy's house, Jay Gatsby is introduced in the novel as a solitary figure standing in his lawn looking at what is described as 'a single green light, minute and far away.' 
 Gatsby is especially known for throwing lavish and opulent parties in his magnificent mansion but among the throngs of people that attend these events, little fact is known about him. Later on, Nick is invited to one such soiree and through a friend of Daisy's he is informed of a rather strange request from Gatsby. The story picks up pace from there and we are introduced to what is considered to be one of the most complicated web of relationships, penned down in a strong, grand style of writing. Gatsby's history with Daisy is revealed and his obsession with her forms the crux of this tale. 
 On the surface, The Great Gatsby is a simple tale of love lost but what makes it deserving of praise is the marvelous manner of storytelling and use of literary devices. The book is generous with splendid characterisations, personification of colours and lucid descriptions. 
 Fitzgerald is capable of handling numerous themes framed within a comparatively simplistic plot. The affluence of America before the Great Depression forms the backdrop for this story of a man consumed by his past and his dedication to making a future out of it. Gatsby is a man who has everything and is still discontent as he sets his sights on things he cannot have. Fitzgerald delves into what the 'Great American Dream' really stands for and what happens when it is actually within reach. He is able to portray a compelling account of man's constant state of 'want.' 
 In the end, it is a novel of humble plot but driven by its exquisitely etched out characters most of whom are unlikable yet persuasive.

 I rarely rate books below three stars, but there were just so many things in both plots that could have been amazing that were too flat! To imitate the multitude of awkward metaphors scattered all throughout it: this book drips with potential, but my imagination was left parched. The concepts are all super intriguing, but none of them are ever fully explored. Imogen is the only interesting character. Darcy is only Indian to give Westerfeld an excuse to use Yamaraj, Lizzie is far from a sympathetic protagonist, and Yamaraj is SO "mysterious" that he is boring. Hardly any of the conflicts in either plot actually cause much obstacle, leaving no doubt that Darcy and Lizzie will achieve their goals. 
 Darcy's unrealistic luck didn't bother me like it did many other reviewers, because there is a certain amount of stretching the truth that an author must do to set things up. We need that feeling of unrealistic luck for Darcy's future to feel unstable. It wasn't very effective, despite her utter disregard for financial prudence, but I see what Westerfeld was trying to do. The dialogue was awkward in both plots, and much information was inconsistent or poorly explained. To be honest, I am really tempted to interpret this whole book as satire against publishers' focus on sales over quality and the romanticized teenage dream of writing. 
 Despite my negative review, I really appreciated the experience of reading Afterworlds. I loved exploring a new and unique (as far as I know, anyway) concept of the afterlife. My main disappointment is that I wanted to be able to explore it more. There are many layers of it alluded to, but we only get to see the very basic workings of it.

If she had a choice, Ellie Hughes wouldn't step foot in Hope Junction again. Too much history lingers there. But Matilda, the woman who raised Ellie, needs her. So Ellie puts her superstar life in Sydney on hold and comes home. She plans on hunkering down in Matilda's cottage, but her history quickly comes to confront her. 
 Flynn Quartermine is the golden boy of Hope Junction. He's a successful farmer in the community and plays for the local football (soccer) team. But in a small town, everyone knows that Ellie Hughes stood him up at the alter 10 years ago. When the rumor mill gets to him that Ellie is back in town, emotions that he constantly tries to repress quickly come to the surface. 
 The plan is for Ellie to nurse Matilda back to health and go back to her life in Sydney without making too many waves. But the need for closure and past secrets are making themselves known. Can Ellie keep her stay in Hope Junction short and sweet? 
 I was very pleasantly surprised with this one. Even though the premise has been done tons of times, I'm a sucker for these kind of stories. There are enough subplots to give the story depth, and the secondary characters really embellish the whole novel. 
 I knocked a star off, because I was irritated about how Flynn reacted to some painful parts of Ellie's past, and it wasn't brought up again. I think some aspects of it were shoved under the rug, and it deserved more conversation. I won't elaborate, as I'd be giving away too much. 
 This was a really fun and sweet romance. Perfect for some weekend reading! 
 Four stars - buy it.

So a slightly lower score, but only marginally, and still a great addition to my Top Reads Bookshelf. 
 This one get's 8.5/10: somewhere between "Excellent read, well written, fell right into the fictional world created" and "Fantastic, left me wanting more" on the NBRS. 
 I'll leave you with a couple of note-worthy quotes (and let's face it, a book is only as good as the paragraphs you can't seem to get out of your head): 
 "Don't you think for a fucking minute you can put all that in your eyes, then die. That's bullshit. I'm not doing this again." 
 "Some things are sacred. Until you act like they're not. Then you lose them." 
 "And here we go. She's bristling and my hackles go up. Bloody hell, I feel fangs coming on."

Whew, I finished this in the nick of time for book club. An autobiography in graphic novel form, about the author's childhood and young adulthood in Iran. This edition is all the Persepolis books published as one volume. Even though the breaks aren't marked in any way, it's very clear where the original book (her childhood) ends. I thought this was clearly the strongest part of the story and I probably would have been just fine reading only this first book on its own. The teen and young adult years, while still interesting, feel more tacked on, the inevitable "so what happened next" and not especially cohesive. It probably doesn't help that I liked the character a lot less when she was older -- I have to say it, she was a bit of a whiner. Even with cutting her a lot of slack for living in a fundamentalist state ... well, she whined a lot and it was tiresome. The great, successful aspect of the book is how well it communicates the variety of experiences that people had during the revolution and regime change, and the multiple ways individuals reacted to it. Despite being incredibly eye-opening and informative about the political state of Iran during these years, it also works as a story about families and friends and what keeps them together and what can potentially drive them apart. As I've mentioned several times, I'm not that great with the graphic novels, so this was a little slow-going but I did think the illustration style was perfectly suited to the story -- harsh in its blocky black and whiteness, and fantastic at showing even subtle emotions though small variations in the scenes. 
 Grade: B 
 Recommended: to people who enjoy women's narratives and world politics.

Back on the beach at Cancun, the same place they were both taken from months ago, Sofia and Ben aren't ready to go home yet. And having missed it for so long, they find themselves trying to soak up as much sun as they can. Having been left with a large quantity of money, they book themselves into the villa they had been staying in previously. After a few days, they feel the time has come to call Ben's parents. When they arrive, they don't tell them where they were and when questioned by the police, they say they just ran away. They say nothing about where Ben got the scars all over his body from his torture at the hands of Claudia, and at Sofia's request, there's no mention of the vampires or The Shade. 
 Ben has a name and number for the hunters, given to him by a hunter who tried to save him on the island, but ended up being killed herself when they were caught. Knowing that his life will never be the same again, and having the need for vengeance and retribution, he plans to contact them. He tells Sofia that he'll give her some time, but that then, with or without her, he'll be making that call. He needs to take his revenge on the vampires, especially Claudia. 
 But Sofia can't seem to forget Derek and The Shade, and when Ben wants to become more than friends, something that she herself had wanted for a long time, she finds that she can't give herself wholly to him. Part of her still belongs to Derek. 
 And without Sofia there, the darkness is overtaking Derek. He's a completely different character than the Derek we met in A Shade of Vampire, and it was interesting seeing this other side to him. But it was also nice to see the effect that Sofia had on him when she returned, to find him in a compromising position with Ashley. 
 Lucas is not in this book too much, though we do get his POV a couple of times. He's on the run from Derek who will kill him for what he did to Sofia. But if he wasn't obsessed with her before, having tasted her blood, he can't stop thinking about her, and won't rest until she is his. 
 Things are getting tough in the Shade. Derek is struggling to keep everyone under control and try to keep Sofia happy at the same time. The vampires are not happy that Sofia, a human slave, is being put before them. But Sofia is not happy with the way things are currently done. She wants the humans who live in the Shade to be treated better and not treated like slaves or food which is exactly how the vampires see them. Sofia has learned a lot about how things are run in the Shade and has read it's history, and it doesn't sit well with her. There are going to be tough times ahead, and revelations throughout this books make for what should be a really interesting third book in this series. 
 I'm also looking forward to learning more about the prophecy made by Cora, the witch, over four hundred years ago, and what it means to Derek and Sofia, and to the Shade. Derek seems to be going to have quite the fight on his hands if he's going to manage to hold onto Sofia.

This book is advertised as taking place in 1830s England. However, once the reader can accept that the setting is not England of the 1830s but rather a finely costumed version of Crazytown, it's easy to let oneself roll into what turns out to be a pretty fantastic read.

As it turns out, Temple fell in with the gaming hell and developed his life as an outsider because he essentially got falsely accused of murder. The book skips right over the niceties of how the Killer Duke somehow managed to evade murder charges and a subsequent hanging in relation to the alleged killing of Mara Lowe, but he did pretty much get exiled from Society. 
 This looks ready to change when the supposedly dead Mara Lowe turns up. Apparently, trying to bail out her worthless brother (and he really is worthless) was a big enough deal to being Mara out of her 12 years of hiding. 
 Is the plot preposterous? Totally. However, I enjoyed this book not so much because of the plotting but more because of the emotion and the characters. The plot is pretty much insane, but the book is well-written and I enjoyed Mara and Temple.

ARC provided in exchange for an honest review. 
 Sometimes there are books that connect with you in every single way and Unveiling The Sky was that book for me. I smiled with the characters, cried with the characters, and even got a little angry right alongside the characters. A lot of times I use the word to describe broken to describe a character, but that word just doesn't seem right anymore. Alara and Gabe believe themselves to be broken, but they weren't at all. They were a little lost, wandering through life, but definitely not broken. Jeannine Allison created two protagonists that were the most realistic characters I have ever read. With dual POV's the reader gets to know the charming Alara and the stubborn Gabe as they both deal with major life events that change the shapes of their lives forever. I adored both of them, I felt like I knew both of them, and I was so emotional this entire story as I felt every little thing they went through. I love that they found each other at what they believed to be the most unlikely time, but really they helped each other find out who they really could be. 
 "Sometims I feel fragmented, like all I have are a bunch of random pieces that don't fit together anymore. I want to give you all of me. But will you want all of me when you realize I'm in pieces?" 
 Unveiling The Sky could easily be described as a heavy book, possibly an ugly cry novel, or maybe even over the top if you're the kind of person that likes happiness, but what it really was for me was incredibly realistic. The book touches on everything from life, death, friendship, family, cancer, depression, acceptance, forgiveness, and more. Jeannine Allison did an incredible job of tackling the subject of depression, bringing it to life, describing it, but also showing so much hope. I didn't expect to relate to it so much, but from page one I understood both Gabe and Alara, their story had parts of my own story. I think every reader will find something in this book that touches them, that connects and resonates. There is a ton of dialogue in this book, but I think the dialogue is what progresses the story, shows the development, and really explains how complex each character is. On top of dealing with a lot of emotionally heavy subjects, we meet 5 friends and get to know them in different ways as well, we see everything from their eyes, and I can definitely say I am glad this is a series, because I want to get to know all of them. 
 "...We all need certain people in our life. Some make sense, some don't, and I don't know where she falls, but I can tell you need her." She stopped suddenly like something just occurred to her. "So maybe you don't need to understand her; maybe you just need to want to." 
 I highly suggest Unveiling The Sky for all readers, fan of any genre type. While it falls in the New Adult category, I think Jeannine Allison successfully wrote a novel that people will find understanding and compassion in, as well as understanding. I might have cried my way through this book (starting at 23%), but I also highlighted countless passages and when I got done I was smiling. This beautiful (not just the cover) novel is absolutely a new favorite and I cannot wait for book two, Naomi's story. 
 I could still believe that happy days were in my future; they were just waiting for me to find them. 
 *Definitely check out the playlist for this book*

Oh gosh Sherman Alexie. 
 Another great one. I think every time I read your books I say to myself "Why am I not a Sherman Alexie completist?" And eventually I hope to be. 
 This book, though ostensibly YA lit, doesn't seem all that different from his grownup stuff about the Indian experience, both the love and joy of family and tradition and the grinding sadness of poverty and alcoholism and cultural isolation. 
 The thing that makes this book YA I guess is that it's about the process of growing up, making friends and falling in love off the Rez, family dying, and so forth. The process of learning to love to learn, learning to embrace being a nerd was great. The friend who says --"If you're good at it, and you love it, and it helps you navigate the river of the world, then it can't be wrong." and also "really good books and cartoons give you a boner."... but "when I said boner, I really meant joy," is a friend we all could have used along the way. 
 And a narrator who recognizes how imperfectly he loves an imperfect girl --- "she was in pain and i loved her, sort of loved her i guess, so i kind of had to love her pain too." and "i'd been thinking about her breasts and she'd been thinking about my whole life." Just sort of makes me swoon.

Wow. I wasn't expecting this. 
 This is an absolutely magical book about the loss of innocence and facing death. I've read a fair amount of Bradbury's stuff over the years, and I even saw the movie made from this novel way back in 83 when it came out, though I can't remember anything about it anymore. 
 But this novel I had somehow ever gotten around to reading until now. 
 And it blew me away. The language in this one, the lyrical quality of it...it grabbed hold of me and wouldn't let go. Just beautiful. 
 And, in reading this book (published the year I was born, and with one of the three main characters a mere two years older than me and concerned about his advanced age), it's easy to see it's influence on Stephen King. When he's at his best, in stories like The Body, and in novels like Salem's Lot, he can conjure some of Bradbury's magic and when he does, when it gets it exactly right, it's drawn directly from Something Wicked This Way Comes. 
 Does the novel show its age? Yes, at times. But can that be forgiven? With the truths buried within, just waiting to be revealed to each new reader? Yes, of course. 
 This book has found a place in my top ten books. A phenomenal read and a phenomenal achievement for Ray Bradbury.

Each chapter in How to Save a Life alternates between two first person accounts: Jill, who grieves the loss of her father by withdrawing from friends and her boyfriend, and Mandy, a pregnant teen who connects with Jill's mom on an adoption website - Jill's mother wants to move on from her loss by adopting Mandy's baby. 
 What Jill and her mother don't know about Mandy is although she's technically an adult at 18, Mandy dropped out of school and ran away from an abusive home situation. The website she and Jill's mom communicate through is for people wanting to handle their own adoptions outside usual channels. Jill warns her mother not to trust an adoption with no real paperwork and social worker, but her mother is convinced and invites Mandy to live with them for her last few weeks of pregnancy. 
 This might seem like a forced premise, but to the author's credit, each character's intentions are detailed so succinctly, I never doubted it. Jill's mother isn't a shrill, irrational woman; she's flawed, but her intentions are to honor her late husband by moving forward with adoption plans they'd already considered before he died. She's aware she could be "filling the void" and embraces this, thinking that helping a struggling teen like Mandy will force her to move on. Jill is rightly confused and angry at her mother. Isn't she enough? Why does her mother need another child? Jill continues to push away the people closest to her, and every day she loses more of the girl she used to be. 
 When Mandy moves in, there's tension between the girls from the start. Mandy is beautiful but simple-minded with no clear goals for after the baby is born. Jill is harsh and judgemental. Jill starts poking into Mandy's past to find out what she's really up to. Jill's mother is aware of how Mandy's presence affects Jill, and she wonders if she's doing the right thing by helping Mandy. It's clear she's feeling the pressure of navigating life without her pragmatic husband. 
 The characters' progressions are expertly written, and I appreciate that elements that could have turned cliche were fleshed out and explored in realistic ways. This is a definite recommended read if you like Young Adult Contemporary. I'm quite a fan of Sara Zarr after reading How to Save a Life, and have since then read her novel Sweethearts from a few years back. 
 Sidenote: Every time I picked up this book, the song by The Fray of the same name popped into my head. Every time!

 "I want to be able to care about clothes and boys, but I want to be good at science too. I want to be both."

I received this book free from Netgalley in return for an honest review.. (Sorry I'm just getting round to it!) 
 Let me start by saying I ADORE Rick Riordans books! I have read and own almost all of them and to receive a copy of this book was a dream come true! 
 This book takes place after the events of The Heroes of Olympus series and is in Apollos point of view. We left off knowing he was going to be punished by Zeus because of events that take place in the previous books.. I won't spoil those for you :) 
 We begin with Apollo hurtling towards earth having been changed into a weak, unattractive loser teen (no offence) where he meets Meg. Let me just say right from the off I got weird vibes from Meg, we know she's a demigod and she has skills in combat but she's very very reserved. She's written so well and she so gradually comes out of her shell and seems to find a friend in Apollo so naturally that I almost didn't notice it happening! Apollo is also fantastically written. We've met him briefly in previous by Riordan and reading in his point of view was so so funny! If you know the books you will know Apollo LOVES himself.. Not as much as Narcissus but it's a close one! One aspect I found great about this book was his way of re-telling events. Several times you knew he was adapting the story a little to make himself seem the like flawless hero and it had me laughing and giggling all over the place! 
 I do feel like maybe the action of the story was lacking a little but as with Riordans other stories a lot of information is given to you in such a short book.. Not short as in lack of pages but a comfortable length because I could happily read ten thousand pages of this! However, when we get to the action it certainly is all systems go! It's exciting and thrilling and so hard to put down! 
 I liked that we got to see more of Nico in these books and finally seeing him happy, the kid deserves a break! The return of a certain hothead demigod filled my heart with such happiness too and his entrance and the actions that follow couldn't have been more fitting!! 
 The villain in this book is going to be so interesting and I'm looking forward to seeing where it goes. We hear about the Beast and know he's someone who's been around a while.. He's violent and a murderer and has a lot of power and influence around the world. His reveal I did not see coming! 
 There's no way I could go through a review and mention the flaming huge plot twist that happens too! I literally gasped out loud! Blimey Riordan did you scare the life out of me!! I'm still in shock writing this now! I felt the fear and the heartbreak from Apollo and completely experienced it myself! 
 I am already struggling to wait for the sequel to this book!!! Overall this book gets a 5/5. I don't think I really had a single problem with this book! It's funny, exciting, interesting, there's so much more mythology and history to learn about and hear from a new perspective! God Rick do I love your books, I don't ever want them to end!

She made me want to be her friend (despite the fact that she pushes all of her would-be friends away). I also thought that Anderson did a fabulous job of giving you just enough information about Alison and her condition that you question her sanity (and humanity) throughout the whole story. 
 As the story moves along, parts one and two were cohesive and captivating, but I found myself a bit thrown-off by part three. I almost knew it was coming but there was just something about it that made it disconnect a bit from parts one and two. In the end, I thought all three parts rolled together for a good story, but it was honestly the first two parts that made me fall in love with the story and the characters. And...that's about all I want to say in case you decide to read it! This is definitely a novel I think you want to go in to without too much information so you can discover everything along the way!

Levana is a young girl of 15 when the novel opens, and still naive and vulnerable enough to elicit hope that she will become a good person. But Levana didn't stand a chance. Within the first few paragraphs I realized that she'd already been set on a path of selfish destruction, sent there by her cruel sister, and her own callous predispositions. Levana's background rivaled the most deviant that can be found on any TV show like Game of Thrones, or the annals of true history. That royal family was fucked. 
 As deplorable as Levana is (and let's face it she's a murderous, sociopathic (view spoiler)[rapist (hide spoiler)]), she's insanely compelling. If you love a good villain, then Fairest will satisfy you immensely. I think it's a great addition to the series, and recommend that you read it in the order I did. It's chronologically a prequel, but it's rife with spoilers, so don't read it first. And don't skip it. It adds to the story. Marissa Meyer doesn't make excuses for Levana, and I don't think her intention is for you to sympathize with her, but for you to see what's boiling underneath. Now that I know who she is, I can't wait to dive into Winter, because I know it's going to be one hell of a ride.

I did this as a mom/daughter read with my eldest (who really isn't all that old). She got the graphic novel version and I got the adult one...or Young Adult one. She got the one that's mostly pictures and I got the one with words. You probably know what I'm saying here. 
 I have to admit to being really impressed with this book. I've heard a lot of praise for it, but it was still better than I expected. It read really well. I really liked Percy as a character and as a narrator. There was an interesting assortment of side characters and a decent amount of greek mythology to be peripherally learned by readers. The whole ADHD/Dyslexic demi-god association was interesting and empowering for kids with such diagnoses and it ended well, despite being the first in a series. 
 I only have two true criticisms. One, Percy never mourns for his mother. Not at all. That felt incredibly unrealistic to me. Now I understand the whole impermanence of the situation, but wouldn't a 12 year old boy still grieve. I also get that as middle grade fiction loss is probably a little too heavy to be address, but I still think it needed a cursory mention. Second, I had a really hard time remembering that Percy was supposed to be 12. He spoke, acted and was treated as if he was much older so I visualised him as such in the story. Again, I get that it's middle grade fiction and tweens are the intended audience and therefore 12 is an appropriate age for the characters, but he did not feel 12. 
 All in all I'm thrilled to have read it. I probably wouldn't have bothered with it if I hadn't been doing it as a parenting activity. That's a shame really. I would have missed out.

 After being consistently disappointed with one of my favourite author's recent offerings, Indigo Spell is the book that restored my faith in Richelle Mead. I found the first two books of the Bloodlines series to be held back by the main character, an alchemist called Sydney who I have described as being too cold, scientific and prudish to be interesting. However, this is the book that changed it all for me as Sydney undergoes some pretty major character developments after she got over her major hang ups in the previous book. 
 There's a lot happening in Indigo Spell, from Sydney being a target of a deadly witch, to struggling against Adrian's affections, and finding out a conspiracy that the alchemists may be involved in that will put the very Moroi she's assigned to protect in danger. After growing attached to Jill, Adrian, Angeline and Eddy, her vampire friends, Sydney is slowly overcoming the barriers to her rigid alchemist prejudice that she has been brought up with. 
 Although Sydney is confused about who she really is, this is the book where her strengths shine as she learns how to wield her 'womanly charms', wields some pretty powerful magic, while using her deduction and scientific skills to uncover some secrets behind the Alchemists. 
 Adrian is back to his old self as he resigns himself to 'loving Sydney from afar', and little does he know that it wouldn't be for long. We get to see how right Adrian and Sydney are for each other as she's pulled him out of his binge-drinking, mopey mess and uses his renewed confidence to chase after her. Even Sydney can't resist his charm and the two finally get together in some sizzling scenes (M rated mind you). 
 The turning point of the book for me was when we learnt that there may be a lot more to the golden lily tattoo that meets your eye. In previous books, I blamed Sydney's prudish, clinical personality on her strict upbringing and her identity as an Alchemist. The tattoo may have more of an impact than we thought, by constricting her thoughts and putting teachings into her mind about why she shouldn't trust a vampire. 
 Should I daresay that Sydney's clinical detachment is actually fun in this book?

This is a fantastic sports romance by Santino Hassell. This somehow also the first football romance book I've read. As much as I've loved the author's other books, I was also a bit hesitant to start this one. I haven't had much luck when it comes to soccer romances because the inaccuracies about the sport in the books completely throw him out of the story, but thankfully, that's not the case here. I think with Illegal Contact, this is much more a character story than one that revolves around football, so that certainly helps. 
 Illegal Contact is about NFL, New York Barons tight end, Gavin Brawley. He's been put under house arrest and suspended from the team for a video that's been caught of him yanking a guy out of his car and slugging him. Now, Gavin lives in a huge house, alone, and can't go out to do simple stuff, like buying food. 
 We soon learn that Gavin isn't an awful person, he just doesn't care what anyone thinks of him. He's had a rough childhood and is past caring what the press think of him and his past when he plays awesome out on the field. He doesn't play into the media's games and so he's the one who gets all the bad press. What the press doesn't know is that for his friends, Gavin is 100% loyal and dependable to his friends. And that's really all he cares about, no matter what his image is to the public. However, that really hasn't worked out in his favor. Now, he needs an assistant, and if his manager has anything to say on the matter, a spy to keep Gavin out of trouble. 
 I was a multimillionaire and a famous athlete, and yet people still treated me like a dirt-poor street kid from Newark. Some things never changed. 
 This is where we meet Noah Monroe. Noah is out of a job at doing something he loves, like working at a LGBT youth center, and now he's scrambling to find any job in order to keep paying rent living in NYC and something temporary while he buys time to look more for something along his career path. Noah doesn't care about football, so he doesn't give the greatest first impression upon meeting Gavin, but that's what sets him apart. When it might be a better idea to hire someone who doesn't care, than to hire someone who's a total fanboy. 
 This is an enemies-to-lovers story, and gives some Beauty and the Beast vibes? I think it's the house arrest part and Gavin's grumpy attitude, to be honest. I love that Noah doesn't take Gavin's shit and talks back every opportunity he gets. I also love that Gavin is actually a big softie who would do everything for his friends. Gavin is bi, and while his manager would love for him to only like women, it doesn't work that ways, and Gavin is super attractive to Clark Kent-lookalike Noah. I was hesitant about this turning into a relationship while Gavin was, technically, Noah's employer, but I'm glad how this relationship developed and worked out in the end. 
 This is a slow burn romance. And the sexual tension is hot. This book has relatively low angst compared to other books I've read, but there's still some in this book between Gavin and Noah. 
 Gavin's friend's Simeon and Marcus are awesome and sweet. And I can't wait to read Simeon's story in Down by Contact!! 
 "What do you like to read?" 
 "Different things. Sometimes science fiction, sometimes mysteries, and right now I'm into romance. It's been a rough month. Happy endings are good for hard times."

 So, this book is about a circus. But instead of "Ooh" and "Aah", my main thought reading it was "Why?" Morgenstern tries to give us something ~magical~ and ~mysterious~ but in the end, the suspension of disbelief is not there, maybe because she constantly talks about how magical it supposedly is. Why is it that we're supposed to care about these characters? Why does this early-1900 farm kid even know how to read, let alone have enough time to go to a circus? Nothing in this book makes any sense when examined through the lens of common sense, but this isn't because it's ~magic~, but because it feels like she didn't care. 
 I wonder if I would have liked this book more if I had read it about 10 years ago. Reading it I found myself picturing the sort of person who would find it interesting: a girl, probably 14 or 15, with pink or purple streaks in her hair who wears necklaces with birdcages or keys or octopi on them, who loves Tim Burton and Neil Gaiman and striped stockings. 
 Sadly I am not that girl. And while there are obviously people who enjoyed this book, I am not one of them apparently. I'm not sure why this was advertised as a best-seller on the cover, or where they found all those Serious Critics to give it such glowing reviews. 
 I humored myself and read the Wikipedia article on Erin Morgenstern the other day, and nothing I read surprised me. Apparently she is a visual artist. Yeah, I can see that. The great majority of this book is just descriptions of circus attractions, people's costumes, and books. Apparently this work came out of a NaNoWriMo project. I am also not surprised. Somewhere around the middle I imagined her exclaiming "Screw plot, I'll write 50,000 words about stuff I like!". 
 And that's exactly what she does. 
 So, if you like the sort of stuff she likes (corsets, stockings, weird circus-y things, fancy dresses, men in vintage suits, etc) you will probably enjoy this book. If you don't, you will find it an agonizingly slow progression of still image after still image, badly written paragraphs, and cliches that everyone knows already.

Last month I made an important resolution; I decided I was reading to much crap and was going to try to read one classic book each month. The great American classic and Pulitzer Prize winner - To kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee was the chosen one for the month of August. 
 A lot as been said about the importance of this book for American society and its symbolism, so for the obvious reasons I'm not going to dwell about that. It's an amazing book one that everyone should read and one that I should have read a long time ago. 
 I made the mistake of watching the 1962 movie adaptation before I finished the book so I was pretty much spoiled about the ending. I found the book and movie to be very different. The movie omits a lot of aspects of the book, lots of little stories and sub-plots, and focuses more on Atticus Finch; portrayed by the amazing actor Gregory Peck, who ended winning an Oscar for it, and less on the children. 
 I also decided I wanted to know more about the book and especially about the reclusive author after finding out this was her only novel apart from a few short essays. I ended watching and definitely recommend the 2010 documentary Hey Boo: Harper Lee and To Kill a Mockingbird.

If you dislike unpopular opinions, then please don't read this review. 
 I'm breaking from the pack on this one. 
 I didn't want to, trust me. But here we are: 
 The book I've been eagerly awaiting since I finished his five-star NOS4A2, only it wasn't. 
 Joe Hill's THE FIREMAN. 
 Rambling, corn-pone, cartoonish. 
 Unlikable characters, interminable dialogue, zero forward momentum. 
 Besides for a mild dislike of the second half of HORNS (which was basically a retelling of the first half), I'm a huge fan of Joe Hill's work prior to this book. 20th CENTURY GHOSTS is one of my all-time favorite collections, and NOS4A2 is a Top-10 novel for me. 
 But THE FIREMAN has left this reader's love affair singed, if not in total ashes. 
 Bear in mind, this review is coming from someone who hasn't been able to find his way to the end of a Stephen King novel since TOMMYKNOCKERS (UNDER THE DOME being the sole exception, and that just barely), so I'm likely an outlier in opinion on this one. I like my fiction lean and mean, and this book was neither. If you're a fan of Stephen King's output from the last couple of decades, then by all means ignore this review and go enjoy THE FIREMAN. This book is for you. It very much emulates the modern King's unhurried storytelling style (although the down-home voice is somewhat less successfully replicated). 
 It's a shame though, at least to this reader, because the premise of this book was certainly intriguing enough and "Book One" (the first 113 pages) delivered on that promise with sleek, gripping prose. 
 Then it appears as though the editor fell asleep on the job or quit altogether, because the story literally ground to a halt, caught in a morass of endless inane character backstories conveyed in some of the corniest cheeseball dialogue I've seen this century. There is some damn fine prose laced throughout this slog of a story, to be sure; like his dad, Joe Hill can write like nobody's business, but Joe Hill deserves an editor with an iron fist and bleeding scalpel-shaped red pen. 
 The unrelenting parade of forced references littered throughout struck me as cloying, not clever, and only served to remind me of the fact that the entertainment value of little Easter egg games diminishes rapidly while literally hundreds of pages are grinding by with nothing more happening than people acting cute while the world burns. Bored to the breaking point, I stoically pushed through to the end after concluding "Book Five" (page 388) hoping to find something of interest, yet my frantic search left me empty-handed. 
 Some serious editing could have turned this book into an exceptional 350 page novel, rather than the 750 page mess it ended up being. Here's to hoping Joe Hill doesn't follow closely in his father's footstep of releasing increasingly muddled doorstop novels, but I'm guessing that ship has already sailed. He's got bigger ambitions than being a horror writer, I suppose, and the success of this book is likely to propel him much further in that direction. 
 Godspeed, Joe. Hope to see you around these parts again someday.

I think this is the worst rating I have ever given a book that thought I was going to love. Because uuuuuuugh 
 Okay so summary plot without spoilers. 
 Cassia is a 15 year old girl who has lived her whole life under the Society's reign. They tell her what to wear, what and when to eat, what to do, who to love, when to die and how to die. Cassia has never doubted the Society because without them there would be no order and chaos would be their leader. Until one day, in Cassia's Matching Banquet, the Society makes a mistake that changes Cassia's life forever. She gets Matched with two boys. Xander and Ky. What is she supposed to do? Who is she supposed to love? Hence commences Cassia's journey to follow what her mind knows is right, but at the same time stay faithful to herself. In the process, she learns things that are better left untouched. 
 I'm really tired of love triangles. Ever since Hunger Games and Twilight, I cringe every time I read about overly-done love triangles. So, naturally when I found out Cassia's dilemma lies in the fact that she can't choose between two damn boys... sigh. 
 The Characters 
 Primarily, there are 6 individual characters, and then the others can be categorized into groups. 
 Cassia. She's the main character and she's what we call an unreliable narrator. She's too polluted with others ideas to think for herself. She's too helpless. A damsel in distress. And I hate the fact that we never see her character develop. Not on her own, I mean. She always needs others to point out the obvious and even then she doesn't know what to do. It was excruciatingly painful seeing her talk or think. I seriously wanted to strangle her every step of the way. 
 Xander and Ky. Since Ally Condie always paired them up in the book, why shouldn't i? I don't have so many problems with these two characters actually. I really like them but I hate the fact that they are so underdeveloped. They have so much potential and just UUUGH. I wish we would've gotten someone else's perspective apart from Cassia's because she is too goddamn unreliable to tell a story straightforward. 
 Reyes Family. 
 I wont even bother saying these were underdeveloped because they all were. 
 I think the highlight of this book for me was Bran. His unrelenting way of rebelling against the Society and not even realizing it. I love the way he stands up for the things he cares about and I love how unflinchingly loyal he is to the people he truly cares about. I think Bran is beautiful and perfect and the best character in this book to be honest. 
 In conclusion, I believe the plot has so much potential. But Condie got caught up in the world building and forgot that it's the characters that move the story forwards. I think thats her fatal flaw. I sincerely hope that Crossed steps up and proves me wrong.

And, speaking of fellow YA authors, it's a lot of fun searching for the names of other authors in the group-name segments. (view spoiler)[So many dead writers! (hide spoiler)] 
 The first issue I had with Gemina is that it shares a lot of striking resemblances to Illuminae, and I'm not talking about format and the fact that's it takes place in space. I don't think I can be any more specific about this without going into heavy spoilers for both, and I don't want to give any big hints for those that have read Illuminae but not Gemina yet. For those who have read both already, here we go: 
 (view spoiler)[While the storylines of Illuminae and Gemina are different, a lot of the overall story and character beats in Gemina are lifted right out of Illuminae. Such as: 
 A monster gets loose on the ship/jump station and starts attacking people: 
 Illuminae: Zombies 
 Gemina: Lanima 
 The leading man getting killed off halfway through: 
 Illuminae: Ezra making it to the wrong escape shuttle. 
 Gemina: Nik getting killed "valiantly"(?) by pausing his running from kill-crazy Kali for a second so he can pick up the journal Hanna just dropped. 
 The leading lady deciding to save everyone else anyway, likely sacrificing herself, even though her love is dead: 
 Illuminae: Kady agreeing to stay with AIDAN, who will be blown apart by the Lincoln and doesn't want to die alone, so he will set the rest of the uninfected free. 
 Gemina: Hanna staying behind on the Heimdall to fix the broken universes, even though if she does save everyone there's still a second drone strike incoming to blow everything left. 
 The twist reveal that the leading man was still alive after all: 
 When I read Illuminae, I was impressed that the story took such a turn, and enjoyed seeing Kady have to grow because of it. I was hooked so much by everything in it that I didn't mind when Ezra turned out to still be ok. I thought the book had earned that back-pedal happy ending. Plus, AIDAN made it out ok, so who cares? (In case anyone hasn't been able to guess my favourite character in these books.) 
 Gemina managed earn its happy ending too, with enough foreshadowing to tell you that something is off here even before Nik apparently gets killed off. I'd initially thought there was something going on after the wormhole malfunction, but after a while of nothing coming of it, I forgot it and started to wonder if this was going to be some clones thing. I'm so happy I was wrong, and the twist was far more creative than that. 
 And yet, Gemina tried to pull that same trick a again shortly after Hanna and Nik are reunited. Only this time, Jackson comes in and kills all three of our new main characters, only there's a twist (again) that their still alive. I understand the explanation for this twist existing, but I didn't like it. 
 Let me explain. There's a show I used to watch called The Mentalist. A lot of it was about using mind games to solve crimes, and I would say that unfortunately probably over half of the episodes would have the characters play the 'Oh no, something terrible has happened to a main character!' card in order to get the villain of the week to mess up and reveal themselves. But they wouldn't tell the audience. Week after week, you'd learn to stop caring pretty quick when something apparently awful happened to the characters you cared about because you knew it wasn't real. Almost ever. You would watch an episode an think, 'Well, there goes the writers playing that card again. I wonder if any new viewers somewhere will get punked?' The point is, if you play that card to many times, especially if there's no real consequences, your audience is going to get annoyed. This is why I'm now worried about Illuminae #3 following too closely to the formula a third time. 
 Speaking of that second twist: 
 The 'other guy' who was the/one of the antagonists having a change of heart because lurv and letting the leading lady go save herself (and her friends, in Gemina's case) and sacrificing themselves in the process: 
 Illuminae: AIDAN revealing that he wasn't really going to let Kady die and giving her an escape from the Lincoln. 
 Jackson deciding that it's time to do as Hanna asked earlier and prove himself with his actions. 
 The difference is that Jackson is most certainly not one of the greatest AI characters ever created (though I hear he has a lovely voice), while I was plenty invested in what was going to happen to Kady and AIDAN. 
 There were more I could think of, but this section is too long already. (hide spoiler)] 
 Whether these similarities bother other readers is going to depend on the individual. For most people who loved Illuminae, I don't think it will be a problem. I'm generally a tough critic. 
 And then there are the new characters. I seem to be alone in this judging from the reviews, but I wasn't a fan of Hanna and Nik, although when that beautiful climax happened I really wished I was. They are the reason Gemina is missing a half star. Hanna and Nik were far too similar to Kady and Ezra. 
 (view spoiler)[Essentially, when you subtract the character quirks and history, they are nearly identical to the couple we met in Illuminae. Both as individuals and their relationship: 
 She's a girl who's already made up her mind about him, and is now immune to his charms. She's a complete badass at something (Kady = hacking, Hanna = 'ninja skills' and battle strategy), which make her valuable in a crisis. She will do whatever it takes to find the truth after her parent is killed. She is independent and can handle the threats well, even when she is alone. 
 Meanwhile, he's a well-meaning jokester who keeps striking out with the girl of his dreams, and greatly lacks her level of skill at anything. Our Constant Analyst is much less favourable when describing him (Ezra = clumsy klutz, Nik = slow and dimwitted) and he's the butt of the jokes of many characters. He's the devoted screw-up in way over his head compared to Madam Badass, and he's gonna use his charms in this crisis to open up to her and win her over in the end and she'll realize it was him all along. 
 I was disappointed that Gemina was doing nearly the same thing over again, and just decided to hope that Hanna and Nik would end up working for me the same way Kady and Ezra did. Here's why it worked for me in Illuminae and not in Gemina: 
 When we meet Kady and Ezra, they're exes. They have history we don't see and we don't need to see. We know they worked, at least for a time, and what brings them together in the end is the both of them coming to terms with why they broke up. We get to learn so much about them this way. 
 In Gemnia, we get to see how Hanna and Nik met: He hit on her, she didn't like it, she told him so, he didn't listen, she broke his arm. The End. Yet now, according to her diary, she thinks of him as this great puzzle to solve and she does plenty of flirting with him when we see them together. I felt like I'd missed a chunk of the book here. I think this is one of the unfortunate downsides of this format: we don't get to see how they see each other from their point of view. We don't get to see why they are interested. After reading the whole novel, I still have no idea why they are interested in each other. He likes her because . . . she's hot and rich and badass, I guess, and flirts with him. But I have no idea why he's got this deep devotion to her. He never says why he's into her and so we never learn. 
 Hanna doesn't really say why she's attracted to Nik either, but from what I can discern, it isn't very flattering. First off, Hanna already has a devoted boyfriend! I don't care if he turned out to be the bad guy, she didn't know that, and neither did Nik (who also knew she had a boyfriend). Yet, she keeps stringing Nik along like her and Jackson are in an open relationship (Jackson definitely doesn't seem to think so). That's not fair to Jackson or Nik, and to make matters worse, the book has several brief discussions on how wrong it is for a guy to cheat on his girl, but there's nothing about what Hanna's doing. I don't like double-standards. 
 Anyway, at the start of Gemina, Jackson appears to be the perfect guy. Perfect looks, great voice, devoted, good job, Dad approves, etc, while Nik is the scoundrel drug dealer. Then, some reveals later, we find out that Jackson is working with the bad guys and Nik, who first appeared to be a murderer, is innocent of all charges and selfless enough to confess to his little brother's crimes, so it turns out Nik was the perfect one all along. Now Hanna chooses Nik, because he's the perfect guy now. 
 Side-note, I'm really tired of the apparent bad boys who, it turns out can do no wrong. They brush the crime off when it turns out to be his brother's crime, like he didn't know what he was doing and was misled. If they were going to make that excuse anyway, why not have it that Nik did the crime, and use those excuses on him. I think it would add another detention to his character if he did the crime (maybe lessen said crime slightly, if that makes everyone more comfortable), and genuinely regret what he did and try to recover and go straight from then on. But then he wouldn't be perfect enough for Hanna, I guess, meaning she'd either have to: 1) Come to some realization that somewhere along the line she wasn't so perfect either, and grow from this knowledge, or, 2) Realize that the other true perfect character was really Ella all along, and Hanna has to go to extreme lengths to win over her true equal. (hide spoiler)] 
 Even with these problems, I loved a lot of Gemina and I look forward to Illuminae 3. Definitely check Gemina out if you were a fan of Illuminae.

 Sol was a wonderful heroine. She was strong and very determined to get what she wanted, even though her plans weren't always rational. She was clever and definitely held her own in a world of secrets and betrayals. My only issue with her was that she was a a tad too impulsive, getting herself into ridiculous situations, and prickly, seeing insults and enemies when there weren't any. Otherwise, I really liked her. 
 D'Arcy was the love interest and he was wonderful. He was very sweet and very intelligent. He was just wonderful. I loved how determined he was to help Sol, just because, at first, he thought it was the right thing to do. I absolutely adored him. 
 The romance was lovely. Despite their rocky start, Sol and D'Arcy were very sweet together and one hell of a bad ass team. I loved the twist of how far their relationship actually stretched. And, I loved how they were willing to go through so much for each other and, ultimately, willing to wait for each other when it seemed things weren't going to go their way. I thought they were a wonderful couple. 
 The pace was the weak point in this book. It started off slow. The first half dragged a bit, but something kept me interesting, so I kept reading. And, I'm glad I did because, about halfway through, the plot picked up and I got totally hooked. There were tons of thrills, surprises, secrets, and betrayals and it all kept me on the edge of my seat. I really enjoyed the story and the ending had me excited to see what happens next. 
 Plus One was a fantastic YA romance. It was thrilling, romantic, and full of deeply hidden secrets. I really enjoyed reading this wonderful book. Romance lovers, this is definitely a book not to be missed.

"For the first time ever, I felt ashamed of my species. The volcano had taken our homes, our food, our automobiles, and our airplanes, but it hadn't taken our humanity. No, we'd given that up on our own." 
 Define Humanity: hu*man*i*ty, noun, plural -ties. 
 1. all human beings collectively; the human race; humankind. 
 2. the quality or condition of being human; human nature. 
 3. the quality of being humane; kindness; benevolence. 
 Define survival: sur*viv*al, noun 
 1. the act or fact of surviving, especially under adverse or unusual circumstances. 
 2. a person or thing that survives or endures, especially an ancient custom, observance, belief, or the like. 
 Define monstrosity: mon*stros*i*ty, noun, plural -ties. 
 1. the state or character of being monstrous. 
 2. a monster or something monstrous. 
 Define Monster: mon*ster, noun 
 1. a legendary animal combining features of animal and human form or having the forms of various animals in combination, as a centaur, griffin, or sphinx. 
 2. any creature so ugly or monstrous as to frighten people. 
 3. any animal or human grotesquely deviating from the normal shape, behavior, or character. 
 4. a person who excites horror by wickedness, cruelty, etc. 
 5. any animal or thing huge in size. 
 I finished reading the book, then the author's notes at the back, and still I kept thinking about this all... I felt so sad, I can't even put into words how much disappointment and anger I have felt. Not for the book, or the characters, but for the whole damn human kind. 
 Like the character in this book, I felt ashamed... Because what would we be without our humanity? 
 Would we be better than anything surrounding us? Because we keep thinking that we are the kings of the world, but are we? 
 How low can you get when you've already hit the bottom? 
 How fast can you run, when you have nowhere to go? 
 How long can you survive when the nature rebels against you? 
 How hard would you bite the hand that have fed you? 
 In a world that doesn't resemble at all the world as we know it, where it is raining with ash, and it's freezing to death, and sun is only a memory from before the volcano eruption, Alex has one purpose: to find his family that left him behind (there was no drama in the act: in fact they just left him at home for the weekend while they went visiting some relatives. It was supposed to be just another weekend - casual, sunny, not different from all the others.. only the eruption has changed everything), but his journey is not as easy as he might think. 
 After the eruption people are starting to starve, and they transform themselves in predators, they hunt, they steal, and they kill. They have weapons and they are not afraid to use them, because when there is only one mouthful of food, nobody wants to share it with strangers. 
 In one encounter with such a beast, Alex finds himself face to face with death, and it's only because of an wonderful woman (Mrs. Edmunds,) and her daughter Darla, that he is still alive. But a price is needed to be paid. And when tragedy strikes, Alex and Darla has no one but themselves, and they need to stay together and work together hard to stay alive. 
 I liked their relationship and the way they tried to help each other. 
 Of course, sometimes they were just lucky, some other times it was all too good to be true, but in the end it felt so damn real, and it hurt so badly to witness this madness called survival. It's a tricky thing to survive, because your life might mean the death of someone else, and if you are not strong enough to kill, then you might be weak enough not to survive... 
 So where do you draw the line between humanity, sacrifice, and survival? 
 Are you human enough to leave someone die by hunger/cold, are you strong enough to sacrifice a dear animal just to have something to eat, are you enough of a beast to kill someone before he kills you? 
 But above all these questions, is there a real need to kill? All those characters can put a gun in front of your face, ready to shoot, but isn't it another way? How can you tell the difference between a good man a bad one (generically speaking).. How can you tell the difference between a human and a person? 
 Listen to me... 
 When this book comes out, pick it up people, and read it. And if somehow this world comes to an end, just remember this book (if you still can), just remember that you are still human.. Just remember...

It was the summer of 2006 when I first heard of this story. First, let me tell you, I was only ten years old and had no interest in reading a book. I liked books. I liked how they had fancy, appealing covers that attracted the eyes of my ten year old self. I was big on buying books but never once had I cracked it open, or flipped through pages. I would just buy them and stack them in my shelf. 
 My library collection at that time held many great classic literature such as Oliver Twist, Da Vinci Code, yadda yadda yadda. If I invited you to my ten year old self room you'd have thought I was a smart kid. I even had little women and Around the world in 80 days. All unabridged version. You would have thought I was some child prodigy. Here is the truth- I hated reading. I was a little slow in deciphering words up until eighth grade. So naturally I was a slow reader, eventually skipping lines and pages here and there. Also, I'd start drifting into my own dream world while reading a book and I wouldn't have even finished the first page. 
 My sister and I never really got along. We fight all the time. We take sibling rivalry to a whole new level. I kid you not. We still don't get along, but on one rainy summer night in 2006 my parents had gone out and it was just my sister and I. She had borrowed The series of Unfortunate events by Lemony Snicket from our school library. She had finished reading this book only that evening, I think. So when my sister and I were stuck at home, with our parents out and no electricity for six agonising hours she forced me to listen to this amazing book she had recently read. She narrated the entire story in the space of three hours time. And the more she told me about the book, the more intrigued I got. By the time she finished her narration I was hooked. 
 The following week I went into my school library to borrow this book again and read it for myself. Alas! I read it (of course, I took two months to finish reading). The first book I finished reading without growing bored. So I have sentiments with this book. And then weeks later I was telling the younger kids in my bus about this book, forcing everyone into the library to borrow it.

 When I first heard about this book I was in. I loved 'Wonderland' growing up - or the Disney version at least - and tend to eat up variations of the story. When we were promised a "true story behind the story" type of thing, even darker and more mad than the original - well, what Wonderland aficionado could pass it up? 
 And I was into it pretty much from the beginning. I liked the voice of the story, even though first person isn't my favorite, and I liked the sort of madness of it. I even liked Alyssa, for the most part. I related to her mixture of insecurity and strength. 
 But then we meet Jeb and the first twitterings of romance are felt... and I was like, ok, I can deal with a bit of romance, and, hey, at least they were long time friends and not insta-love, which I hate - though the whole 'two people who secretly love each other but stay away for X stupid reason' is a bit tired, too. 
 But, aside from that, the story of a growing family insanity, the language and whatnot was good. 
 Then we get to Wonderland, and I loved parts of it. The way the characters are taken from the book but twisted and different. I especially liked the Twid Sisters, thought the Mad Hatter analog was pretty cool, and enjoyed the adventure, danger and insanity of the whole thing. 
 What I did not enjoy, however, is the love triangle. 'Cause, see, Jeb comes along on our adventure and is ever so tiring and annoying, constantly "protecting" Alyssa and sort of putting her down and generally being a giant ass, even though I think we're meant to be rooting for him as the "good guy" of the triangle. He's just so patronizing and domineering and annoying. I kinda worry about what it means for young girls if this is the good guy. 
 Then we have Morpheus. Morpheus is also an ass, but of a different kind. He has an agenda and he's kind of obviously pulling Alyssa's strings. And maybe it's 'cause I tend to go for the dark, broody types... or maybe it's 'cause Morpheus was actually honest about his treachery, in a weird sort of way, but I actually preferred him over Jeb. 
 But, regardless, the biggest issue isn't just that the triangle exists, but that it becomes such a huge focus of the book. So much of the awesome stuff is sort of swept away by the constant alpha-posturing and, even worse, Alyssa goes from being sort of willful and spunky, chasing away to Wonderland despite her mother's warning, to a typical damsel in distress, her biggest issue being which boy to trust/love/whatever. 
 She's constantly getting saved, constantly dithering and unsure, and becomes downright helpless when she's on her own. Gone is the spunk of the girl at the beginning of the book. 
 When Alyssa uses a (view spoiler)[wish and wishes that Jeb hadn't come along, I couldn't help but wish we'd gotten that story instead. (hide spoiler)] 
 That said, I did like the ending, for the most part, and Alyssa did step up. Finally. 
 So, overall, I'm a bit conflicted. The overall plot and the characters and the whole twist of Wonderland was really cool. The love triangle was way overplayed and tiresome. And some of the middle could've been tightened up... but the beginning and end were pretty strong, and the adventures were cool, overall. 
 I just can't help but being a bit disappointed because of the book that might've been if only we'd focused more on the story, if Alyssa had stayed more spunky throughout, and if there was a lot less romance. I'm not saying all of the romance had to have been cut - but it certainly shouldn't have been the focal point that it became.

 1.5 Stars - This is a science-fiction romance that didn't quite make the mark. It wasn't a bad book, but it wasn't a good book either. My overall thoughts of this book are just... bleh. 
 The book centers around a romance between two characters who have no chemistry to speak of. Their entire relationship is based on the fact that the guy loved her in a past life. This could have been an opportunity for some interested discussions between them, but instead the girl gazes at him starr-eyed and asks to hear memories of their other life, when they were married and pregnant. It comes off as really creepy. The guy has basically found a replacement who looks exactly like the woman he loved - but she is NOT her. They talk about this only a very, very small bit, and I never felt like they really dealt with it. 
 The rest of the book deals with the relationships between the protagonist and her friends and family. Parts of this was interesting but none of their arcs were really seen through in a satisfactory way. Especially Jo's. The protagonist accepts what happens to Jo REALLY quickly. I found her situation the most emotionally compelling, and it was hardly even explored. 
 Lillie herself is not an interesting or likeable person. She treats the people in her life in a dismissive, if not just uncaring and rude way, especially with her running commentary on her friends - one is too "mannish" and the other is too slutty. The only person she likes is Tom, who I couldn't tell you anything about except that he's supposedly "sexy and mysterious." 
 Throughout the book is a sci-fi element that only loosely makes sense. I felt confused throughout most of it, and had a LOT of questions. Different characters give the protagonist different information, especially the love interest, who only tells her the half-truth until the end - and yet she doesn't REALLY hold him accountable for the misinformation, and is madly in love with him again awfully fast. At one point the author says that there is no such thing as imagination (as explained by her sci-fi world) and it was at that point I couldn't even pretend to believe in her world anymore. 
 The writing wasn't bad and it wasn't good either. I feel like that's my overall impression of this book, that it just (pardon the pun) fell flat. It was just ... eh. This book could have been an okay book, but it really did not pull it off, and was a lackluster, mediocre attempt overall.

Despite these two awesome elements, Insatiable didn't quite quench my thirst for a fantastic adult paranormal novel. (Get it? Quenching my thirst? Vampires? Hardy har har. I'm done now.) 
 The one thing I can't complain about in Insatiable is the plot. Cabot tells an unpredictable story that was wrought with suspense until the final page. I read this book while traveling and it made my four hour delay (three of those spent on the plane) s and time sitting in airports pass much more quickly.

I appreciated the way Meena handled herself at the conclusion of this story, but I think Cabot wound up making her sound preachy. Even if you believe in the message you're sending through a character, preachy just doesn't work for me. 
 One of my biggest problems with Insatiable was the insta-love, and I'm not talking about the physical intimacy that Lucien and Meena quickly shared. What I mean is that I didn't like how after having just met Lucien, Meena couldn't stop talking about how in love she was with him and vice versa. However, I loved reading about Alaric. Even though I wasn't sure about him at first, he grew on me by the end of the novel. Let's just say that while I started of who I was rooting for, I finished on Team Alaric. 
 As far as vampire books go, Insatiable isn't a total dud. However, there were some things in here that seriously clashed with my tastes. I'll be curious to see where the story, especially the romance, goes in Overbite.
