The Sleeper and the Spindle is a gorgeous book: the illustrations are all in black and gold, and there are some really beautiful pages. Riddell was just the right illustrator to bring the story to life, I think. The copy I have is really great: the dust cover is transparent, with the pattern of roses on it; the cover of the book itself is the sleeping woman. 
 If you know Neil Gaiman's work, the rest of this is perhaps not surprising. It takes both Snow White and Sleeping Beauty, and puts them in a unified world that is a little darker, a little different, a little more mature than the sanitised stories we see so much of now. This ain't Disney. It's still a fairytale, but it's something different, too -- something a little bit creepy, even. 
 The LGBT representation that I have seen this book being lauded for is... not exactly. There's one kiss which appears to be so if you see the illustration on its own -- and it's a gorgeous illustration -- but it doesn't mean what it seems to mean, in context. Which is a little bit of a cop-out, really, since there's excitement around this book on the back of it. 
 But really, romance isn't at the heart of this fairytale. A search for autonomy is really what's going on; a shrugging away from the familiar fairytale 'happy ever after'.

Avow is the last installment in the enchanting series, The Archers of Avalon. And on that note, let me cry like a baby and freak the hell out. I am a HUGE fan of this series and I am in love with AVOW. Chelsea Fine, you have just become one of my favorite authors ever. Words cannot express how dearly I love this story, okay they can, I was just being dramatic. But really, I can't believe I have to say goodbye to Team Awesome. Sniff sniff. And what an end to a wonderful journey to the Fountain of Youth. I feel like crying happy tears. 
 The Archers of Avalon is definitely a beautiful read filled with a great romance between century-long star-crossed lovers, mystery, brotherly love, true friendship, magic and curses, heart-breaking sacrifices, moments that will squeeze your heart to pieces, and banters that will make you laugh out loud. 
 In AVOW, Scarlet finally got her memories back and the transition was completed. Meaning, the connection she and Tristan had was reversed. This time, it's Scarlet's touch that might kill Tristan and she's the one who suffers in pain when they're apart. Color me and them FRUSTRATED! Raven, the crazy witch, kidnapped Heather and Gabriel in exchange for the map of the fountain. You know what I love the most in this series? FLASHBACKS! And this book is full of them. WOOT. There we see how Tristan and Scarlet suffered through their fatal connection, how Tristan heart shattered to pieces, how Gabriel suffered life without love, and how Nate really got addicted to the video game. I can't believe it was Tristan's fault. Chuckles. 
 I can absolutely tell you that I will really miss the characters. They're all amazing and I really loved the bond these crazy group have. 
 SCARLET JACOBS. Oh, I am so amazed by this girl. In the first book, we were introduced to a Scarlet with amnesia, who woke up in forest with no memories of who she was. Then from being the lost girl, torn between her feelings for two brothers, we met the Scarlet in the flashbacks and, OH MAN, was she buckets full of awesome! She's way badass. And by badass, I mean she's the hunter who threatened Tristan's life to steal his hunt, same girl who stole ( or "borrowed" as she would say) Tristan's weapons and vials of blood in the middle of the night like a creep to go on a suicidal mission, and the girl who will go the great lengths to protect the ones she love without thinking twice. See what I mean? She's hilarious, brave, and oh so stubborn. She's damn perfect. 
 TRISTAN ARCHER. Oh my freaking wow! Just gimme a second to pause and swoon, okay? This guy, you guys! Green-eyed hottie? Check. Dangerously sexy and intense? Double check! Will do any crazy-ass stunt to save his girl like hiring people to mutilate him and trying every goddamn weapon to literally break his immortal heart? CHECK! Yeah, this is the guy! Talk about true effin' love. I guess watching the girl you love die over and over and over again definitely push a guy off the deep end. But Tristan hadn't always been the brooding, suicidal mess that he was. In fact, he was the responsible, kind-hearted Archer who hunted his father's forest to provide food for the poor.The guy who captured Scarlet's heart and owned it since. Scarlet's Hunter. Same guy who broke his own heart and asked his brother to marry his girl so she'd be kept safe. Who can beat that, huh? Swoooooonnnn..... 
 GABRIEL ARCHER. This Archer I did not like at first. I thought he did not deserve being with Scarlet. He's good-looking like Tristan. Duh, twins. Charming and nice but him and Scarlet together was not right. At all. I felt like he only loved her because of the curse, He couldn't find love without Scarlet so he had to settle for her. And that's just terrible for them both. But somewhere along the way, Gabriel won a place in my heart. I was actually crossing my fingers that he eventually finds his happiness. And then in AVOW, I realized he really did love Scarlet in his own ways and that he's willing to let Tristan make peace with her even after he'd broken her heart to stop Scarlet from hurting. Just proved that he's not selfish and he wanted his brother and Scarlet to be happy even if it hurt him, too. Then he was so protective of Heather and the two of them were amazing and I just want them to be in love. Screw the curse and all. I've been hoping for this since book two and thank you, Chelsea Fine for granting my wish. You're the best. 
 HEATHER BAXTER. OMG! This perky girl I heart so much. She's the best girlfriend Scarlet has ever had. She's super hilarious and cute. I was super mad at that lunatic witch-bitch when she got Heather addicted to the fountain water and almost sending her to the nut-house. And she's brave and smart. Butcher knife and all. Oh, and the fact that she made Gabriel feel something for her and not empty at all , curse and all, that earned her huge points. Go, Tomb Raider! With pink boots. 
 NATE I DUNNO HIS LAST NAME. This geeky immortal is definitely my favorite. He's crazy hilarious and though he sucked at being a witch, he made up for being an awesome friend. He was a great help to finding a cure for Scarlet. He's the bestfriend who stood by Tristan during his darkest, broodiest times. He's become like a brother to the Archers and Scarlet. And most importantly, his Comic-Con purchased thingies that Gabriel underestimates? Totally life-saving! OMG, love the whip! And trust him to recognize an awkward moments when he's in one. He's the best. 
 MOST HEART-BREAKING MOMENT: Nate's sacrifice. I can't even. Sob. 
 Overall, this series is on the TOP of the best I've read. Can't you tell? It's a bittersweet story of sacrifice, loss and love. Definitely a page-turner and if you're a sucker for happily ever after, pick up this series. Like now.

It was Krishnamurthi who said that 'it is no measure of good health to be well-adjusted to a profoundly sick society'. What he might have added is that there are forces within society: corporations, the government and - as is the case in Ken Kesey's 'One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest' - the medical community, that actually thrive on making us believe we are sick. In this era of quick fixes, synthetic treatments such as electro-shock therapy, lobotomy, or (serious) addiction-forming psychotropic antidepressants are used in an attempt to 'normalise' human behaviour. 
 In this book (of which near perfect justice was done as a movie), events in an unnamed state hospital in Oregon are seen through the eyes of the patient Chief Bromden. We never really know why he has ended up there; in fact, most of the patients themselves don't know why they have been committed, except that one day they found themselves unable to adjust to the world around them due to its innate sickness, were diagnosed as 'mentally ill', and shunted off - like criminals - to an institution. In the words of the patient Harding: 
 'I don't think I can give you an answer. Oh I could give you Freudian reasons with fancy talk, and that would be right as far as it went. But what you want are the reasons for the reasons, and I'm not able to give you those.....I indulged in certain practices that our society regards as shameful. And I got sick. It wasn't the practices, I don't think, it was the feeling that the great, deadly, pointing forefinger of society was pointing at me-and the great voice of millions chanting, 'Shame, Shame, Shame'. It's society's way of dealing with someone different.' 
 The world doesn't give a damn that there are seeing, feeling humans with beating hearts and throbbing pulses; as long as the soul and individuality has been squeezed out of the different and therefore dangerous ones, it's a good night's rest for those who prefer to go through life with their eyes closed and their minds numbed. Therefore, misfits gravitate towards other misfits. Or, to continue Kesey's avian analogy, 'Birds of a feather flock together'. 
 According to the Chief, the hospital - and the world at large - is controlled by intricate machinery known as The Combine, with Nurse Ratched behind the controls, preying on the inner inadequacies and paranoia of her patients to keep them in a perennial state of fear. All is bleak until the hospital receives a new 'inmate' in the form of Randle McMurphy, a straight talking con man and hustler with a desire to shake things up and bring back a breath of life to the dying hopes of fellow patients. McMurphy is a genuine representation of the flawed, free American spirit - a farm boy, and a man of the soil, a war hero, a gambler, and an alcoholic; the very same sort of spirit that society seeks to suppress for the danger it represents to conformity. To the Chief however, McMurphy with his freethinking ways is a potential saviour from the cold grasp of institutional control. 
 Without giving too much away, the winner in this duel of the individual against the omnipotent machine has only one (inevitable) winner. Although largely tragic, the novel does end with some semblance of hope, but with the caveat that freedom of any kind - even if it is simply the freedom to be considered normal in a world that has been going mad for some time and is only getting worse - is far from easy. 
 Footnote: Overall, it's a beautifully done book full of moments of warm joy, pain and shining truth. However, I've taken a star off the ratings because of the strong racist overtones: I thought Kesey unfairly objectified black people as villains, and lackeys of the state.

A quick and easy read that will get you thinking long and hard. What do we want our interconnected society to be? Should we let entertainment companies write our laws governing how computers and connections work? Is privacy a right for people or just for corporations? Short segments give good explanations and history of copyright, piracy, how computers have worked and work now, but the solution bits at the end weren't as fleshed out as I could wish. Guess I'll have to do the thinking.

I dunno...this one was kind of Meh. There was too much of "the chosen ones" going on for my liking. As a number of other people have said, this is coming on a little too strong, too late in the dystopian genre and just has too many cliches. 
 Might still do well, but I wasn't a fan.

What would happen if you woke up one day just to find out that you were a clone made to keep a singular man alive forever? Well, that's pretty much the storyline in The House of the Scorpion. Matteo Alacran (Matt) is the younger clone of El Patron, the extremely rich owner of an opium empire who thinks he deserves an eternal life. Matt is to give him his organs when he's old enough but some people with good hearts are willing to save Matt from his horrible fate. Will Matt escape his destiny? Will he find himself a decent life even if most people treat him like garbage? (Come on, he was harvested from a cow, how can he possibly be human right?...right?) 
 Although I didn't think the story was amazing, I have to admit that it is quite different from any other YA book that I've read. Set in a futuristic country of Mexico, I think Nancy Farmer did a really good job with the setting. It didn't feel fake or anything. Hell, I think I might as well have been born there! In addition to that, I really love the relation between Maria and Matt. In spite of the fact that I think that the third quarter of the book was a little boring, I'm sure that Nancy will make a better job in the sequels.
This book was everything I wanted it to be and more! Loved Ash and Tory's section, their romance was so sweet!

First of all, please do not read my review if you have not read Obsidian because otherwise this review will come as a spoiler to you. This leads me to say that I do recommend reading Obsidian first though chronologically this one happens first. 
 I have put off reading this book for the longest time because I am such a coward. Yep, went there! In our family we call it 'Old Yeller' cowardice as in 'great movie, heroic dog, heroic dog dies cue the tears' type of emotional cowardice. Now that you are going 'what the heck???' I'll explain. The popular Lux series began with Obsidian telling the story of a spunky human girl who happens to blog about books (my kinda gal) and the irascible alien hottie and his twin who live next door. In the story, the human girl learns about the Luxen race and in the process, she learns of the ill fated love affair between Daemon's twin Dawson and the human girl Bethany. Now knowing the bare bones of Dawson's story and that it doesn't end well, I was a bit skittish about reading said story with all the details knowing full well that I'd probably require a box of tissues nearby. And yes, I did tear up in the end, but I am glad I tugged up my big girl panties and read this one finally. I adored Dawson. He's so fun-loving and full of hope which really had me cheering for him to finally break free and win his chance at happiness even though I knew the outcome. 
 The story begins when Dawson spies the new girl in school. He is attracted to her smile from day one. For Bethany's part, she has just moved to West Virginia from Nevada so her mom could take care of her terminally ill older brother. She knows nobody and has all the trepidation of starting school in the midst of a bunch of strangers. One gorgeous stranger isn't shy and welcomes her with his friendly smile and chitchat. Shock of all, Dawson wants to spend time with her and go out on a date. 
 Soon Dawson and Bethany are doing the 'can't stop thinking about, staring at, texting, phoning and casual dating' phase. Dawson's luxen family and friends take quick notice of his interest in the human girl and they don't like it. He is warned away from her, but he doesn't care and takes his stand that he will continue to see Bethany. 
 Bethany can't help, but notice the odd things about Dawson when she spends more time with him. Its not until they share a kiss that she is suddenly brought to realize that odd just doesn't cover the half of it. The story dives into deeper more serious waters for Dawson and Bethany with his kind openly hostile toward the relationship, the Dept of Defense who monitor the Luxen sniffing around and the ever dangerous alien Aron race nearby hoping to tap the energy of a Luxen. 
 The plot was gentle for the most part as Dawson and Bethany's relationship progressed. It offered up scenes of typical high school teen relationship fare especially on Bethany's part, but it also had the layer of tension that the alien element added. Bethany could be described as your average pretty teenage girl with the exception being her love for art and her open-hearted acceptance of Dawson. Bethany is sensible of the risk and the sacrifice Dawson is making to be with her. I loved that she wasn't the needy, clinging type. I found the opportunity to get to know the Dawson that Daemon and Dee grieved for in Obsidian probably the best part of the story. Then there are those scenes with the triplets together- priceless stuff. I can report that apparently Andrew and Ash were always jerks even before Katy's arrival. 
 This classifies as Young Adult, but I would recommend this for older teens because the content does contain moderate language and moderate violence. 
 So, though it took me a while to get up my courage, I am so glad I read this novella length telling of Dawson's story. So much makes more sense now! Fair warning- have a tissue handy if you're an emotional-type like moi. Those who enjoy YA level Science Fiction Romance should give this story/series a try.

This book should be required reading for EVERYONE. If you're an introvert, or if you know an introvert, this book will be beneficial to you. They should teach it in schools, and I think it would be especially useful for managers, teachers and parents. I'd been wanting to read Susan Cain's book since I saw her TED talk some time ago, and I'm so glad that I finally got around to it. Cain is pretty magnanimous and diplomatic toward extroverts, but I tend to think a little more harshly in the sense that I think our society's propensity toward what Cain calls the "Extrovert Ideal" is poisoning our culture. Quiet explained about my own personality and helped me to understand why I do some of the things I do, including the way I relate to others, how I've operated in the work environment and what I should truly be doing with my life. Cain is right when she asserts that introverts have so much to offer. I just hope that our culture can come to realize it and stop crippling them with unrealistic expectations. Anyway, I'm still processing everything I read in this book and still drawing my own conclusions. I wish I'd been able to read this years ago.  The only real complaint I have is that Katniss is...well, I used a very derogatory word when I said it aloud, but let's substitute a stubborn house goat instead. The crux of the story is that there are various people who live in the Pendleton which is a Gilded Age mansion that has been converted into apartments. Unfortunately for the residents of the Pendleton, the dwelling has been built on a fault in the space time continum. Every thirty eight years the residents are propelled to the future which is filled with killer Pogromites which can best be described as the creatures such as those from Aliens. If you survive the Pogromites you get to return to your time and if you don't you become a permanent resident of the Pendleton. As if all of this wasn't terrible enough, the residents of the Pendleton are living with a homicidal maniac by the name of Mickey Dime. At the end of the novel there is an explanation of why the events unfolded at the Pendleton and it is very reminiscent of a science gone wrong ala Michael Chrichton. You could probably call this the Dean Koontz ode to Michael Chrichton novel. For the majority of the story the reader is left to wonder just what exactly is happening at the Pendleton. To further confuse matters, there is a large cast of characters to keep remember and keep track of. In the end the work pays off as the novel reaches it's climatic conclusion.

(Review originally posted at Fictionally Inclined.) 
 *4.5 STARS 
 Jill Shalvis is easily my favorite recent discovery. Her Lucky Harbor series is exactly what I needed in my life right now. I will review the first two soon, but I just finished this one. Since I actually have time to write a review, am inclined to do so, and am seriously feeling the need to gush about this book, though, you are getting the reviews for this series out of order. Sorry! 
 Last night, I was at a leadership overnight, and everyone went to bed at 4 AM. Despite having been exhausted half an hour earlier, I was wide awake. I decided to relax by reading for a few minutes, then go to bed. I finally went to bed just after 5, having finished reading The Sweetest Thing (Lucky Harbor #2) and the first chapter of Head Over Heels. And let me tell you: If I had had Head Over Heels at that moment, I absolutely would have stayed up the rest of the night. No doubt in my mind. That is how invested I was in Chloe and Sawyer. From the first time they appeared in the first book of the series, I wanted to know more about them, both as separate characters and together. The dynamic between the two of them fascinated me, and by the end of the second book, their chemistry was practically sparking off the pages of my book. I have been impatiently waiting for their book since I first met them less than a week ago, and after reading the sneak preview last night (this morning?), I was absolutely rabid in my desire for this book. Let me put it this way: Hallowed FINALLY came into the library today. I read Head Over Heels first without even a second thought. 
 As excited as I was for this book, though, I was equally nervous. Sometimes, an amazing couple is built up in the background of a series. Then they finally get their own book, but it's disappointing because even if the book itself is fine, it just doesn't live up to the build-up. This has happened to be twice in my recent reading history. I didn't want that to happen in Head Over Heels, or I would be heartbroken. Thankfully, this was absolutely not the case. I loved this book! I loved everything about it. Every character, every argument, every so-much-sexual-tension-it-will-curl-your-toes-and-they-haven't-even-had-sex-yet interaction, every scorching kiss, every family bonding moment, every joke, every revelation, every piece of advice, every romantic moment. Here, have a list. Lists are always the answer. 
 Things I loved in/about Head Over Heels: 
 * Chloe. Oh, Chloe. She is one of those characters that you start out the series thinking she's just another free spirited character. Then, as you learn more and more about her, you understand all these layers and complexities that make her unique and fun and wonderful. I usually despise the "I can't say 'I love you,'" hang-up. But she had legitimate reasons, and Shalvis made me believe it. I also like how she used it, but I won't go into that. 
 * Sawyer. His confusion about Chloe and how he felt about her in the beginning was just so adorable. He was so stoic and straight arrow, and she disturbed his world. Always one of my favorite tropes. He was just such a legitimately good guy. 
 * Chloe and Sawyer's relationship! I don't frequently read law enforcer/trouble maker romances, but this owe was wonderful. Even though the relationships are quite different, they reminded me of Stephanie and Ranger (my OTP) from the Stephanie Plum series a couple times, which was a definite plus for me. But they were completely unique, and their relationship just had such an endearing quality. I loved the progression of it, from the confusion and the fighting against their feelings and the arguing and cautious stand-offs to the moment they finally cave to the HEA. I believed it every second of the way. 
 * Lance's background story, even though it made me happy and broke my heart all at the same time 
 * Severe asthma is not generally an issue addressed in books. I know practically nothing about asthma, but I thought it was handled well. Chloe's asthma was also something different about the book that made it memorable. 
 * It dealt with everyday things like morning breath in a cute and realistic fashion. 
 * Maddie, Tara, Jax, and Ford all stayed the same. They were friends and family and cracked jokes and picked on each other and interacted like people really do. They didn't become sickeningly sweet or corny or unrealistically wise. They just were. 
 * They referenced Friends! 
 * Shalvis continued starting each chapter with a little bit of wisdom, and the wisdom selections she chooses somehow really fit the main character of the book. Chloe's cracked me up, of course. Exhibit A) 
 Always remember, you're unique. Just like everyone else. * While I do, of course, enjoy the sexy!times, I like that this one was a little lighter on them than the first two. It worked better with the story that way, although I can't talk about why without going into spoilers. Let me say, though, the sexy!times that were there? I definitely needed a cold shower a couple times! 
 * Chloe's continuing obsession with the Magic 8 Ball app. 
 (view spoiler)[ * This one specific moment in the book that just hit me. At one point in the book, Chloe wakes up, and the first thing she feels is Sawyer. She thinks he is there, even though there's no reason for her to think that, but once she opens her eyes, she realizes he isn't. This was the moment I truly believed she had fallen for him. I've read the "reached for him but he wasn't there and it felt wrong" scene a million, but this was different. Even though it could be explained in a million ways -- she had been dreaming about him, she subconsciously recognized his lingering scent in the room, etc. -- I just felt like this revealed her innate desire to be with Sawyer. All the time, both sleeping and awake. And this was a huge step for her, so far beyond all previous relationships. Her expectation and disappointment were tangible, and I felt what she felt at that moment. It was a brilliantly written little moment. 
 * This quote. It is from Sawyer's POV after Chloe passed out from lack of oxygen due to her asthma during sex with him. Normally, I wouldn't bring something like this up because I try to keep spoilers to the minimum. But this was another of those little lines that got to me with its simple, stark power. 
 Earlier, in his shower, her breathing had started out quiet like this, but then she'd gone up in flames for him. He'd loved it, loved the way she'd panted for more, clutching at him as if she was afraid he'd stop... And then in the very next beat, when she'd started to suffocate, all he'd wanted to do was breathe for her. 
 (hide spoiler)] 
 Overall, Head Over Heels was a wonderful read! I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys a cute, fun romance with depth and sizzling chemistry. I would also suggest that you read the first two in the series first because Chloe and Sawyer have fantastic build-up, particularly in the second one.

 ...I do kind of wish I'd waited, though. 
 There were so many ups and downs to the rollercoaster of Sevin and Evangeline. I loved Sevin for the most part -- he's the brooding alpha male, but he's also the guy who isn't afraid to shed a tear (and those tears certainly brought on a few of my own). However... That is not to say the book was all peaches and roses for me. While I won't pretend to understand the lifestyle these characters live in (however, it does intrigue me), I did feel that the whole Elle-Sevin, Sevin-Evangeline thing was a bit much. The want and the desire Sevin had for Evangeline should have been enough; when things with Elle went terribly wrong, though, he should not have taken emotions out on Evangeline. 
 I also felt a bit jilted at the end... The last chapter was emotional and the epilogue? The first part of it had me seeing through a veil of tears. However, the view point's (vp) thoughts on Evangeline weren't exactly just in my mind -- the vp didn't have a whole lot to go on and it bothered me how welcoming vp was toward Sevin, yet still not sold on Evangeline. This would have been one of the few cases where I wasn't a fan of the epilogue, and that makes me sad. I wanted so much for Evangeline and Sevin, and I just didn't feel that they got everything they deserved (and was completely heartbroken about Sevin's thoughts for the reason as to why their life ended up the way it did). 
 All in all, though, the writing was easy to follow, the dialogue (internal and external) was realistic, and the emotion? The emotion was there.

I seriously would give this book 6 stars if I could. 
 Reader thoughts: This world is so rich. Part of me thinks I can see Robert Jordan's influence. All of the cultures and side characters carry their own importance (even the little details, like the way the safe hand is treated or the length of the eyebrows!). Part of me thinks this is just Sanderson at his best. Somehow, he continues to get better and better, which just excites me so much for the rest of the Stormlight series. I've heard there will be 10. 
 One of my favorite quotes: "Palanquins are for women." 
 "Ain't nothing wrong with women. Some of my relatives are women." 
 (Lopen has some of the best lines.) 
 Every time Kaladin and Shallon spend more than a page together (indeed, whenever they say more than two words to each other), there's a flurry of witty responses and hilarious insults. "I offend! Give boots!" and "Stealer of women's virtue! No, not virtue, wrong word. Stealer of women's vestiture!" HAHA! 
 And there were plenty of sad parts too. Syl! I was so mad at Kaladin, the storm-stubborn fool. Moash! Jasnah! 
 So many moments I wanted to jump and shout, "hurray!" because the characters finally accomplished what they had been trying. So many moments I wanted to shake sense into them (esp Kaladin, who claims the lighteyes are prejudiced, but really he's the worst). 
 Writer thoughts: These characters have some dark pasts. A writer does that because it can make the characters stronger and more relatable. Neither one of those happened here. Kaladin and Shallon have pasts so dark that they are broken characters, and I doubt any reader could really relate with what they went through. So, why? Because darkness is interesting, in a way. Readers don't want characters to get off easily. It's satisfying, in some way, when a character goes through metaphorical hell and still comes out a hero. Encouraging, because at least real life isn't that bad. 
 Plus, when the broken characters show they can be reforged, I want to cheer for their strength. This is personality at its best. A strong character isn't one who can punch someone's brains out, but one who can take everything life throws and still stand up and defend what is right. That is true strength.

I would recommend it on those merits alone, but it is also a key book in American history literature as most will agree!

2008 Printz Award winner! 
 I'm going to echo several other reviews here: this is beautifully written, atmospheric, and engrossing, and yet it just didn't do it for me. 
 When Symone's generous uncle offers to whisk her and her mom away to Paris, Sym jumps at the chance--and when her mom's passport goes missing at the last moment, Sym looks forward to exploring Paris with Uncle Victor. But after one night, he reveals that the trip is bigger than Paris. They're going south. Very far south. Antarctica-south, where Sym has dreamed of going. But Uncle Victor isn't just going for the tourism--he's bringing Sym on his expedition to find proof that the Earth is hollow, and that there is an entire society living just under the outer crust. As Victor's obsessive madness becomes more apparent, Sym talks over the situation with someone who understands it all: Titus Oates, the explorer who died here over 90 years ago, whose voice lives in her head and is her confidant, her sounding board, her only friend. 
 Yeah, they're pretty much all crazy. But that's the thing: I'm honestly not sure at what point I was supposed to realize that. At 14 years old, Sym has an imaginary friend, a 90-years-dead explorer, and that's right from the beginning. Read this review and more on my blog From A to Z. 
 Shut Out is a modern retelling of the Greek play Lysistrata, which is the story of a group of women who decide to withhold sex from their husbands as an incentive to end a war. I'd never heard of Lysistrata before reading Shut Out, and it's such an interesting idea to me. Sex is undeniably a very powerful and influential tool in our society and I was intrigued to see what Keplinger would do with the storyline in a modern high school context. 
 I thought Lissa was a little annoying when we first meet her at the start of the novel. She's understandably frustrated with Randy, but she feels like an overbearing parent in the way she communicates with him, and she's generally very naive about him throughout the course of the story. 
 Things really get interesting when the boys start fighting back against the sex strike, and that's when I found myself really enjoying it. I love Cash, the leader of the boys, and his interactions with Lissa are great. Despite leading the guys against her, he is a total sweetheart, and I found myself torn between wanting Lissa to stick to her guns and lead the girls to victory, and wishing she would just give in to her awesome chemistry with Cash. 
 I also really loved the strong female friendships that Lissa developed with the other girls participating in the strike, particularly Chloe and Ellen. So many YA novels are focused so intensely on the romance aspect, so I'm always happy to find good friendship networks along with the swoony guy and fun romance. 
 The main issue that I had with Shut Out was the way it handled the girls' discussions and revelations about sex, which is unfortunate since that was such a huge focus of the novel. It's not that I don't think it's important to talk about these things, and I think the overall message was good, but there's an art to doing it subtly and tastefully, and I felt like I was just being hit over the head with it. The girls' conversations (and Lissa's inner monologues) were incredibly forced and ended up feeling preachy and obvious instead of natural. It was enough to make me roll my eyes while reading. 
 Though somewhat disappointed, I did enjoy the novel overall, and I'm interested to try another of Keplinger's stories, especially since I've heard good things about The DUFF. I'd recommend Shut Out if you're looking for a light, contemporary romantic read and you don't mind a slightly heavy-handed message along with it.

Synopsis 
 Seventeen year old Meg's been at loggerheads with her father all her life, and this time she's gone and done something so outrageous he's given up all hope: she got arrested. Just her luck, her 'cop', has a lesson to teach her. He makes sure that Meg and her associate trespassers each spend a weeks worth of nights, during spring break, with one of the emergency services their little escape disturbed. Guess what? Meg gets the 'police', or rather Officer After, the officer who arrested her high, drunk, and pre-sex on an off limits railway bridge, in the first place. 
 A week with John After will open her eyes and ultimately make her face the consequences of her past behaviour and the unhealthy, lonely direction her life is heading in. Of course the irritating, sexy way he manages to scrape under her skin and singe her doesn't impede this process although it does lead her to push both of them right to the edge... 
 Just how hard is it to break a cop? And does she want to break him after all? Especially when sitting back and baking cobbler for him seems so much more appealing. 
 My Review 
 I haven't read anything by Jennifer Echols before, except 'The Boys Next Door' which was okay but not 'punchy'. This novel is definitely 'punchy', it's got attitude. I loved the character of Meg, even if she's not really anything like me, well not in the life experience arena. Meg's self-analysis and eventual 'growth' were all believable and raw, they made me feel shallow truth be told, and I love the book for that. I think it has some very worthwhile things to say. 
 The scenes in this novel and the way they were portrayed were all very fresh. The novel did make me smile. It's a page-turner - I stayed up quite late for the first half and came right back to it the next day. For a chick lit summer read it makes the list, and even better I can say it is cleverly written. It didn't make me laugh out loud or cry, it wasn't as good as it could have been, but it was GOOD. I was fully engaged throughout and Meg and John made an interesting 'high tension' combination - Jennifer's writing is spot on (and dreamy!). I will recommend this book to my friends. I did feel that the novel came to a rather abrupt ending, although it was 'fairytale' and optimistic. 
 Personal Verdict 
 I'm hoping for a sequel and I'll be looking out for anything new published by Jennifer in the future!

Let me tell you a story about a boy.. his name is Cole Walker and soon he is going to become somebody's hero... 
 Samantha Young does it again in an impressive way. Echoes of Scotland Street is my favorite book from the series, in which you can read the story of Cole and Shannon. Cole is Jo's brother from the second book, all grown up and ready to steal out hearts permanently. Shannon is newly introduced, but as soon as you'll meet her you will realize how good she is for Cole. 
 First thing to keep in mind while reading this book: appearances can be deceiving!! When you see a hot guy with tattoos, rocking a wonderful smile and looking at you with piercing eyes, you think he is a player!! WRONG!! Cole is everything of those above minus the player part. Having had a though childhood, abused my his mother and raised practically by his big sister, he is now a grown up who is trying to figure things out. Discovering his passion for tattoos thanks to Cam (book 2), he takes on a hob at a tattoo parlor and there he meets Shannon. Well, they already know each other but I will let you explore that on your own. 
 As in all the books when you have a gorgeous guy and a beautiful girl, sparks fly, but Shannon is not letting her attraction to Cole get ahead of her. She is hurt by the bad choices made in relationships in the past and won't allow anybody to physically or emotional hurt her anymore. From this point on, a truly powerful struggle begins, where Cole has to prove Shannon that love is worth the risk although life wasn't always gentle with you. 
 Cole in my opinion is the best male character from all the books. You can clearly see him evolve from the shy boy presented in the second book to the man he is today. Jo is the main reason he managed to get away from the darkness in which he could have ended because of his mother. He grown up so well, focusing on his talent, having an objective in life that guided him. His love life wasn't so lucky, but everything settles down when he sees Shannon. Despite the player look, he believes in true love, in loyalty and in treating women well. Cam and Jo where the perfect example for him in terms of relationships and family, giving him a goal to achieve. 
 Shannon on the other side doesn't believe in love any more because of the abused she suffered in past relationships. I understand her reluctance in approaching someone, and nevertheless a person that reminds you of a certain type of guy. I love the way Cole managed to break her barriers and show her what true love can reached once you let it in. 
 I liked that Samantha introduces a certain theme in the book- physical abuse. A women should never go through what Shannon went through. This is a lesson to learn for all girls and women out there who tolerate violence. Everybody deserves tenderness and love no matter the mistakes they make and second chances have to be taken in order to live a happy life. 
 Echoes of Scotland Street present us our favorite characters from the past books, we get to see them all-together in the wonderful unity they created. Their bond is even stronger than before and I liked the way they embraced Shannon as their own, without judging or asking questions. Everything is so natural with them that you kind of wish you have such friends in real life to stand by you and accepting your true colors. 
 One of my favorite parts was the ending because I have never read one such as that before. It was unique and exciting. 
 I love the book and recommend all the series with an open heart! 
 5 stars!!

 Full Review: Everybody knows Cate Cahill and her sisters are eccentric. Too pretty, too reclusive, and far too educated for their own good. But the truth is even worse: they're witches. And if their secret is discovered by the priests of the Brotherhood, it would mean an asylum, a prison ship--or an early grave.

Agnieszka is a challenging daughter to her villager parents. Her father is the woodcutter. She is constantly tearing her clothes, and messing them up and she also strays too far into the woods that surround the village. The woods are not safe, and they seem to infect animals and people with a kind of madness that sometimes literally transforms them, and not in a good way. It has been this way for so long that the villagers are used to it. They live in a war zone and it seems the wood is winning lately. 
 The wood took over an entire village recently; just up the road. 
 Twenty years ago, the queen ran into it - allegedly holding the hand of her lover, a prince from the rival kingdom - and she never came back. Both countries are still at war but currently have an uneasy truce. Her sons are now adults and heroes to the common people, and the king still rules alone. 
 But when the wood attacks the village, it is the Dragon that they call. 
 He always comes, and he always helps, but he is only one man. 
 And the wood is winning. 
 *** 
 I saw a promo for this book a long time ago and the first paragraph just grabbed me. Recently it was half price on book depository and I lashed out and got the hardback. (being thrifty, I usually wait for the paperback edition.) 
 "Our Dragon doesn't eat the girls he takes, no matter what stories they tell outside our valley. We hear them sometimes, from travelers passing through. They talk as though we were doing human sacrifice, and he were a real dragon. Of course that's not true: he may be a wizard and immortal, but he's still a man, and our fathers would band together and kill him if he wanted to eat one of us every ten years. He protects us against the Wood, and we're grateful, but not that grateful." 
 The person that everyone thinks the Dragon will take is Agnieszka's best friend, Kasia. She is so pretty and accomplished that her parents have raised her sure in the assumption that it will be her that is the chosen one. But he chooses Agnieszka when she shows an unexpected magic ability. 
 Kasia tells her that she has seen a tree reach for her that's why she is so clumsy, but she didn't say anything at the time. Agnieszka always found food in the wood, as if the forest gave it to her, or conjured it for her. 
 The dragon looks like a young man but has to be at least 150 years old. He lives in a massive castle, all alone and he has forgotten how to train a person, or how to comfort a homesick girl. Especially one who was ill prepared to be chosen. He's traditional, rigid, happy with order and things in their proper place, and Agnieszka is chaos incarnate in his well-ordered world. 
 She messes up constantly and he always shouts at her. 
 For Agnieszka certain books in the library clamour to be read and they are often the works of witch women rather than the formal schooling of the men. She finds a tiny notebook that belonged to baba yaga. The Dragon tells her the books are useless. She tries to explain to the Dragon that he does it wrong. It's as if you walk in the forest and you need to change your path if there is a fallen tree; but the Dragon finds it hard to use her green, living, and changing magic. 
 I thought this idea of women's magic was fantastic. 
 Within months of her arrival at the castle, there is an incident and the Dragon has to leave. That night, she sees the warning lights go up in her village. She raids his potion cupboard and goes to help, rationalizing that she is better than nothing. 
 Somehow she gets through the attack. He grouses at her that she has wasted expensive potions. 
 But days later her friend Kasia is taken by some walkers (a kind of praying mantis like wood creature). She and the Dragon rescue Kasia and drag her out of the heart tree that holds her, but she is forever changed by it, and the two magic wielders working together have thrown an almighty stone into the magic pond and the ripples reach everywhere. 
 Next, princes and political emissaries are knocking at their door.

The Goldfinch starts out a bit strangely, but I soon got immersed in the story of Theodore Decker. Narrated in the first person, an adult Theo recounts his life starting with the the moment his life took its most dramatic turn. At 13, Theo is a victim of bombing inside the Metropolitan Museum of Art. He survives but loses his mother. While escaping the aftermath of the museum bombing he takes a masterpiece painting, The Goldfinch by Carel Fabritius (1654) which remains with him on many levels for the rest of the novel. We follow Theo as he gets sent to live with his wealthy nerdy childhood friend, Andy Barbour, befriends Hobbie a friendly man in the antique and furniture restoration trade, develops a love for the red-headed Pippa - similarly struck with tragedy, goes to live in Nevada when his father and his new girlfriend when he eventually turns up, and develops a close friendship to Boris - a classmate and hard-living Russian world traveler. Theo struggles to deal with the loss of his mother, assimilate into a complete unfamiliar settings, and navigate an unclear world ahead. This all culminates in the thriller portion of the book which takes place in Amsterdam where Theo kills a man, contemplates/attempts suicide, and eventually gets a solution to the worry that has haunted him since he was 13. 
 This is a immense work spanning almost 800 pages. It has been widely popular since its publication in late 2013 and been very polarizing among readers and critics. It won the 2014 Pulitzer Prize for fiction. In my opinion the book has a feel very much like The Catcher in the Rye. Some people would love this book, others would hate it. I loved most of it. Even though, its told in the retrospective first person, to me it felt like a omniscient first person narration where I almost didn't realize the agency of the narrator, but was engulfed in the description of the present scenes and the fully formed thoughts and feelings of Theo in those specific moments. 
 The writing is indeed beautifully constructed. Tartt does an amazing job conveying the little things. Descriptions of the social workers, the doormen, the boyfriends, the girlfriends, the roommates, the dog, the bodyguards, the Nevada landscape, modern day New York, a piece of furniture, the things that real people would latch onto, the emotions and thoughts and actions - they are all painted so real. The descriptions are substantial, but also substantive. The writing never felt overly embellished (not everyone's opinion) and the plot did not drag. It is appropriately referential and has some elements of humor interspersed with a more tragic, melancholy and at times philosophical quality. The dialogue is genuine, appropriately emotional, and captures moments well. 
 I immensely enjoyed the small moments in the book, the moment where your foster dad stands up for you as if you were his biological son, the moment your dorky friend covers for you, the moment you are able to fulfill someone else's promise when the promiser is disbelieved, the way a dog remembers someone after 10 years, remembering how someone else remembered something so dear to you, the little objects or thoughts that recurred through the book and so many more things. 
 The story at times seems fantastical and improbable. The low lows of drugs and alcoholism and constant death occupy many of the pages in this book. At times, The Goldfinch is not a "fun" read, and rather more anxiety inducing. Theo becomes more and more a jerk. Its hard to find sympathy towards him towards the end of the book. How can you continue the book when you hate its hero? Theo is dumb, has almost no redeeming qualities, and yet I think overall the book worked. Towards the end I felt the structure and style of the writing itself instead of being immersed in the setting myself. I began to feel Tartt's hand for the first time in orchestrating the plot ending. In the end I give Theo a pass as the narrator, but Tartt as an author diverted from the tone of the work a bit. This ending may be purposeful and I respect the attempt, but it doesn't quite work for me. 
 Stray observations: 
 1. The ending has a lot of philosophizing. I enjoyed how despite being alcoholics and drug addicts, Theo and Boris are portrayed as cultured - reading classic novels, being familiar with classical music etc. They philosophize based on real works/ideas and real emotions and real thoughts. It makes the philosophical ending believable. 
 2. I was being educated a lot. On furniture restoration, aristocratic life in New York, drugs and alcohol, art history and many other topics. Moreover, there are tons of references and many I wanted to look up in the middle of reading this book. 
 3. Again, there were so many small moments and details that made me smile. Some moments were also heartbreaking especially in retrospect. 
 4. I can understand why some found no emotional latch that resonated with them and hated the book. 
 5. The Amsterdam plot was the weakest. Too fast paced and not developed as the rest of the plot. 
 6. My relationship to many of the characters were more intense than long-lasting. I had strong emotions attached to many of them. Yet, the timing of the ending was good for me. I didn't need to find out what happened next for them. 
 Rating: For me 4 / 5. I related with Theo. Many will not.

I'd say its a cross between Chick Lit and Contemporary Romance. 
 We follow the story between the 2 women who have this very handsome doctor (Nick) in their lives. One is Tessa, Nick's wife, the other is Valerie, the mother of his most recent patient. I don't want to give the whole story away, but you can probably guess what happens and why its set up this way. This is the 2nd time Emily Giffin has shown both sides of an affair. The first was Something Borrowed--we got to see "the other woman," Rachel's side of things. Then she wrote a book called Something Blue and we got to see Darcy, the fiance's side of things. Speaking of Rachel, she and Dex are small bit characters in this book, which was a huge bonus! Anyways, I think its really interesting how this story played out. In the Darcy-Rachel-Dex Triangle, I totally rooted for Rachel, because Darcy was such a B----!  Emily Giffin is great at whipping out her magnifying glass, and really showing us all the hidden agendas in relationships. Not just marriages and affairs, but also friendships and parents and their children. She does it masterfully again here, so even if you are not big on reading a book about an affair, I think you will enjoy this book! 
 I also really liked the way she handled the affair--unlike Dex and Rachel's affair, this one was a lot less about sex and the physical. I give this book 4 stars!

 The fatal flaw, I believe, were the characters. They lacked depth. Sofia, summed up, was infuriating. I know characters cannot always act the way in which you would in situations, but Sofia defied reason. She is kidnapped from her home, sexually and physically abused throughout and shown a world that is more frightening and dangerous than anything she could of ever imagined. Yes she was beautiful, yes she has a tormented past, yes she is wonderfully creative. But that was it, her past was not delved into, other traits not explored. 
 Derek was no better; conflicted, he stands idly by whilst his supposed amour is sexually abused and emotionally spent by his manic brother. 
 Bens turn up seemed too easy and I find I did 
 not take a liking to him due to the fact he turned up at the end. Kudos to him though for being the only level headed character in the book. 
 I would of loved to have met the other girls more, but all I got were a few sparse mentionings and lines of their going on's. As well as the guards Kyle and (forgive me, his name has slipped my mind). 
 Due to the length of the book the world of The Shade is not explored, such as Derek's father, The Hunters, Cora and Derek's past. I know there are other books but an enthralling first is the best. 
 I found time passed too quickly and there were not enough events and occurrences to keep the plot alive. 
 Insta love is a pet hate for me, and even though time passes in this (I think), her feelings were not expressed therefore not justified enough to warrant the title of -true- love. 
 I've been a tad brutal, but I am not utterly bashing this book. It was an enjoyable read and I found sections to be interesting and action filled. It was a tad irksome but enjoyable nonetheless. Choosing the latter, I recommend this to anyone favouring quick, easy reads.

I have read many books set in and around the Holocaust and all are devastating in their own way, but this story cuts to the heart of the issue then and now. A young nine-year-old German boy full of adventure, hope for the future and innocence befriends a young Jewish boy from the Auschwitz concentration camp. Bruno, the German boy, is the son of the commandant of the camp and has none of the hatred and prejudicial feelings that brought about that horror in history. He is open and honest and good and pure and willing to see the good in others. 
 Their friendship evolves with the wire fence separating them. Only twice do they meet without the barrier and both times end with bad results. 
 This is a book that will tear your heart out, but yet tells such an important story. It tells this story of the Holocaust in a way that would appeal to readers of every age. Bruno will be one character that I will never forget.

It would seem I'm beginning the year by deep diving into comforting, non-challenging reads! I just really haven't wanted to read anything too demanding or that might stress me out or be terribly sad, and have decided to embrace the fact that reading for pleasure is a completely valid way to spend my time. Not every book has to make my brain bigger or dazzle me with its literary prowess; sometimes you just want a book that whisks you away and take you on a romp that makes you smile. 
 That's pretty much what When a Scot Ties the Knot did perfectly. I like that Dare's historicals have a sense of whimsy to them and don't take themselves too seriously. That said, I tried to read the two previous books in this series and was disappointed to find that I could not get into them AT ALL (I found the writing mawkish and the stories/characters just really uninspiring). This one felt more like her Spindle Cove series (which I really love) and worked MUCH better for me; I was hooked from the start. It's super fluffy and gentle and has a lot of heart. A marriage of convenience + half-hearted blackmail + a bluestocking & a brawny dude in a kilt, all of it taking place in a castle... what's not to like? 
 A note: I know some others have complained about the anachronistic dialogue in parts, but that didn't bother me one bit or really seem all that noticeable to me. I mean, you wouldn't confuse the dialogue for something out of Jane Austen or even Georgette Heyer, but it didn't jar me from the story. And for those that say these might as well be contemporaries, I guess it's a failure of the imagination, but I just don't really see how most of her novels would work as they are all about women dealing with the strictures of society and the fact that they either don't fit the mold or don't wish too. I'm not saying this has no modern parallels, but I think that having to work within the more restrictive boundaries of what was expected of women and how tightly their futures were tied to marriage back then makes these stories more compelling when set in a historical setting. But, maybe that's just me and my preferences. I guess I just see these as escapist fantasy, really, and as long as they feel emotionally accurate, I suppose I don't much care if they're historically precise.

 But as I found out it's based on a book, I was really excited.

 Did I really want to support a story that lived off the "I have to change so that guy falls in love with me" cliche? Not really. 
 I support self love. NO ONE should change who they are to get someone to notice you. 
 Well, I started to read the book anyway, SO ready to tear it apart. But I was surprised that the story was everything but that!

It doesn't seem like too many new Urban Fantasy series are coming out lately. Authors are either expanding beloved series, ending them, or moving into Paranormal Romance and Young/New Adult. So that's why The Line caught my eye. It takes place in Savannah, one of my favorite Urban Fantasy cities next to New Orleans. Then it threw witches into the mix. And if I'm honest witches are my guilty pleasure for Urban Fantasy. True, I'm a hard core werewolves and vampires fan. Deep down witches will always hold a secret place in my heart. Sadly very few things that utilize witches make them believable and well . . . not childish. Or over the top Satan's spawn!! 
 That's why within a few pages of The Line I was hooked. Ohhhh, so hooked. Mercy Taylor is promptly introduced while giving her Lair's Tour. While it's unclear if she really needs the money, one thing is clear this book is gonna have drama! The main character is from a prominent--filthy rich--family. The Lairs Tour is a job Mercy created where she goes around taking people on tours lying about the city and places. Making up or spinning stories off the top of her head. To be honest I think it's brilliant and I would hands down take that tour! With the rich writing, I felt like I was sweating it up in Savannah and indeed on that tour. After the tour was done I was all to ready to enjoy the rest of Mercy's life and world. 
 Boy is The Line all about the drama. Crazy soap opera family drama! One Life to Live and All My Children may be off the air, but The Line finally delivered the fix I've been hungering for! All the character's have some serious issues, and what I'd fondly refer to as zany personalities. From Mercy's crazy as hell head of the house, slushed up aunt, and gay uncle there's plenty of personalities to butt heads. Though the big fail for me was how evil Mercy's sister is, and at no point was there any love on the sister's part towards Mercy to make me feel for the relationship. In that one huge wicked-sister plot point was the books fatal flaw. 
 Yet, the drama mixed in with all the mysteries, multiple plots, and drama--yes loads of drama--made it all better. Yes. There was plenty of predictable points, but Horn definitely made up for it and pulled a few over my eyes. Now I'm not going to ruin anything and won't dig to much into the plot. However, I will say there are plenty of players here and it kind of made me think of Game of Thrones witches edition. While there wasn't any dramatic deaths, everyone is a player and the succession for the "throne" is on. (OK, I was watching Game of Thrones while I read The Line, so take the comparison with a grain of salt. They both definitely have drama.) 
 Mercy is a pretty nice character, at times she comes off as a martyr and I wished she'd get her bitch on and smack down on some people! But there in lies the breath of fresh are that The Line brings to the genre. Mercy is a genuine and nice person, one who wants to see the best in people. Even when her own romance is tanked and everyone she knows has betrayed her somehow. The drama, characters, plot, and the magic here is soooooooooooo refreshing. When the last page turned this unearthly glowing happened and I was transported to my happy book place that had been unreachable this year with my book funk. (At least from new titles/authors.) The Line made me feel refreshed and brave to go out and try new authors again! Bravo Horn! Bravo. Take my money.

This was a different kind of YA novel where the female protagonist has her head screwed on pretty straight. There was some pretty slow lead up to the more exciting and fun-to-read shenanigans, but I liked the ending quite a bit. Sometimes the stories that try to buck the "Happily Ever After" come off sounding a bit try-hard and empty; this does a good job of avoiding that. 
 The writing style was a bit odd at times, and there were many occasions that I doubted whether many 15 year old girls would be able to attain this particular level of self awareness, self assuredness, and intelligence. It felt like a bit of adult wish fulfillment in this way, almost like the author was rewriting her less than feminist, less confident past with all the wisdom and hindsight of adulthood. 
 The main character, Frankie, DOES act in predictably teen ways: she finds Matthew attractive and enjoys kissing him, she yells at an ex in a public place, she stays with Matthew even though their relationship is built on lies & little more than physical attraction, but I also found her introspection about it all pretty far beyond a typical 15 year old's years. 
 Still, I especially enjoyed Frankie's large scale prank, and liked how the boys' reaction to said prank was pretty realistic. Her boyfriend did not understand, did not magically appreciate her deeper thought processes despite their very superficial relationship, and I appreciated that. 
 In all, it's a quick, fairly light read. If you can make it to the last third of the book, I think you'll like the ending.

There's something Marcus Zusak wrote in "The Book Thief" which describes my sentiments perfectly: 
 "Sometimes you read a book so special that you want to carry it around with you for months after you've finished just to stay near it." 
 That's it. That's Anna for me. 
 When I was invited to read and review Anna and the French Kiss, by Stephanie Perkins, I was delighted. When I finished reading it, I felt... what did I feel, exactly? Happy? Warm? Hopeful? Satisfied? Seventeen again? All those and certainly quite a few of those good adjectives you can think of, too. 
 The book is about a girl who is sent to study in Paris against her will. Of course that would a bad thing for Anna. No teenager enjoys having other makind decisions for them, 
 Wrong. 
 Anna soon meets the most perfect boy in the world, Etienne, and he shows her that life is so much more than the things we're used to considering important. Because things are not important. People are. Life is all about friendship. It's about trying new things. It's about being brave. And it's about caring. 
 Anna and the French Kiss is a love story, in the pure sense of the world "love". No appellations required. The characters are sarcastic, funny, honest, lovable, and struggle with issues that we all can identify with. The narrative is hilarious (even Harry Potter is the victim of a joke) and easy to read. You start a chapter, and you don't want to stop until you reach the last page. 
 Go read it too!

I began my journey with Harry in 2002, a late bloomer with the series by all respects. I read the first four in a row, then read them again each time a new book came out. I suffered the same grief as everyone else when I finished The Deathly Hallows. In the nine years since I have reread the books and watched all of the movies several times. I've been sorted into Ravenclaw on Pottermore and envisioned the day when I can walk down the streets of Diagon Alley at Universal Studios. So it was with much excitement, and some trepidation, that I picked this book up the day it came out, July 31, 2016. 
 Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is easily one of my favorite additions to the Harry Potter series. Although it was written as a stage play, it doesn't read like one at all. There is plenty of description to bring readers back to the wizarding world that we know and love, while leaving us to fill in the gaps through our own imagination. Harry, Ginny, Hermione, and Ron have all returned along with several other familiar faces you would expect to see and one or two that you might not. It contains what we've come to expect from Harry's world - a race against time in order to save the world from being picked up, turned over, and rearranged by a most dark and improbable force. But there's also a new world that Harry and his friends need to battle, which sometimes feels as difficult to manage as a blast ended skrewt - marriage, parenthood, and careers. 
 If you haven't read the book, please be aware that spoilers follow. Proceed at your own risk. 
 (view spoiler)[ 
 Harry and Ginny have a pretty normal relationship - after many years of wedded bliss, they're in need of couples therapy and a communication workshop or two. Harry's anxiety requires a few of Luna's yoga classes along with consultation from Molly and Arthur on what not to say to your children. But I'm a working parent too. I get it. Sometimes you lose your cool and say things you don't mean. Sometimes your family lets you down. Sometimes your job sucks. And I don't even have to deal with the guilt of letting everyone die for me and saving the world. It's no wonder Harry's having a hard time with it all. His reactions weren't what we would have expected when he was 19 years younger, but they were what I would expect from a 40-year old man in his situation now. 
 In comparison, Hermione and Ron were a bit of a let down. Rowling's later regret over pairing them up seemed pretty apparent throughout the story. Ron lost so much of his strong character development from the seventh book, and spent most of the book attempting to provide comic relief. Hermione is now consumed by her role as Minister of Magic, leaving little time for her marriage or her family. She even admits that she spends more time at the office than with Ron. It's no wonder then that they ended up with some relationship troubles. Also Hermione didn't quote Hogwarts: A History even once. Who else will remind me that I can't apparate inside Hogwarts grounds? 
 If you've stuck with my review this long, I thank you as this last bit is my favorite. In between all the wonderful dialogue of Days of Future Past...erm I mean Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, one character stood out to me amongst all the others. And, no, it wasn't Harry. 
 Draco stole this book for me. Draco was always one of my favorite characters from the first seven books. He was the bad boy that you hated to love, and you just loved to hate. He didn't try to hide the fact that he was a complete git; for the first five books he was loud and proud about his feelings surrounding pure blood superiority. He even became a death eater, but instead of destroying the last of his humanity, that move in my opinion, brought him back from the brink. Book six and seven only showed barely visible conflicts in his character, but they were enough to convince me that his inner turmoil would eventually transform him for the better. 
 Cursed Child redeemed Draco in the way that I always hoped he'd be redeemed. It proved everything I believed about him since the moment he didn't kill Dumbledore in Half-Blood Prince. Many of the reviews I've read said that Draco's transformed character was unrealistic, but I found him to be one of the most authentic, well-developed characters in this play. 
 Draco's wife wasn't even physically in the story, but his love for her was more evident than the other couples in the story. You could feel Draco's heartache at the loss of his wife and his desire to love his son in all the ways that Lucius had not loved him. It pains him to hear the rumors that his son is actual Voldemort's, all the while knowing the great sacrifices that he and his wife suffered to have their son. Draco even beseeches Harry to help him prove that he is indeed Scorpius's father, an act that would have required much desperation and humility. Draco also admits how he always envied the trio while they were at Hogwarts as they had the type of friendship that he never thought he could have. It was truly beautiful to see Draco and Harry finally working together as a team to find their sons after so many years lost. 
 People have been trying to convince me for years that even though all dark wizards (save Peter Pettigrew) came from Slytherin, it doesn't mean that all witches and wizards in Slytherin are bad. I suppose it's akin to the "A square is always a rectangle, but a rectangle is not always a square" comparison. Well, everyone can stop pushing. I'm now convinced. Draco's transformation paired with the dynamic duo of Albus and Scorpius plus Snape's undertaking to save the world from a horrible Voldemort-run reality showed that Slytherin house has the potential to be much more than they're given credit for. Of course one can argue that Albus and Scorpio's stupidity was the cause of two alternate realities and the possible return of Voldemort, but in the long run their mistake is what cemented every relationship in the story back together including their own. Can't say this was an enjoyable read exactly, but it was a gripping read for sure. It's one of those disaster survival tales; in this case the what-if scenario focuses on a meteor strike moving the moon and wreaking havoc with the earth's tides and climate. 
 It's told from the point of view of Miranda, a teenage girl who goes from being worried about her changing friends and the pressures of schoolwork to just hoping somehow her family will have enough food, water, and firewood to make it through the disaster. The story is presented as Miranda's diary, although it's doubtful anyone would keep such a detailed account of conversations as presented in the book. But she does have a strong voice, and the intensity of the situation keeps the book moving (or at least kept me moving through the book) at a fast pace. 
 While I felt that things were for the most part portrayed pretty realistically, I could see there being worse (and better) things happening if the imagined event was a reality. But part of the limitations here come from the story coming from the isolated viewpoint of just what one family experiences. 
 Probably will scare some people into stockpiling, but the point I think is more about family and hope outweighing fear. Ended a bit abruptly and left some things hanging, but there's two more books in the series, so perhaps things are wrapped up more there.

I need the next book in this series NOW! What an amazing ending! Anna Godbersen is one of my all-time favorite authors, so I was really excited to read Bright Young Things. While I did not like this novel as much as The Luxe, it was still fantastic. It is packed with drama and romance--two things I love in a novel. 
 One of the things I liked so much about The Luxe series was the relationship between Diana and Henry--I wanted to find something similar in Bright Young Things, but I don't think Cordelia and Thom have that same undeniable chemistry that Diana and Henry do. All around, the characters in Bright Young Things are not nearly as relatable as the characters in The Luxe (which was one of the factors that made it such an amazing series for me). Even though I didn't like the characters as much, I think that this will change as the story progresses. I started to like Cordelia, Astrid, and Charlie much more towards the end of the book because I had a better understanding of their personalities. 
 The best part about this novel is hands-down the plot. I kept turning to the pages because I was dying to know what happened next. The prologue was also really well-done, what a way to start a novel! From the very beginning, Godbersen tells us that one of the girls will be famous, one will be married, one will be dead. I don't think I've ever started a novel that told me right from the beginning that one of the main characters would be gone by the end of the book, but it really drew me into the novel. If the next book was already available, I would have picked it up immediately. Luckily, even though the next book isn't available until September, Anna Godbersen will be signing advanced copies at Book Expo America in a few weeks! I am so excited to meet her :). The writing is beautiful, the plot is fantastic, the end is amazing, and the beginning is intriguing--if you haven't read Bright Young Things yet, I don't know what you're waiting for!

I'm not sure it's possible for me to write an unbiased review of the Northern Lights (probably known as The Golden Compass to my American friends). I have loved this series since about 2000 and still own my original paperbacks that have been read countless times over the years so it's hard to be completely objective about a story that has been a part of your life for such a long time. Anyway, I'll do my best to try and explain why this story has always been one of my favourites but surely the fact that it's still on my shelf after 17 years is enough to hint at how good it is! 
 When her best friend, Roger, goes missing along with numerous other young children, Lyra and her daemon Pantalaimon, set out to find them and bring them home. What follows is an epic journey that takes her from her home in Jordan College, Oxford all the way to the frozen wastes of the North. She has help from numerous sources along the way - the gyptians who are also searching for their missing children, the witches of the North and even an armoured bear called Iorek Byrnison - but what she finds when she eventually catches up with the child snatching gobblers is something more horrific than she could ever have dreamed of. 
 Lyra is a brilliant character, she's fierce, stubborn and a little bit reckless, as an accomplished liar she can be cocky and thinks she knows everything but she's also very intelligent and will quickly learn from the mistakes she makes. I love how feisty she is and the way she jumps straight into the action because she is so determined to save Roger and the other children, she faces things that would terrify even adults and she does it with a great deal of bravery. The bond between her and Pantalaimon is brilliant, he's a bit more sensible than she is and is often the voice of reason when she's about to get herself in trouble, unfortunately for him she doesn't always take his advice but he is always there as her backup when she needs him. 
 While Lyra's world initially seems very similar to our own it quickly becomes clear that Philip Pullman has used his wonderful imagination to create something very different. Every human is born with their own daemon, a living, breathing entity that is basically the other half of their soul. Daemons can take any form throughout childhood, Pantalaimon often changes shape depending on the situation that Lyra finds herself in, but once puberty is reached it will choose one form to settle as. The bond between human and daemon is unbreakable and killing one will cause the death of the other so there are lots of strict taboos in place about not touching other people's daemons even though you can communicate with them. I love the sheer variety of different daemons found in these books and I've spent the last 17 years waiting for my own daemon to turn up! Unfortunately it's still nowhere to be found but I still live in hope. 
 Along with daemons this world also contains the panserborne, a race of warrior polar bears who have an affinity to metal and who are known to be brilliant protectors. Lyra is able to make friends with Iorek Byrnison, an exiled panserborne who has been living amongst humans for far too long, and he agrees to help her try to rescue the missing children after she frees him from captivity. Iorek is another brilliant character and a great ally for Lyra as she travels across the frozen wastes of a land similar to the arctic. Although this series has a lot of fun characters it also has some surprisingly dark elements, I'd actually forgotten how upsetting some parts of the story were so be warned it's not for the faint of heart but that darkness doesn't make it any less of a wonderful journey. There are lots of amazing elements to this story and from what I remember the series only gets more fantastical in the next two books. 
 I started this reread because I want to be ready for the new companion trilogy (the first book La Belle Sauvage will be released in October) and I can't wait to read new stories set in this world but I'm just as excited to continue with the original trilogy and remind myself of the rest of Lyra's adventures. There is a reason that this series holds up so well since it was originally published, it's something special and if you've not already read it you're really missing out.

 After middle son Jace jumps onto her roof one night, Samantha is sucked into his family-heart and soul. Everything is perfect, but Samantha can't seem to tell her mom she's dating the boy next door. Thankfully her mom is focused on her reelection campaign and a budding romance with a smarmy campaign manager, but one night Samantha's world collides with Jace's in the worst way possible.

 False Memory begins with our protagonist, Miranda, waking up alone with no memory of who she is. She finds herself in a mall, tries to get help, and inadvertently unleashes some kind of energy burst that causes everyone in the immediate vicinity to panic. Everyone except for one boy, who seems to know a hell of a lot more about Miranda than she does herself. 
 This is one of those books that reeled me in with exciting potential, only to quickly turn around, punch me in the face, and take off with that potential into narrative hell. 
 Miranda's memory loss is the most interesting concept here, and it should have been the driving force behind the entire story, especially at a character level. But sadly, other than its use in the introduction and as a basic plot point, it doesn't get nearly the narrative weight or attention it deserves. The characters, which all could have easily had indepth, moving build up and development surrounding Miranda's memory loss, are instead flat and unmemorable. And the plot surrounding their "superpowers" and the organization they are apart of isn't nearly interesting enough to make up for the boring characters. 
 Basically, False Memory wasn't at all what I expected, disappointingly so, and I didn't feel the need to wade through the last half of the book when what I was expecting (a character driven story based on memory loss with a side of scifi superpowers and shady science experiments) was so much more interesting than what I got.
